notes.subject: CP01
notes.title: Piping Fundamentals and Design
notes.content:
PURPOSE AND FUNCTION: Transports fluids and fluid/solid mixtures between equipment. Design must account for temperature, pressure, flow rate, chemical/physical properties, contamination, and shock loads.

DESIGN FACTORS:
• Temperature affects material properties, expansion, and thermal stress
• Pressure determines wall thickness, material selection, support design
• Flow rate/velocity affects erosion, corrosion, and pressure drop
• Shock loads (water hammer, steam hammer, thermal shock, seismic) require robust design
• Changes in direction require proper support and restraint

MATERIAL SELECTION:
• Low-carbon steel: economical, prone to rust/corrosion
• Low-alloy steel: high-temperature applications, improved wear/fatigue/corrosion resistance
• Stainless steel: corrosion resistant, minimizes corrosion product buildup
• Copper alloys: excellent corrosion resistance, good conductivity
• Nickel alloys: high temperature/pressure applications, high cost
• Plastic: corrosion resistant, lightweight, limited temperature range

PIPE SUPPORT SYSTEMS:
• Rigid restraints: fixed, prevent movement
• Spring hangers: support vertical gravity loading, allow thermal movement
• Snubbers: limit seismic motion while allowing thermal growth

THERMAL EFFECTS:
• Thermal loops/bends: accommodate thermal expansion
• Expansion joints: allow controlled linear expansion
• Insulation: controls heat loss/gain and protects personnel

notes.subject: CP01
notes.title: Valve Functions and Basic Construction
notes.content:
1. STARTING/STOPPING FLOW: Isolation to completely stop or start fluid flow (gate valves, ball valves, plug valves)

2. THROTTLING FLOW: Control flow rate without stopping completely, requires throttling-capable design (globe valves, needle valves)

3. CONTROLLING DIRECTION OF FLOW: Routes fluid to different paths (directional control valves, check valves)

4. REGULATING PRESSURE: Maintains desired system pressure (pressure regulators, pressure-reducing valves)

5. RELIEVING PRESSURE: Protection against overpressure (relief valves, safety valves)

BASIC VALVE CONSTRUCTION:
• Body: contains internal flow path, seats, and internal parts
• Bonnet: upper section that seals the body
• Disk: moves to open/close or throttle flow
• Seat rings: provide seal surface for the disk
• Stem: connects disk to actuator/handwheel
• Backseat: allows packing adjustment without system depressurization
• Packing/stuffing box: compression seal prevents stem leakage

STEM DESIGNS:
• Rising stem: stem moves upward when valve opens (visual position indicator)
• Non-rising stem: stem does not move (position not visually obvious)

notes.subject: CP01
notes.title: Pressure Types and Relationships
notes.content:
DEFINITION: Pressure = Force / Area (P = F/A). Units: psi, Pa, bar, atm. Normal atmospheric pressure = 14.7 psia = 101.3 kPa.

HYDROSTATIC PRESSURE: Pressure from weight of fluid column above reference point. Formula: P = rho x g x h. Increases with depth. Acts in all directions equally.

ABSOLUTE PRESSURE: Measured from perfect vacuum (zero reference). Units: psia. Thermodynamic calculations require absolute pressure. Example: 10 psig = 24.7 psia.

GAGE PRESSURE (PSIG): Pressure above atmospheric. Formula: Pgage = Pabsolute - Patm. Common pressure gauge indication.

VACUUM PRESSURE: Pressure below atmospheric. Formula: Pvac = Patm - Pabs. Used in condenser and pump suction applications.

DIFFERENTIAL PRESSURE (PSID): Difference between two locations. Used for filter drop, valve throttling, level measurement.

PASCAL'S LAW: Pressure applied to confined fluid is transmitted undiminished throughout in all directions. F1/A1 = F2/A2.

HYDRAULIC PRESS APPLICATION: Input force on small piston creates pressure throughout system. Pressure acts on larger piston producing larger output force. Work In = Work Out: F1 x d1 = F2 x d2.

notes.subject: CP01
notes.title: Valve Operational Issues and Prevention
notes.content:
CAUSE: Valve body cools faster than disk during system cooldown. Differential thermal contraction binds seat against disk. Can make valve impossible to reopen until reheated.

PREVENTION:
• Periodically crack valve open and re-shut during cooldown
• Use proper closing torque (avoid over-torquing)
• Allow gradual cooling when possible

PRESSURE LOCKING:

CAUSE: Liquid trapped in valve bonnet pressurizes as it heats. Pressure buildup prevents valve opening. Common in high-temperature systems during startup.

PREVENTION:
• Provide relief or vent path on valve bonnet
• Equalize/reduce pressure buildup
• Design relief path to lower trapped pressure

OPERATING EXPERIENCE LESSONS:

1. Valve Handling: Never use wrench on valve handwheel for extra leverage. Can overstress actuator gearing/casing. Has caused catastrophic actuator failure.

2. Manual Operation Verification: Reaching hard stop on handwheel does NOT confirm full travel. Verify full designed number of turns. Position limit switch not reliable sole indicator.

3. Manual Override Precautions: Manually operating past designed open limit can slip position limit switch. Requires leak rate/stroke time retest after manual operation. Document any manual override operations.

KEY MAINTENANCE PRACTICES:
• Regular inspection for leakage
• Packing maintenance using backseat feature
• Periodic exercise to prevent stiction
• Monitor position indicators for consistency
• Track valve operation history

notes.subject: CP01
notes.title: Valve Actuators and Position Verification
notes.content:
• Fail Open: opens on loss of power/control (safety for emergency drainage)
• Fail Closed: closes on loss of power (safety for isolation)
• Fail As Is: remains in current position (most Motor Operated Valves)
• Fail Safe: the position required to protect the system/equipment

MANUAL ACTUATORS:
• Handwheel or lever: direct mechanical operation
• Reach rods: extends control distance
• Gearing: provides mechanical advantage for higher torque

ELECTRIC ACTUATORS:
• Motor Operated Valves (MOVs): Fail As Is, gear reduction for torque, declutch lever for manual/motor switching
• Solenoid Operated Valves: Two-position (on/off only), spring placement determines fail position

PNEUMATIC ACTUATORS:
• Gas cylinder, piston, diaphragm, or vane designs
• Quarter-turn designs for butterfly/plug valves
• Spring action determines fail position on air loss

HYDRAULIC ACTUATORS:
• Piston-driven for high-force applications
• Spring action determines fail position on pressure loss

VALVE POSITION VERIFICATION METHODS:
• Light indication: Red = Open, Green = Closed, Both lit = Mid-position/Throttled
• Travel indication: Rising stem position, local mechanical pointer
• Actual verification: Visual stem observation, handwheel turn count, quarter-turn valve lever position

HUMAN ERROR PREVENTION:
• Verify all local/remote indications before and after manipulation
• Follow procedures and require independent verification
• Confirm valves and instrumentation are labeled correctly

notes.subject: CP04
notes.title: Definition: Pumps and Flow Resistance
notes.content: Pumps are devices used for moving and/or altering the pressure of fluids in confined spaces using suction or pressure. The fundamental function of a pump is to move a given volume flow rate of fluid at a specific pressure from one level to another, while overcoming all flow resistance encountered between the fluid levels. Flow resistances can be caused by height differences, valves, piping, system geometry, fluid properties, and friction.

notes.subject: CP04
notes.title: Pump Purpose: Moving Fluids Through Systems
notes.content: No matter the size, shape, or design of a pump, its basic purpose remains constant: to move fluids. However, "moving fluids" means different things in different situations. Moving water between points at the same level is relatively simple. But moving fluid from ground level to a tank 50 feet above requires significant pressure and demands more sophisticated pump designs.

notes.subject: CP04
notes.title: Diverse Pump Applications and Functions
notes.content: Different pumps are designed to fulfill different functions. Some pumps are designed to move large volumes of fluid at relatively low pressure; others are made to pump small volumes at very high pressures. Some pumps handle thick, heavy fluids like fuel oil or slurry, while others are devoted to moving clear, light fluids like water, or gases like air. Despite these variations, all pumps share the same basic purpose: moving fluids through systems.

notes.subject: CP04
notes.title: Pump Classification: Kinetic vs Positive Displacement
notes.content: Pumps are classified into two main categories: Kinetic (dynamic) pumps and Positive displacement pumps. Kinetic pumps operate by converting mechanical energy into kinetic energy (velocity), then converting that velocity into pressure energy. Positive displacement pumps work by trapping a fixed volume of fluid and forcing it into the discharge line. Both categories include several different designs for different applications.

notes.subject: CP04
notes.title: Kinetic (Dynamic) Pumps - Centrifugal Type
notes.content: Kinetic or dynamic pumps use rotating impellers to impart velocity to the fluid. The fluid enters the pump at low velocity and low pressure, gains velocity from the impeller, then the pressure increases as the fluid exits. Common types include centrifugal pumps which are the most common in plant applications. These pumps are best for moving large volumes at moderate to low pressures.

notes.subject: CP04
notes.title: Positive Displacement Pumps - Fixed Volume
notes.content: Positive displacement pumps trap a fixed volume of fluid and force it through the discharge. As the displaced volume is replaced, a new volume is trapped and the cycle repeats. These pumps are best for moving small volumes at high pressures, or for moving viscous fluids. Types include gear pumps, screw pumps, piston pumps, and diaphragm pumps.

notes.subject: CP04
notes.title: Pump Capacity - Volumetric Flow Rate
notes.content: Capacity is a fundamental pump characteristic describing the amount of fluid a pump moves. Pump capacities are normally expressed in gallons per minute (gpm) or cubic feet per second (cfs). The amount moved for a given set of operating conditions is plotted on a pump operational curve (performance curve). The rated volumetric flow rate for a specific set of parameters is defined as the pump's capacity.

notes.subject: CP04
notes.title: Static Head - Elevation Difference
notes.content: Static head is a difference in fluid levels (elevation head) and is normally stated in feet of water column. For example, if the discharge point is 25 feet higher than the suction point, there is a 25-foot static discharge head. Static head represents the pressure energy needed to lift fluid vertically against gravity and does not account for friction or flow velocity.

notes.subject: CP04
notes.title: Dynamic Head - Velocity and Friction Effects
notes.content: Dynamic head is the energy required to set the fluid in motion and to overcome any resistance to that motion. Dynamic head includes velocity head (kinetic energy of moving fluid) and friction head (energy lost to friction in pipes, fittings, and equipment). Dynamic head is also expressed in feet of water column. Total head is the sum of static head and dynamic head for a given condition.

notes.subject: CP04
notes.title: Total Suction Head (Hs) - Equation and Components
notes.content: Total suction head (Hs) is the amount of pressure, expressed in feet of water column, that is available at the suction of a pump. Total suction head equals the static suction head minus the dynamic suction head of the pump. When the suction source fluid level is above the pump centerline, suction head is positive. When below the pump centerline, the pump must "lift" the fluid, creating a negative suction head called "suction lift."

notes.subject: CP04
notes.title: Suction Head Formula and Pressure Considerations
notes.content: The equation for total suction head is: Hs = hs – hfs + ps, where Hs is total suction head, hs is static suction head, hfs is pressure drop in suction line, and ps is vacuum or pressure in a tank on the suction side. When the suction source is under vacuum or pressure, that pressure is included in the total suction head calculation. The dynamic head includes both friction losses and velocity head effects.

notes.subject: CP04
notes.title: Total Discharge Head (Ht) - Equation and Components
notes.content: Total discharge head (Ht) is the sum of static discharge head and dynamic head of piping downstream of the pump, expressed in feet of water column. Static discharge head is the elevation difference between the pump centerline and the fluid level on the discharge side. If the pump discharges to a pressurized tank, the total discharge head includes that tank pressure. The discharge side dynamic head includes friction losses in discharge piping.

notes.subject: CP04
notes.title: Discharge Head Formula and Tank Pressure
notes.content: The equation for total discharge head is: Ht = ht + hft + pt, where Ht is total discharge head, ht is static discharge head, hft is pressure drop in discharge line, and pt is pressure in a tank on the discharge side. This equation accounts for both the elevation the fluid is raised (static) and the resistance to flow on the discharge side (dynamic). Accurate calculation requires knowledge of pipe diameters, lengths, and fitting losses.

notes.subject: CP04
notes.title: Total Head (H) - Pressure Difference Calculation
notes.content: Total head is the total pressure difference between total discharge head and total suction head of the pump. If pressure gauges are installed on the suction and discharge of the pump, the total head equals the difference in the two gauge readings. Total head can be calculated using the equation: H = Ht – (+Hs). Total head is also called total developed head or total dynamic head (TDH). This is the pressure rise the pump must produce.

notes.subject: CP04
notes.title: Head Calculation Example - Suction and Discharge
notes.content: Example calculation: Given a pump with suction source at 580 ft elevation, pump centerline at 592 ft, discharge destination at 617 ft, suction line pressure drop of 3 ft, and discharge line pressure drop of 6 ft. Total suction head = (580 – 592) – 3 = -15 ft. Total discharge head = (617 – 592) + 6 = 31 ft. Total head = 31 – (-15) = 46 ft. This total head represents what the pump must overcome to move fluid through the system.

notes.subject: CP04
notes.title: Net Positive Suction Head (NPSH) Definition
notes.content: Net positive suction head (NPSH) or available NPSH (NPSHA) is the absolute pressure at the suction of the pump minus the vapor pressure of the fluid at the same point. NPSH is critical for pump operation because it determines whether cavitation will occur. The required NPSH (NPSHR) is determined by pump design and supplied by the pump manufacturer. To prevent cavitation, available NPSH must be greater than required NPSH.

notes.subject: CP04
notes.title: NPSH Equation and Saturation Pressure
notes.content: The NPSH equation is: NPSH = Psuction – Psat, where NPSH is net positive suction head, Psuction is absolute pressure at pump suction, and Psat is saturation pressure (vapor pressure) of the fluid. When NPSH equals zero, a partial vacuum forms in the liquid and the fluid begins to flash (boil) into vapor, risking cavitation. The saturation pressure varies with temperature; higher temperatures increase saturation pressure, reducing available NPSH.

notes.subject: CP04
notes.title: Cavitation - Formation and Vapor Bubbles
notes.content: Cavitation occurs when pump suction pressure approaches the saturation pressure of the fluid in the pump. Vapor bubbles begin forming at saturation pressure, causing the pump suction and casing to become vapor bound. Cavitation reduces fluid capacity in the pump and can cause noise, vibration, and severe pump damage. When cavitation occurs, capacity of the pump decreases and significant damage can occur quickly. Equipment damage from cavitation is one of the most serious operational failures.

notes.subject: CP04
notes.title: Cavitation Effects - Damage and Performance Loss
notes.content: Cavitation causes pitting and erosion of the pump impeller as vapor bubbles collapse or implode under high pressure at the discharge. This erosion can significantly reduce impeller efficiency and create imbalance. In addition to physical damage, cavitation results in flow oscillations, excessive pump vibration, pump overheating, and lower than normal flow rates. The reduction in capacity depends on the amount of vapor formed. Long-term cavitation can render a pump unusable.

notes.subject: CP04
notes.title: Cavitation Indicators - Noise and Vibration
notes.content: Indicators of cavitation include distinctive noise that sounds like the pump is pumping rocks or has a solid object inside, vibration due to impeller imbalance from erosion, motor current fluctuations as flow varies, and fluctuations in discharge pressure and flow rates. Operators must be able to identify cavitation because early detection can prevent catastrophic pump failure. As cavitation occurs and damages the impeller, it cannot add the same kinetic energy, reducing pressure and flow.

notes.subject: CP04
notes.title: Cavitation Prevention Methods
notes.content: Several methods prevent cavitation. Using a head tank to create static pressure at pump suction raises absolute pressure above saturation pressure. A booster pump can increase pressure at the suction of a main pump. Using large diameter suction piping converts kinetic energy to pressure energy, increasing pressure. Reducing system temperature where possible decreases saturation pressure. Reducing suction line restrictions and length minimizes friction losses. Proper system design and operational procedures are critical.

notes.subject: CP04
notes.title: System Preparation to Prevent Cavitation
notes.content: Cavitation prevention requires system preparation before pump startup. All air must be vented from suction lines because vapor bubbles and free air are much more compressible than liquid, leading to flow instability. Filling suction lines completely with fluid before starting the pump ensures liquid contact with the impeller. Operating procedures must include gentle startup to establish flow gradually, preventing sudden pressure fluctuations. Operators must monitor pump discharge pressure and flow patterns.

notes.subject: CP04
notes.title: System Design Features for Cavitation Prevention
notes.content: System design features for cavitation prevention include adequate suction tank sizing with adequate freeboard, proper water level control, temperature management to keep saturation pressure low, suction strainers with low pressure drop, short and large-diameter suction piping to minimize friction losses, and proper valve placement. In closed systems, maintenance of air removal during startup is essential. In open systems, atmospheric pressure aids in preventing cavitation. The relationship between temperature and saturation pressure must be understood.

notes.subject: CP04
notes.title: Pump Performance Curves and Operating Points
notes.content: Pump operational curves show the relationship between flow rate and the head (pressure) a pump can develop. These curves are provided by manufacturers and show pump performance at different operating points. The pump's operating point occurs where the pump curve intersects the system resistance curve (sometimes called the system head curve). Understanding pump curves helps select appropriate pumps and predict performance at different operating conditions. Curves vary significantly between different pump types and designs.

notes.subject: CP04
notes.title: Pump Efficiency and Design Operating Range
notes.content: Pump efficiency is a measure of how effectively a pump converts input mechanical power to useful hydraulic power. Efficiency decreases as flow rate deviates from the pump's design point. Most pumps operate at peak efficiency in a specific range of flow rates and heads. Operating a pump outside this range wastes energy as heat, accelerates wear, and can cause cavitation. Selection of an appropriately sized pump is important for plant efficiency and reliability. Part-load operation reduces efficiency significantly for many pump types.

notes.subject: CP04
notes.title: Fluid Properties and Temperature Effects on Pumps
notes.content: Pump performance depends on several factors including system design, fluid properties, temperature effects, and pump condition. Water properties like density and viscosity affect pump performance. Temperature affects fluid viscosity and saturation pressure. As temperature increases, viscosity decreases and saturation pressure increases, both affecting pump operation. Fluid contamination and degradation affect viscosity and can cause erosion of internal pump components. Regular system maintenance including filtration keeps fluid properties stable and protects pump life.

notes.subject: CP04
notes.title: Centrifugal Pump Impeller Designs
notes.content: Centrifugal pump impellers can be designed in different configurations to handle different fluid types and operating conditions. Radial flow impellers are the most common and best for low-viscosity fluids. Axial flow (propeller) impellers are designed for high-flow, low-pressure applications. Mixed-flow impellers combine radial and axial characteristics. Special impeller designs handle abrasive slurries or liquids with gas content. Understanding impeller type helps operators recognize pump capabilities and limitations in their plant systems.

notes.subject: CP04
notes.title: Positive Displacement Pumps - Types and Applications
notes.content: Positive displacement pump operation is fundamentally different from centrifugal pumps. These pumps deliver a fixed volume of fluid with each cycle, regardless of discharge pressure (up to their designed maximum). This makes them excellent for moving high-viscosity fluids or when constant flow is required. However, they are more complex, more expensive, have higher maintenance requirements, and are more susceptible to cavitation. Gear pumps, screw pumps, and piston pumps are common types, each with distinct advantages and limitations.

notes.subject: CP04
notes.title: Pump Reliability and Preventive Maintenance
notes.content: In plant systems, pump reliability and availability are critical for operations. Understanding pump theory helps operators recognize abnormal conditions early and take corrective action. Common problems include cavitation, seal leakage, bearing wear, vibration, and performance degradation. Preventive maintenance includes regular inspection, vibration monitoring, thermal monitoring, and fluid analysis. Operators trained in pump theory can better diagnose problems and work with maintenance personnel to ensure pumps operate reliably and efficiently throughout their service life.

notes.subject: CP04
notes.title: Pump Theory Application - Key Concepts Summary
notes.content: Summary of key pump concepts: Pumps move fluids by overcoming system resistance. Capacity is flow rate; total head is pressure rise required. Static head is elevation difference; dynamic head is friction and velocity effects. Suction head can be positive (above pump) or negative (below pump, called lift). Cavitation occurs when suction pressure drops to saturation pressure, causing vapor bubble formation and equipment damage. Prevention requires maintaining adequate NPSH through system design and operational procedures. Understanding pump theory is essential for safe, reliable operation.

notes.subject: CP06
notes.title: **SECTION 1.0 - INTRODUCTION**
notes.content: Heat exchangers are particularly important in power plant operation. A heat exchanger is a device designed to transfer heat from one fluid to another. Two key concepts: (1) Heat can only be transferred when there is a temperature difference between substances; (2) Heat always transfers from higher temperature substance to lower temperature substance. Heat is transferred primarily by conduction (heat transfer between adjacent molecules through material) and convection (heat transfer by bulk motion and mixing of fluid portions).

notes.subject: CP06
notes.title: **SECTION 2.0 - TYPES OF HEAT EXCHANGERS**
notes.content:
**OBJECTIVE 1: Explain the difference between direct contact and indirect contact (surface) heat exchangers.**
Two general types of heat exchangers: Direct contact heat exchangers - the two fluids come in contact with each other (examples: cooling towers, lakes, rivers). Indirect contact (surface) heat exchangers - the two fluids are separated by a solid surface such as a tube or metal plate (examples: steam generators, main condensers). Direct contact is less common; indirect contact more commonly used in power plant applications.
notes.objective: Explain the difference between direct contact and indirect contact (surface) heat exchangers.

notes.subject: CP06
notes.title: **SECTION 2.1 - COOLING TOWERS**
notes.content:
**OBJECTIVE 2: Describe the principles of operations of Forced Draft and Natural Draft Cooling Towers.**
Cooling towers exchange energy from cooling water into air flowing through the tower using evaporative cooling. The cooled circulating water serves as heat sink for main condensers. Two main types: open-circuit and closed-circuit. Two basic flow configurations: Cross-flow (air enters side, flows across, exits opposite side) and Counter flow (air enters bottom, flows upward; water enters top, flows downward). Towers may be forced-draft (fans blow air in), induced-draft (fans draw air through), or natural-draft (uses convective chimney effects).
notes.objective: Describe the principles of operations of Forced Draft and Natural Draft Cooling Towers.

notes.subject: CP06
notes.title: **COOLING TOWER DESIGN AND FILL MATERIAL**
notes.content: Tower fill material traditionally redwood but now mostly PVC or plastic. Critical factors for efficiency: (1) effectiveness of spray or splash in atomizing water, (2) internal tower volume for air-water contact, (3) airflow rate through tower, (4) water flow rate. Cooling tower systems are open and need makeup water to replace evaporated water or blowdowns. Closed systems use expansion tanks to compensate for volume changes due to temperature changes.
notes.section: COOLING TOWER DESIGN AND FILL MATERIAL

notes.subject: CP06
notes.title: **SECTION 2.2 - SHELL AND TUBE HEAT EXCHANGERS**
notes.content:
**SECTION 2.2.1 - CROSS FLOW HEAT EXCHANGERS**
**OBJECTIVE 3: Describe the four basic flow paths for shell-and-tube heat exchangers (Cross Flow, Parallel Flow, Counter Flow, U-Tube).**
Crossflow occurs when two fluids flow perpendicular to each other. Main condensers are classic crossflow examples - exhaust steam flows downward perpendicular to tubes containing cooling water. Often used to condense or evaporate liquids. Steam at temperature T condenses to condensate at same temperature (phase change). Temperature outside condenser tubes is constant; circulating water enters at temperature (t) and exits at higher temperature. Greatest temperature difference where water enters tubes; most steam condenses at this end.
notes.section: SECTION 2.2 - SHELL AND TUBE HEAT EXCHANGERS
notes.objective: Describe the four basic flow paths for shell-and-tube heat exchangers (Cross Flow, Parallel Flow, Counter Flow, U-Tube).

notes.subject: CP06
notes.title: **SECTION 2.2.2 - PARALLEL FLOW HEAT EXCHANGERS**
notes.content: Parallel flow occurs when fluids flow in parallel paths and same direction. NOT commonly used because material requires larger surface area than other types for given heat load. When cold fluid enters, rate of heat transfer is large because temperature difference (ΔT) is large. As heat transfers, temperatures converge and ΔT becomes smaller. Therefore, rate of heat transfer decreases as fluids travel through parallel exchanger.

notes.subject: CP06
notes.title: **SECTION 2.2.3 - COUNTER FLOW HEAT EXCHANGERS**
notes.content:
**OBJECTIVE 4: Explain why a counter-flow heat exchanger will produce a higher rate of heat transfer than an equally sized parallel-flow heat exchanger.**
Counter flow heat exchangers have parallel flow paths but fluids flow in opposite directions. Temperature difference and fluid flow rates determine heat transferred. Temperature profile changes throughout exchanger. Designers use logarithmic mean temperature difference (ΔTlm) to calculate overall heat transfer rate. Heat transfer rate: Q = Uo × A × ΔT, where Q = rate of heat transfer (Btu/hr), Uo = overall heat transfer coefficient (Btu/ft² hr°F), A = surface area (ft²), ΔT = temperature difference (°F). Larger temperature difference, surface area, or heat transfer coefficient = more heat transferred. Counter flow can transfer large amount of heat for its size compared to parallel and crossflow types.
notes.objective: Explain why a counter-flow heat exchanger will produce a higher rate of heat transfer than an equally sized parallel-flow heat exchanger.

notes.subject: CP06
notes.title: **SECTION 2.2.4 - U-TUBE HEAT EXCHANGERS**
notes.content: U-tube heat exchangers extensively used in plants. May be mounted horizontally or vertically. Performance like crossflow heat exchangers. Tube side working fluid enters waterbox, directed into one end of U-tubes, flows through tubes, exits through channel head. Divider plate separates inlet and outlet sides. Shell side flow enters shell, passes over outside of tubes, exits shell. Baffles normally used to force flow to zigzag across tubes. Advantages: expansion simplified, half as many tube-to-sheet joints needed. Disadvantage: difficult to mechanically clean tube surfaces.

notes.subject: CP06
notes.title: **SECTION 3.0 - REGENERATIVE AND NON-REGENERATIVE HEAT EXCHANGERS**
notes.content:
**OBJECTIVE 5: Describe regenerative and non-regenerative heat exchange processes.**
Regenerative heat exchanger transfers heat from high temperature fluid into low temperature sections of same system (example: Feedwater Heaters in secondary system). Minimizes energy loss since heat not rejected to separate system. Non-regenerative heat exchanger transfers heat between liquids in two distinct systems (examples: Turbine Lube Oil Coolers, Residual Heat Removal HX). Used to transfer heat out of particular system; heat removed is rejected and not returned. Typical application: regenerative HX in Chemical and Volume Control System reduces letdown temperature from 540°F to 250°F using charging flow returning to RCS.
notes.section: SECTION 3.0 - REGENERATIVE AND NON-REGENERATIVE HEAT EXCHANGERS
notes.objective: Describe regenerative and non-regenerative heat exchange processes.

notes.subject: CP06
notes.title: **SECTION 4.0 - HEAT EXCHANGER CONSTRUCTION**
notes.content:
**OBJECTIVE 6: Describe major components of a heat exchanger.**
Shell and tube heat exchanger consists of: shell (casing around heat transfer region), multiple tubes forming tube bundle, tubesheets (perforated metal plates at shell ends), waterboxes or channel heads, baffles, inlet/outlet nozzles, vent and drain connections. Two separate fluids flow: tube side fluid (usually higher pressure, flows through tubes) and shell side fluid (usually lower pressure, flows outside tubes). Shell houses internals and directs shell side flow. Tubes direct and separate tube side fluid. Two common tube types: Straight tubes and U-tubes.
notes.objective: Describe major components of a heat exchanger.

notes.subject: CP06
notes.title: **SECTION 4.1 - HEAT EXCHANGER TUBES**
notes.content: Tubesheets separate two fluids and provide tube support. Waterboxes enclose tubesheet areas at each end, direct flow through tube bundles, removable for cleaning. Nozzles are where fluid systems connect to shell or waterboxes. Vents remove air and non-condensable gases improving performance. Drains remove liquid before maintenance. As tubes heat up they expand - typical 30-foot feedwater heater tube expands 1.4 inches if heated from 70°F to 470°F. To prevent damage, one end of tube bundle designed to expand/contract. Floating head design allows one tubesheet to slide, absorbing expansion.

notes.subject: CP06
notes.title: **HEAT EXCHANGER TUBE ARRANGEMENTS**
notes.content: Tube types: Straight tube - arranged in bundle enclosed by shell, allows easy mechanical cleaning and replacement. U-tube - advantages include simplified expansion and half as many tube-to-sheet joints. Coil tube - one or more coils inside shell, expansion absorbed like spring, no seals needed, suitable for high pressure. Bowed tube - solidly bolted to shell at each end, bow allows thermal expansion.

notes.subject: CP06
notes.title: **SECTION 4.2 - HEAT EXCHANGER SHELLS AND TUBE SURFACES**
notes.content: Plain surface tubes are smooth (examples: condenser, feedwater heaters, lube oil coolers). Extended surfaces have fins, rings, studs, grooves or other extensions. Advantages: increase surface area for heat transfer. Gas-to-liquid heat exchangers often use extended surface tubes with gas on finned side. Shell may be oriented horizontally or vertically per operational needs. Main condenser is one of largest shell and tube HX - rectangular shaped with thousands of tubes. Most other shell and tube HX in plant are cylindrical.
notes.section: SECTION 4.2 - HEAT EXCHANGER SHELLS AND TUBE SURFACES

notes.subject: CP06
notes.title: **HEAT EXCHANGER PASSES AND BAFFLES**
notes.content: Shell and tube HX can have any number of tube or shell passes. Pass occurs each time either fluid flows across or along heat exchanger length. Multiple passes allow shorter HX with same tube length. Shell side fluid takes shortest route from inlet to outlet without baffles. Baffles direct flow over tubes and serve as lateral support. Cause fluid to cross tubes several times while maintaining overall counter flow direction. Resulting HX has combination of cross and counter flow heat transfer.

notes.subject: CP06
notes.title: **SECTION 5.0 - HEAT EXCHANGER OPERATION**
notes.content:
**SECTION 5.1 - HEAT EXCHANGER STARTUP**
**OBJECTIVE 7: Explain the following regarding Thermal Shock of a heat exchanger: Description of thermal shock, Conditions or situations that make thermal shock more likely, Operational concerns for a heat exchanger that undergoes thermal shock.**
Before operation, HX must be filled with operating fluids. Differential thermal expansion between tubes and shell minimized by gradually introducing fluids by throttling inlet valves. Warming done gradually to prevent thermal shock (temperature change inducing excessive thermal stress). Thermal shock occurs when temperature suddenly increases/decreases causing differential metal expansion/contraction, challenging integrity. After sudden temperature decrease, brittle fracture possible due to additional thermal stresses if internal pressure high.
notes.objective: Explain the following regarding Thermal Shock of a heat exchanger: Description of thermal shock, Conditions or situations that make thermal shock more likely, Operational concerns for a heat exchanger that undergoes thermal shock.

notes.subject: CP06
notes.title: **HEAT EXCHANGER STARTUP PROCEDURE**
notes.content: To place HX in service: (1) Cold fluid circulated first using vent connections for air evacuation. Air-containing HX is less efficient since air reduces heat transfer surface area. (2) Hot fluid valved in after cold fluid to prevent thermal shock. (3) Air evacuation again accomplished using vent connections. Inlet valve throttled to limit flow and minimize pressure spiking. Once full, vent valves closed. Vent valves opened while filling to let air escape and prevent air binding. Pressure spike called water hammer occurs when fluid velocity suddenly changes. Causes pipe movement and damage. Minimized by slowly operating valves.

notes.subject: CP06
notes.title: **SECTION 5.2 - HEAT EXCHANGER SHUTDOWN**
notes.content: Procedures for shutting down heat exchangers involve controlled cooling and draining. As HX cools, metal contracts. Drains should be opened to prevent water hammer and pressure spikes. Procedures ensure safe cooling and maintenance access without damage to equipment.

notes.subject: CP06
notes.title: **SECTION 5.3 - DYNAMICS OF HEAT EXCHANGER OPERATION**
notes.content:
**OBJECTIVE 8: Explain how the following operational factors affect heat exchanger performance: Flow rates that are too high or too low; Scaling or tube fouling; Heat exchanger tube failure.**
Multiple operational factors significantly impact heat exchanger performance. Flow rates that are too high create excessive pressure drops and energy loss. Flow rates too low result in inadequate heat transfer. Scaling or tube fouling deposits reduce heat transfer surface area. Deposits include mineral scale, corrosion products, biological growth. Heat exchanger tube failure can result in cross-contamination of fluids, loss of heat transfer capability, and potential operational hazards.
notes.section: SECTION 5.3 - DYNAMICS OF HEAT EXCHANGER OPERATION
notes.objective: Explain how the following operational factors affect heat exchanger performance: Flow rates that are too high or too low; Scaling or tube fouling; Heat exchanger tube failure.

notes.subject: CP06
notes.title: **HEAT TRANSFER COEFFICIENT AND SYSTEM OPTIMIZATION**
notes.content: Heat transfer rate depends on U (overall heat transfer coefficient), A (surface area), and ΔT (temperature difference). Deposits reduce coefficient. Tube failure reduces effective surface area. System operators must maintain flow rates, monitor for fouling indicators, and detect tube failures through temperature, pressure, and flow monitoring. Maintaining clean surfaces and proper flow ensures optimal performance.
notes.section: HEAT TRANSFER COEFFICIENT AND SYSTEM OPTIMIZATION

notes.subject: CP06
notes.title: **SECTION 6.0 - CONDENSERS**
notes.content:
**OBJECTIVE 9: Explain the relationship between condenser vacuum and backpressure.**
Condenser vacuum and turbine backpressure are directly related. Higher vacuum in condenser means lower pressure, which creates greater pressure difference between turbine inlet and outlet. This pressure difference drives more work from steam, improving turbine efficiency. Vacuum is measured as absolute pressure. Better vacuum (lower absolute pressure) reduces backpressure, improving plant efficiency. Degraded condenser performance reduces vacuum, increasing backpressure, reducing turbine output and efficiency.
notes.objective: Explain the relationship between condenser vacuum and backpressure.

notes.subject: CP06
notes.title: **SECTION 6.1 - CONDENSER CONSTRUCTION**
notes.content: Main condenser is one of largest shell and tube heat exchangers - rectangular shaped with thousands of tubes carrying circulating water. Condenser tubes designed for efficient heat transfer with steam on shell side and cooling water on tube side. Tube bundles arranged for maximum heat transfer. Hotwell collects condensed steam. Condenser designed as crossflow with steam flowing downward perpendicular to tube bundles containing circulating water.

notes.subject: CP06
notes.title: **CONDENSER VACUUM SYSTEM**
notes.content: Condenser vacuum maintained by air removal systems. Non-condensable gases (primarily air) cannot condense and accumulate in condenser. Buildup of non-condensable gases increases pressure and reduces vacuum. Air removal systems (jet air ejectors or vacuum pumps) continuously remove non-condensables, maintaining vacuum. Effective air removal is critical for sustained condenser performance and efficient operation.

notes.subject: CP06
notes.title: **SECTION 6.2 - CONDENSER OPERATION**
notes.content:
**OBJECTIVE 10: Explain the principle of operation of condensers.**
Condenser operation depends on steam contacting cold condenser tubes where condensation occurs. As exhaust steam contacts cold condenser tubes it condenses, forming condensate. Condensate falls and collects in hotwell, then pumped through secondary plant components requiring cooling and to feedwater heater trains. Circulating water through tubes keeps them cold and provides condensation surface. Latent heat of condensation transferred through tube walls, warming circulating water. Large quantities of cooling water needed - approximately 65 to 100 pounds or 8 to 12 gallons of cooling water needed per pound of steam condensed.
notes.objective: Explain the principle of operation of condensers.

notes.subject: CP06
notes.title: **CONDENSER PERFORMANCE MONITORING**
notes.content: Condenser efficiency monitored by measuring vacuum, outlet water temperature, and flow rates. Degradation indicated by: (1) Reduced vacuum despite stable load, (2) Increased outlet water temperature, (3) Fouling of tubes, (4) Air in-leakage. Regular monitoring detects performance degradation early, allowing corrective action before significant efficiency loss. Maintenance includes tube cleaning and air system maintenance.

notes.subject: CP06
notes.title: **SECTION 7.0 - OPERATING EXPERIENCE**
notes.content: SOER 84-1: Cooling Water System Degradation Due to Aquatic Life - Cooling tower and condenser performance can be degraded by aquatic organism growth in cooling water systems. Biofouling can reduce cooling effectiveness, increasing condenser backpressure and reducing turbine efficiency. Control measures include chemical treatment and system monitoring to maintain performance and prevent fouling-related operational issues.

notes.subject: TH01
notes.title: Systems of Measurement and Unit Conversion
notes.content:
TWO PRIMARY SYSTEMS:

AMERICAN ENGINEERING SYSTEM (ENGLISH ENGINEERS SYSTEM):
• Force: pounds force (lbf), Mass: pounds mass (lbm)
• Length: feet (ft), inches (in)
• Temperature: Fahrenheit (°F)
• Pressure: psi (pounds per square inch), psf (pounds per square foot)
• Energy/Work: British Thermal Units (Btu), where 1 Btu = 778.16 ft·lbf
• Power: horsepower (hp), where 1 hp = 550 ft·lbf/s
• Flow rate: gallons per minute (gpm), pounds per hour (lbm/h)
• Density: pounds per cubic foot (lbm/ft³)
• Viscosity: pounds per foot-second (lbm/ft·s) or centipoise (cp)

INTERNATIONAL SYSTEM (SI/METRIC):
• Force: Newtons (N), where 1 N = 1 kg·m/s²
• Mass: kilograms (kg)
• Length: meters (m)
• Temperature: Celsius (°C) or Kelvin (K) - required for thermodynamic calculations
• Pressure: Pascal (Pa), kilopascal (kPa), or bar (1 bar = 100 kPa = 14.5 psi)
• Energy/Work: Joules (J), where 1 J = 1 N·m
• Power: Watts (W), where 1 W = 1 J/s or 1 N·m/s
• Flow rate: cubic meters per second (m³/s), kilograms per second (kg/s)
• Density: kilograms per cubic meter (kg/m³)
• Viscosity: Pascal·seconds (Pa·s) or centipoise (cp)

ADVANTAGES OF EACH SYSTEM:
English System advantages:
  • Familiar to engineers with traditional training
  • Practical units often match real-world dimensions
  • Historical database and references available

SI Advantages:
  • Decimal-based conversions (powers of 10)
  • Used internationally in modern applications
  • Simpler calculations (no conversion factors like 778)
  • Standard in most modern research and new equipment

UNIT CONVERSION PROCESS:

Step 1: Identify given units and desired units
Step 2: Write conversion factor with given units in denominator, desired units in numerator
Step 3: Multiply original value by conversion factor
Step 4: Cancel units algebraically and solve

EXAMPLE: Convert 50 psi to kPa
→ 50 psi × (6.895 kPa/psi) = 344.75 kPa

COMMON CONVERSION FACTORS (Memorize these):
• Length: 1 ft = 0.3048 m, 1 inch = 2.54 cm
• Mass: 1 lbm = 0.4536 kg, 1 kg = 2.205 lbm
• Pressure: 1 psi = 6.895 kPa, 1 bar = 14.5 psi, 1 atm = 14.696 psia
• Energy: 1 Btu = 1055.06 J = 778.16 ft·lbf
• Power: 1 hp = 0.7457 kW, 1 W = 1 J/s
• Flow: 1 gpm = 6.309 × 10⁻⁵ m³/s, 1 gpm = 0.06309 L/s

DIMENSIONAL ANALYSIS:
Method to verify equations are dimensionally consistent:
• Each term in an equation must have same dimensions
• Example: Velocity (ft/s) = Distance (ft) / Time (s) ✓ Correct
• Use to catch errors in calculations
notes.section: SYSTEMS OF MEASUREMENT AND UNIT CONVERSION:

notes.subject: TH01
notes.title: Temperature Scales Comparison
notes.content:
ABSOLUTE ZERO AND MOLECULAR MOTION:
Absolute zero = point where all molecular motion theoretically stops
• 0 K = -273.15°C = -459.67°R = -459.67°F
• NO temperature below absolute zero is physically possible
• All thermodynamic equations REQUIRE absolute temperature for correct results

RELATIVE TEMPERATURE SCALES (Reference Point Based):

FAHRENHEIT (°F) - American Standard:
• Freezing point of water: 32°F
• Boiling point of water (at 1 atm): 212°F
• Temperature interval: 180 degrees between freeze and boil
• Used in American Engineering System
• Familiar to US population but poor for calculations
• Formula for conversion: °F = (°C × 1.8) + 32
• Inverse formula: °C = (°F - 32) / 1.8
• Resolution: Decimal fractions of degrees possible
• Applications: Building temperature control, weather reports, cooking

CELSIUS (°C) - International Standard for Relative Scale:
• Freezing point of water: 0°C (convenient reference)
• Boiling point of water (at 1 atm): 100°C (convenient reference)
• Temperature interval: 100 degrees between freeze and boil
• Smaller degree interval than Fahrenheit = more precise
• International standard for non-thermodynamic applications
• Formula for conversion: °C = (°F - 32) / 1.8
• Applications: Scientific work, weather, building control, food storage

SCALE COMPARISON EXAMPLE:
Room temperature (68°F):
= (68 - 32) / 1.8 = 36 / 1.8 = 20°C
Both scales show same physical temperature, just different numbers

ABSOLUTE TEMPERATURE SCALES (Zero = No Molecular Motion):

RANKINE (°R) - Absolute Fahrenheit Scale:
• Corresponds directly to Fahrenheit
• Absolute zero: 0°R = -459.67°F
• Boiling point of water: 671.67°R = 212°F
• Formula: °R = °F + 459.67
• Maintains same degree interval as Fahrenheit (1°F = 1°R interval)
• Rarely used, but appears in some engineering equations
• Used when working with English Engineering System in thermodynamics

KELVIN (K) - Absolute Celsius Scale:
• Corresponds directly to Celsius
• Absolute zero: 0 K = -273.15°C
• Boiling point of water: 373.15 K = 100°C
• Formula: K = °C + 273.15 (simplified: K ≈ °C + 273)
• Maintains same degree interval as Celsius (1°C = 1 K interval)
• STANDARD for all thermodynamic calculations
• Required in ALL scientific and engineering equations
• Example: Steam table calculations MUST use Kelvin

WHY ABSOLUTE TEMPERATURE IS REQUIRED:
Thermodynamic equations use temperature ratios and relationships that only work with absolute scales:
• Ideal Gas Law: PV = nRT (T must be absolute)
• Efficiency calculations: η = 1 - (T_cold/T_hot) (requires absolute T)
• Temperature-dependent rates: k = A × e^(-Ea/RT) (requires absolute T)

COMMON ERROR: Using relative temperature in thermodynamic equations produces wrong answers
Example Error: Assuming Δ°C = ΔK
• Temperature difference: ΔT is same in both scales
• But equation T₁/T₂ requires absolute temperature (K or R)

TEMPERATURE CONVERSION QUICK REFERENCE:
32°F = 0°C = 273.15 K = 491.67°R
212°F = 100°C = 373.15 K = 671.67°R
Room temp (68°F) = 20°C = 293.15 K = 527.67°R

notes.subject: TH01
notes.title: System Types and Properties
notes.content:
DEFINITION OF A THERMODYNAMIC SYSTEM:
A quantity of matter or space separated from surroundings by a boundary.
• Everything within the boundary = THE SYSTEM
• Everything outside the boundary = THE SURROUNDINGS
• The boundary separates system from surroundings (real or imaginary)

THREE SYSTEM TYPES:

ISOLATED (CLOSED) SYSTEM:
• Definition: No mass transfer across boundary, no energy transfer
• Theoretical ideal; true isolated systems do not exist in reality
• All real systems exchange something with surroundings
• Used for theoretical calculations and limiting case analysis
• Example (closest to ideal): Perfectly insulated, sealed container

CLOSED SYSTEM:
• Definition: No mass transfer across boundary; energy transfer (heat/work) may occur
• Mass inside remains constant
• Boundary allows heat and work to transfer
• MOST COMMON for thermodynamic analysis
• Real-world examples:
  - Fixed mass of gas in a cylinder (internal combustion engine)
  - Sealed reactor vessel with piping for steam/water but no inlet/outlet
  - Closed piping section between two isolation valves
  - Accumulator with fixed charge of nitrogen or gas
  - Constant pressure cooker (no mass enters/leaves)

OPEN SYSTEM (CONTROL VOLUME):
• Definition: Mass transfer across boundary (inlet and/or outlet flows); energy transfer occurs
• Mass inside changes over time as flow enters and exits
• MOST REALISTIC for practical power plant equipment
• Requires mass balance and energy balance across control volume
• Real-world examples:
  - Turbine with steam inlet and exhaust outlet
  - Compressor with air inlet and discharge outlet
  - Boiler with water inlet, steam outlet, and fuel input
  - Pump with inlet and discharge piping
  - Condenser with exhaust steam inlet and hot cooling water inlet
  - Heat exchanger with two fluid streams

SELECTION GUIDE:
Use CLOSED SYSTEM when: analyzing fixed mass of substance (single piece of equipment in isolation)
Use OPEN SYSTEM when: analyzing flow through equipment (practical equipment in power plant operation)

WORKING FLUID:
The medium (substance) within a system that stores, transfers, or absorbs energy.

Characteristics of Working Fluid:
• Must be able to absorb and reject heat
• Must be compatible with system materials
• Must have predictable properties across operating range
• Should have high specific heat (stores more energy per unit mass)
• Should have low viscosity (flows easily, reduces pumping work)

Common Working Fluids in Power Plants:
• Steam (most common) - absorbs heat in boiler, rejects in condenser
• Water (liquid form) - circulates through boilers and condensers
• Refrigerant - absorbs and rejects heat in refrigeration systems
• Gas (air, nitrogen) - used in gas turbines and auxiliary systems
• Oil - used in lubrication and some heat transfer systems

SYSTEM PROPERTIES - FUNDAMENTAL CLASSIFICATION:

INTENSIVE PROPERTIES (Independent of Mass):
These properties do NOT change with the amount of material.
• Pressure (P) - force per unit area [psi, kPa, Pa]
• Temperature (T) - measure of molecular motion [°F, °C, K, R]
• Density (ρ) - mass per unit volume [lbm/ft³, kg/m³]
• Specific volume (v) - volume per unit mass = 1/ρ [ft³/lbm, m³/kg]
• Velocity (V) - speed of fluid motion [ft/s, m/s]
• Height/Elevation (z) - vertical position [ft, m]
• Enthalpy (h) - specific heat content [Btu/lbm, J/kg]
• Entropy (s) - specific disorder/unavailable energy [Btu/(lbm·R), J/(kg·K)]
• Specific internal energy (u) - specific energy stored in substance [Btu/lbm, J/kg]

Why Intensive: These properties are same regardless of how much material you have.
Example: Water at 100°C has same temperature whether you have 1 kg or 100 kg.

EXTENSIVE PROPERTIES (Dependent on Mass):
These properties CHANGE with the amount of material.
• Volume (V) - total space occupied [ft³, m³]
• Mass (m) - total matter content [lbm, kg]
• Weight (W) - gravitational force on mass = m × g [lbf, N]
• Internal energy (U) - total energy stored = u × m [Btu, J]
• Total enthalpy (H) - total heat content = h × m [Btu, J]
• Total entropy (S) - total disorder = s × m [Btu/R, J/K]

Why Extensive: Doubling the material doubles these properties.
Example: 1 kg of water has half the volume of 2 kg of water (at same T and P).

RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN INTENSIVE AND EXTENSIVE:
Specific properties (intensive) = Total properties (extensive) / Mass

Examples:
• Specific volume (v) = Total volume (V) / Mass (m) = V/m
• Specific enthalpy (h) = Total enthalpy (H) / Mass (m) = H/m
• Specific internal energy (u) = Total internal energy (U) / Mass (m) = U/m

PRACTICAL APPLICATION:
When analyzing a steam system:
• Intensive: Steam at 400 psia and 600°F has specific properties from steam tables
• Extensive: 100 lbm of that steam has 100 times the total internal energy
• Calculation: U_total = 100 lbm × u_specific(from steam table)

IMPORTANT NOTE:
All thermodynamic equations use SPECIFIC (intensive) properties, requiring division by mass for correct results.

notes.subject: TH02
notes.title: First Law of Thermodynamics
notes.content:
FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLE:
"Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only converted from one form to another."

MATHEMATICAL STATEMENT (For Closed System):
Q - W = ΔU_system
or
E_in - E_out = ΔE_system

Where:
• Q = Heat transfer to system [Btu, J]
• W = Work done by system [Btu, J]
• ΔU = Change in internal energy [Btu, J]

UNIVERSAL PRINCIPLE:
This law applies to ALL energy transformations:
• Chemical combustion → thermal energy
• Thermal energy → mechanical work
• Mechanical work → electrical energy
• Electrical energy → light, heat, motion

POWER PLANT APPLICATION (Open System Energy Balance):

Thermal-to-Electrical Conversion Process:
1. Fuel Input: Chemical energy from coal/gas/oil/nuclear
2. Boiler: Chemical energy → Heat transfer to steam
3. Steam Generation: Heat absorbed raises steam temperature and pressure
4. Turbine: High-pressure steam expands → Mechanical work extracted
5. Generator: Mechanical work → Electrical power output
6. Condenser: Low-pressure steam → Heat rejected to cooling water/atmosphere
7. Pump: Mechanical work returns condensate to boiler

ENERGY BALANCE FOR POWER CYCLE:
Total Energy In (Fuel/Heat) = Electrical Energy Out + Heat Rejected + Losses

Efficiency = Electrical Power Output / Total Thermal Energy Input × 100%

Typical Plant Efficiency: 33-40% (coal), 45-55% (gas), 60-90% (nuclear)

FORMS OF ENERGY IN POWER SYSTEMS:

STORED ENERGY (Energy a substance HAS - state-dependent):
Properties of matter that depend only on current state, not on how the substance reached that state.

POTENTIAL ENERGY (PE):
Energy due to position in gravitational field
Formula: PE = m × z × g / gc
Where:
  • m = mass
  • z = height above reference point
  • g = gravitational acceleration (32.174 ft/s² or 9.81 m/s²)
  • gc = conversion factor (32.174 lbm·ft/(lbf·s²) in English system)

Example: Water elevated in tower stores PE relative to ground level.

KINETIC ENERGY (KE):
Energy due to motion/velocity
Formula: KE = m × V² / (2 × gc)
Where:
  • m = mass
  • V = velocity
  • gc = conversion factor

Example: Rotating pump impeller, flowing steam, moving piston.

INTERNAL ENERGY (U):
Sum of all microscopic forms of energy within a substance:
• Molecular motion (kinetic at molecular level) - increases with temperature
• Molecular vibration - increases with temperature
• Electron orbital motion
• Nuclear binding energy (constant for most processes)

Specific Internal Energy (u):
• u = U / m (energy per unit mass)
• Units: Btu/lbm, J/kg
• Changes with temperature and pressure
• Steam tables provide direct values
• Example: Saturated steam at 100 psia has u = 1187.8 Btu/lbm

Why Internal Energy Matters:
Internal energy must change for any temperature change to occur, and represents the energy available from the substance.

FLOW ENERGY (PV WORK):
Energy required to push a fluid into or out of a control volume
Formula: PV = P × V (specific: Pv = P × v)
Where:
  • P = pressure
  • V = volume (specific: v = volume per unit mass)

Physical Meaning: Work done against pressure to inject fluid into system.

Example: Pump must do 100 psi work just to push water into a 100 psi line (plus kinetic/potential changes).

ENTHALPY (H) - MOST IMPORTANT FOR FLOWING SYSTEMS:
Definition: H = U + PV
Combined measure of internal energy and flow work energy.

Specific Enthalpy (h):
h = u + Pv
Units: Btu/lbm, kJ/kg
This is the enthalpy found in steam tables.

Physical Meaning:
Enthalpy represents the TOTAL energy content of a flowing fluid, including:
• Internal energy (energy stored in substance)
• Flow work energy (energy to push fluid into/out of system)

WHY ENTHALPY IS CRITICAL FOR POWER SYSTEMS:

Turbine Work Calculation:
W_turbine = m × (h_inlet - h_outlet)
Example: Steam enters turbine at h₁ = 1400 Btu/lbm, exits at h₂ = 1200 Btu/lbm
Specific work = 1400 - 1200 = 200 Btu/lbm
For 100 lbm/s flow: Power = 100 × 200 = 20,000 Btu/s = 28.3 MW

Pump Work Calculation:
W_pump = m × (h_outlet - h_inlet)
Example: Liquid water inlet h₁ = 50 Btu/lbm, outlet h₂ = 60 Btu/lbm
Specific work = 60 - 50 = 10 Btu/lbm

Condenser Heat Rejection:
Q_rejected = m × (h_steam_inlet - h_liquid_outlet)
Example: 100 lbm/s steam at h₁ = 1200 Btu/lbm, exits as liquid at h₂ = 50 Btu/lbm
Heat rejected = 100 × (1200 - 50) = 115,000 Btu/s = 163 MW

Boiler Heat Addition:
Q_added = m × (h_outlet - h_inlet)
Example: Liquid water inlet h₁ = 100 Btu/lbm, steam outlet h₂ = 1400 Btu/lbm
Heat added = m × (1400 - 100) = m × 1300 Btu/lbm per unit mass

Advantages of Using Enthalpy:
• Simplifies energy balance for flowing systems
• Eliminates need to calculate Pv work separately
• Steam tables provide direct values - no calculations needed
• Applies to all open systems (turbines, pumps, heat exchangers)
notes.section: FIRST LAW OF THERMODYNAMICS - ENERGY CONSERVATION:

notes.subject: TH02
notes.title: Energy Components and Enthalpy
notes.content:
REVIEW OF STORED ENERGY TYPES:

1. POTENTIAL ENERGY:
   Calculated: PE = m × z × g / gc
   Significance: Important for elevation changes in piping, but usually small compared to enthalpy changes
   Example: Water elevated 100 ft = 100 ft × 1 lbm/lbf = 100 lbm·ft/lbf per lbm (small)
   vs. Steam enthalpy change in turbine = 200+ Btu/lbm (much larger)

2. KINETIC ENERGY:
   Calculated: KE = m × V² / (2 × gc)
   Significance: Often negligible in power plants but important in jet flows, nozzles
   Example: Water at 10 ft/s = (10²)/(2×32.174) = 1.55 Btu/lbm
   vs. Enthalpy change = hundreds of Btu/lbm
   Exception: High-velocity flow in nozzles or diffusers requires kinetic energy consideration

3. INTERNAL ENERGY:
   Not usually calculated directly; its change is represented by enthalpy change
   Temperature change = Internal energy change for substance
   Used in closed system analysis (piston-cylinder)

4. FLOW ENERGY (Pv):
   Always considered through enthalpy calculation
   Implicitly included in "h" values from steam tables

TRANSIENT ENERGY (Energy IN TRANSIT - Process-dependent):
Not properties of matter, but energy crossing system boundaries during process.

HEAT (Q):
Definition: Energy transfer due to temperature difference.
Characteristics:
• Transfers spontaneously from hot to cold (no work required)
• Does NOT flow through perfect insulation
• Path-dependent (same initial/final states can have different Q depending on process)
• Units: Btu, kJ, calories
• Sign convention: Q > 0 = heat added to system, Q < 0 = heat removed

Physical Process:
• Random molecular motion of hotter substance → Random molecular motion of cooler substance
• Molecular collisions transfer kinetic energy across boundary

Power Plant Example:
• Boiler: Q_in = heat from combustion to steam
• Condenser: Q_out = heat from steam to cooling water

WORK (W):
Definition: Energy transfer due to organized force acting through distance.
Formula: W = F × d
Characteristics:
• Organized transfer (vs random molecular collision in heat)
• Path-dependent (same states can have different W depending on process)
• Units: Btu, kJ, ft-lbf, J
• Sign convention: W > 0 = work done BY system, W < 0 = work done ON system

TWO MAJOR TYPES OF WORK:

1. MECHANICAL WORK:
   W_mech = F × Δx
   Solid object moved by force
   Examples:
   • Piston moving in cylinder
   • Shaft rotating in turbine
   • Pump impeller pushing fluid

2. FLOW WORK (PV WORK):
   W_flow = P × V
   Energy to push/pull fluid against pressure
   Already included in enthalpy calculation (h = u + Pv)
   Do NOT calculate separately for flowing systems

TURBINE WORK:
Process: High-pressure steam expands through turbine
Work = ṁ × (h_inlet - h_outlet)
Energy Conversion: Internal energy of steam → Mechanical work → Electrical energy
Example: Turbine with 100 psia inlet, 1 psia outlet, 500 lbm/s flow
  From steam tables: h_inlet = 1279 Btu/lbm, h_outlet = 1105 Btu/lbm
  Specific work = 1279 - 1105 = 174 Btu/lbm
  Total work = 500 lbm/s × 174 Btu/lbm = 87,000 Btu/s = 123 MW

PUMP WORK:
Process: Pump adds pressure to fluid
Work = ṁ × (h_outlet - h_inlet)
Energy Conversion: Mechanical work from motor → Fluid pressure increase
Note: For incompressible liquids, Wp ≈ v × ΔP (specific volume × pressure change)
Example: Pump takes water at 50 psia, delivers at 2050 psia
  Pressure increase = 2000 psi
  Water specific volume v ≈ 0.01613 ft³/lbm
  Pump work = 0.01613 × 2000 / gc = 1.0 Btu/lbm (liquid water)

SIGN CONVENTIONS:
Turbine: W = h_in - h_out (positive for work output)
Pump: W = h_out - h_in (positive for work input)

POWER (P or PWR):
Definition: Rate of energy transfer
Formula: Power = Energy / Time
Units:
• Btu/s (common in power engineering)
• Watts = J/s (SI standard)
• Horsepower (hp) - historical
• 1 hp = 0.7457 kW = 2545 Btu/h = 745.7 W

Power Conversions (Memorize):
• 1 Btu/s = 1.415 hp
• 1 hp = 0.707 Btu/s
• 1 kW = 3412 Btu/h
• 1 MW = 3.412 MMBtu/h

TURBINE POWER CALCULATION:
Power_turbine = ṁ × w_turbine = ṁ × (h_in - h_out)
Example: 100 lbm/s steam, work = 200 Btu/lbm
Power = 100 × 200 = 20,000 Btu/s = 28.3 MW

PUMP POWER CALCULATION:
Power_pump = ṁ × w_pump = ṁ × (h_out - h_in)
Note: Actual power > theoretical because pumps have efficiency < 100%
Actual Power = Theoretical Power / Pump Efficiency
Example: Theoretical = 1000 Btu/s, Pump efficiency = 80%
Actual motor power = 1000 / 0.80 = 1250 Btu/s

GENERATOR POWER OUTPUT:
Generator Power = Turbine Power × Generator Efficiency
Typical turbine efficiency: 85-90%
Typical generator efficiency: 95-99%
Combined: 80-90% of shaft power becomes electrical power

notes.subject: TH02
notes.title: Heat, Work, and Power
notes.content:
HEAT TRANSFER (Q):
Fundamental Mechanism: Random molecular motion transfer across temperature gradient

Three Modes of Heat Transfer:

1. CONDUCTION:
   Heat transfer through solid material
   Formula: Q = k × A × ΔT / L
   Where:
   • k = thermal conductivity of material
   • A = contact area
   • ΔT = temperature difference
   • L = thickness
   Example: Heat through boiler tube wall from hot gas to cooler water inside

2. CONVECTION:
   Heat transfer from surface to moving fluid (or vice versa)
   Formula: Q = h × A × ΔT
   Where:
   • h = convection coefficient (depends on fluid, velocity, geometry)
   • A = surface area
   • ΔT = temperature difference
   Example: Steam giving up heat to cooling water in condenser

3. RADIATION:
   Heat transfer via electromagnetic waves
   Formula: Q = σ × A × T⁴
   Where:
   • σ = Stefan-Boltzmann constant
   • A = surface area
   • T = absolute temperature
   Example: Heat loss from hot pipes to environment without direct contact
   Note: Only significant at very high temperatures; often negligible in power plants

HEAT TRANSFER CALCULATIONS IN POWER CYCLES:

Boiler Heat Transfer:
Q_boiler = ṁ × (h_out - h_in) = heat input to steam from fuel

Condenser Heat Transfer:
Q_condenser = ṁ × (h_in - h_out) = heat rejected from steam to cooling water

Heat Exchanger (General):
Q = ṁ_hot × (h_hot,in - h_hot,out) = ṁ_cold × (h_cold,out - h_cold,in)
Heat leaving hot stream = Heat entering cold stream

WORK IN THERMODYNAMIC CYCLES:

Turbine Work:
W_turbine = ṁ × (h_in - h_out) = mechanical work extracted from expanding steam
This work drives the generator

Pump Work:
W_pump = ṁ × (h_out - h_in) = mechanical work required to increase fluid pressure
Must be provided by electric motor

Compressor Work:
W_compressor = ṁ × (h_out - h_in) = mechanical work required to increase gas pressure
Must be provided by turbine or motor

Net Work for Cycle:
W_net = W_turbine - W_pump - W_compressor
This net work is converted to electricity

POWER CALCULATIONS FOR ACTUAL EQUIPMENT:

Turbine Mechanical Power:
P_shaft = ṁ × w × η_turbine
Where η_turbine = isentropic efficiency (85-90%)

Generator Electrical Power:
P_electrical = P_shaft × η_generator
Where η_generator = electrical efficiency (95-99%)

Overall Plant Efficiency:
η_overall = P_electrical / Q_boiler = (W_turbine - W_pump) / Q_boiler × η_generator × η_transformer
Typical: 33-40% coal, 45-55% gas, 33% nuclear

ENERGY CONSERVATION CHECK:
For any process: Q_in - Q_out - W_out + W_in = ΔE_system
Sum of all energy transfers must equal change in system energy.
notes.section: ENERGY TRANSFER MECHANISMS IN POWER CYCLES:

notes.subject: TH03
notes.title: States, Phases, and Phase Diagrams
notes.content:
DEFINITION OF STATE:
A substance is in a specific thermodynamic state when its condition is uniquely defined by two independent intensive properties.
Once ANY TWO independent properties are known, ALL other properties can be determined.

PRINCIPLE OF STATE:
Two properties required because any substance has multiple properties:
Temperature, Pressure, Density, Specific volume, Internal energy, Enthalpy, Entropy, etc.

Not all pairs work equally:
• GOOD PAIRS (independent): (P, T), (P, v), (T, v), (P, h), (T, s)
• BAD PAIRS (not independent): (P, x) in wet region - pressure and quality NOT independent for saturation
• Avoid if possible: Using h and s together - less direct table access

PRACTICAL STATE DETERMINATION:
Given state → Look up other properties in tables (steam tables for water)
Example: If you know P = 100 psia and T = 350°F
  → Look in superheated steam tables at 100 psia, 350°F
  → Read off: v, u, h, s, and all other properties

PHASE: DESCRIPTION OF MOLECULAR STRUCTURE

Definition: Physical condition determined by intermolecular forces and molecular spacing.

FOUR PHASES OF MATTER:

1. SOLID STATE:
   Molecular Characteristics:
   • Molecules vibrate in fixed positions (tight bonds)
   • Intermolecular forces very strong
   • Rigid crystalline structure

   Physical Properties:
   • Fixed shape - maintains geometry without container
   • Fixed volume - molecules cannot move closer or farther apart
   • Very high density - molecules closely packed
   • Incompressible - pressure cannot reduce volume significantly

   Thermodynamic Properties (water as example):
   • Lowest specific volume (smallest v)
   • Lowest specific enthalpy (h is most negative)
   • Lowest internal energy

   Power Plant Applications:
   • Ice formation in cooling systems (undesirable)
   • Solid fuels (coal, biomass)

2. LIQUID STATE:
   Molecular Characteristics:
   • Molecules in contact but can slide past each other
   • Intermolecular forces still significant
   • Random molecular arrangement

   Physical Properties:
   • No fixed shape - conforms to container
   • FIXED VOLUME - cannot compress significantly (much denser than gas)
   • High density - molecules close together but mobile
   • Nearly incompressible - used for hydraulic systems

   Thermodynamic Properties (water as example):
   • Moderate specific volume (larger than solid)
   • Moderate specific enthalpy
   • Better energy storage than solid

   Power Plant Applications:
   • Liquid water in boilers and condensers
   • Pump inlet (requires liquid, not vapor)
   • Lubrication systems
   • Cooling water

3. VAPOR/GAS STATE:
   Molecular Characteristics:
   • Molecules separated by large distances (low density)
   • Intermolecular forces negligible except at very high pressures
   • Random rapid motion and collisions

   Physical Properties:
   • No fixed shape - fills entire container
   • No fixed volume - expands to fill container
   • Very low density - molecules far apart
   • Highly compressible - pressure changes volume significantly
   • Flows easily

   Thermodynamic Properties (water as example):
   • Largest specific volume (largest v)
   • Largest specific enthalpy (h is most positive)
   • Highest internal energy

   Important Distinction:
   • VAPOR: Gas in vicinity of saturation (can recondense easily)
   • GAS: Substance far from saturation (difficult to condense)
   • Example: Steam at 100 psia is "vapor" (close to saturation), Air is "gas" (far from saturation)

   Power Plant Applications:
   • Steam exiting boiler for turbine inlet
   • Exhaust steam from turbine to condenser

4. PLASMA STATE:
   Molecular Characteristics:
   • Gas ionized into electrons and ions
   • High-energy state with significant electromagnetic forces

   Conditions Required:
   • Extremely high temperatures (>10,000 K)
   • High energy inputs

   Power Plant Applications:
   • Combustion process (partially ionized)
   • Nuclear fusion research
   • Lightning, electric arcs

PHASE TRANSITIONS (Phase Changes):

Process: Substance changes from one phase to another

SIX POSSIBLE PHASE CHANGES:

1. MELTING: Solid → Liquid
   • Heat absorbed (endothermic process)
   • Temperature remains constant at melting point
   • Intermolecular forces weaken, allowing molecular motion
   • Occurs at constant pressure (1 atm) at fixed temperature
   • Example: Ice at 32°F → Water at 32°F (absorbs heat of fusion)

2. SOLIDIFICATION: Liquid → Solid
   • Heat rejected (exothermic process)
   • Temperature remains constant at freezing point
   • Molecules slow, form crystalline structure
   • Opposite of melting
   • Example: Water at 32°F → Ice at 32°F (releases heat)

3. VAPORIZATION: Liquid → Vapor
   • Heat absorbed (endothermic process)
   • Temperature remains constant at boiling/saturation point
   • Molecules gain enough energy to escape liquid bonds
   • Requires large energy input (latent heat)
   • Example: Water at 212°F → Steam at 212°F (at 1 atm, absorbs heat of vaporization)

4. CONDENSATION: Vapor → Liquid
   • Heat rejected (exothermic process)
   • Temperature remains constant at saturation point
   • Vapor molecules lose energy, rejoin liquid phase
   • Releases latent heat
   • Critical process in power plant condensers
   • Example: Steam at 212°F → Water at 212°F (at 1 atm, releases heat)

5. SUBLIMATION: Solid → Vapor directly
   • Heat absorbed (endothermic process)
   • Skips liquid phase
   • Temperature remains constant
   • Rare in power plants but occurs with some refrigerants
   • Example: Dry ice at -109°F → CO₂ vapor (sublimes at atmospheric pressure)

6. DEPOSITION: Vapor → Solid directly
   • Heat rejected (exothermic process)
   • Skips liquid phase
   • Reverse of sublimation
   • Example: Frost forming (water vapor → ice directly)

PHASE DIAGRAM (PRESSURE-TEMPERATURE CHART):

Axes: Horizontal = Temperature, Vertical = Pressure (logarithmic scale typical)

THREE PHASE BOUNDARY LINES:

1. FUSION LINE (Melting/Freezing Boundary):
   • Separates Solid and Liquid regions
   • Relatively steep slope (strong pressure effect on melting point)
   • Less important in power engineering (unless sub-zero operation)

2. VAPORIZATION LINE (Boiling/Condensation Boundary):
   • Separates Liquid and Vapor regions
   • Critical curve for steam systems (most important for power plants)
   • Pressure INCREASES with temperature
   • Example: At 1 atm, water boils at 212°F; at 100 psia, at 327°F; at 1000 psia, at 545°F
   • Used for saturation steam table indexing

3. SUBLIMATION LINE (Deposition Boundary):
   • Separates Solid and Vapor regions
   • Exists only at pressures below triple point pressure
   • Less common in power engineering

CRITICAL PHASE DIAGRAM POINTS:

TRIPLE POINT:
Location: Where all three phase boundary lines meet (solid, liquid, vapor all coexist)
For water:
  • Temperature: 32.018°F (0.01°C)
  • Pressure: 0.00604 psia (0.0611 kPa)
Significance:
  • Only point where all three phases can exist in equilibrium
  • Used as reference point for Kelvin temperature scale
  • Rarely encountered in power plants (too low pressure)

CRITICAL POINT:
Location: Highest temperature and pressure where liquid-vapor distinction exists
For water:
  • Temperature: 705.4°F (374.15°C)
  • Pressure: 3206 psia (22.064 MPa)
Significance:
  • Above critical point, substance is supercritical
  • No phase boundary, no latent heat required for vaporization
  • Densities of liquid and vapor become equal
  • Some supercritical power plants operate above this point
  • Liquid and vapor properties merge; cannot distinguish between them

PHASE REGIONS:

Region 1: SUBCOOLED/COMPRESSED LIQUID
• Location: Below saturation temperature at given pressure
• Properties: Nearly incompressible, similar to saturated liquid
• Steam table: Compressed liquid tables or saturated liquid properties
• Importance: Pump inlet condition (must be liquid)

Region 2: SATURATED REGION (WET VAPOR)
• Location: Below critical point, between saturation lines
• Composition: Mixture of saturated liquid and saturated vapor
• Quality (x): Mass fraction that is vapor; 0 < x < 1
• Properties: Calculated using quality and saturation properties
  • h_mix = h_f + x × h_fg  (where h_fg = latent heat)
  • s_mix = s_f + x × s_fg
• Steam table: Saturated steam tables indexed by T or P
• Importance: Common in turbines; quality must be >95% to prevent blade damage

Region 3: SUPERHEATED VAPOR
• Location: Above saturation temperature at given pressure
• Properties: Single-phase gas, stable
• Steam table: Superheated steam tables indexed by (P, T)
• Importance: Most desirable turbine inlet condition; higher efficiency
• Degrees of superheat: ΔT = T_actual - T_sat (should be >50°F typically)

notes.subject: TH03
notes.title: Five States of Water
notes.content:
These are the five conditions encountered in typical power plant operations.

1. SUBCOOLED LIQUID (COMPRESSED LIQUID):
Definition: Liquid water at temperature BELOW saturation temperature for the given pressure.

Characteristics:
• Phase: 100% liquid
• Molecular state: Liquid molecules tightly bound, vibrating in place
• Resistance to boiling: Very high - requires significant heating to reach saturation
• Compressibility: Nearly incompressible (density change < 1% for pressure changes up to several thousand psi)
• Flow behavior: Flows easily through pipes and pumps

Physical Properties:
• Density (ρ): Relatively high and constant (~62.4 lbm/ft³ for water at room temperature)
• Specific volume (v): Very small (~0.0161 ft³/lbm for water)
• Specific enthalpy (h): Moderate value (depends on temperature)
• Specific entropy (s): Moderate value (increases with temperature)

Practical Examples:
• Water in pump inlet before entering boiler
• Cooling water returning to cooling tower after condenser
• Liquid water in building plumbing systems

Power Plant Importance:
• Pump inlet MUST be liquid (vapor cavitation if vapor present)
• Initial condition entering boiler
• Desired condition for pressurization systems

2. SATURATED LIQUID:
Definition: Liquid water AT saturation temperature for the given pressure, on verge of boiling.

Characteristics:
• Phase: 100% liquid, but about to vaporize
• Molecular state: Liquid molecules at surface have just enough energy to escape
• Resistance to boiling: Zero - any additional heat causes vaporization
• Heat addition next step: Small additional heat → boiling begins; temperature stays constant
• Pressure-temperature relationship: Unique saturation pressure for each temperature (and vice versa)

Physical Properties:
• Depends on saturation temperature/pressure (indexed in saturated steam tables)
• Density: Still relatively high (~50 lbm/ft³ for 100 psia steam)
• Specific volume (vf): Notation "vf" indicates saturated liquid
• Specific enthalpy (hf): Notation "hf" indicates saturated liquid enthalpy
• Specific entropy (sf): Notation "sf" indicates saturated liquid entropy

Steam Table Access:
Two options for saturation data:
Option 1: Look up by saturation temperature
  If you know T_sat = 300°F, find row in saturated table
Option 2: Look up by saturation pressure
  If you know P_sat = 100 psia, find row in saturated table

Practical Examples:
• Water in boiler just before bubbles form
• Steam-water mixture at the interface (liquid side) in a boiler or condenser

Power Plant Importance:
• Reference state for steam quality calculations
• Represents maximum liquid content before vaporization begins

3. WET VAPOR (TWO-PHASE MIXTURE):
Definition: Mixture of saturated liquid AND saturated vapor coexisting at same temperature and pressure.

Characteristics:
• Phase: Mixture of both liquid and vapor (never pure single-phase in this region)
• Composition: Varying fractions of liquid and vapor depending on heat added
• Temperature and Pressure: BOTH remain constant during phase change (all energy goes to vaporization, not heating)
• Quality (x): Defines composition - mass fraction that is vapor
  • x = 0: 100% liquid
  • x = 0.5: 50% liquid, 50% vapor (by mass)
  • x = 1.0: 100% vapor
  • Formula: x = m_vapor / m_total = (m_total - m_liquid) / m_total

Calculating Properties in Wet Region:
Property = (1 - x) × f_property + x × g_property
Or equivalently:
Property = f_property + x × fg_property

Example with enthalpy:
h = hf + x × hfg
If P = 100 psia, x = 0.9 (90% vapor):
  From saturated table: hf = 298.2 Btu/lbm, hfg = 888.8 Btu/lbm
  h = 298.2 + 0.9 × 888.8 = 298.2 + 799.9 = 1098.1 Btu/lbm

Physical Properties:
• Density: Between liquid and vapor density
• Specific volume: Between vf and vg (both phases present)
• Enthalpy: Between hf and hg (increases as x increases)
• Entropy: Between sf and sg (increases as x increases)
• Viscosity: Very complex (mixture behavior)

Steam Table Notations:
• Subscript "f" = saturated liquid property
• Subscript "g" = saturated vapor property
• Subscript "fg" = difference: fg = g - f
• Example: hfg = hg - hf = latent heat of vaporization

Practical Examples:
• Steam exiting boiler during initial vaporization
• Steam-water mixture in a steam separator
• Low-quality steam entering turbine (undesirable, but occurs)

Power Plant Importance:
• Turbine inlet quality must be HIGH (>95%) to prevent blade erosion
• Low-quality steam causes:
  • Impingement erosion from liquid droplets
  • Corrosion from liquid water
  • Reduced turbine efficiency
  • Possible blade failure
• Condenser produces low-quality steam (x ≈ 0.10-0.15) being condensed
• Steam quality is carefully controlled through superheating and reheating

4. SATURATED VAPOR:
Definition: Vapor at saturation temperature for the given pressure, with last liquid just evaporated.

Characteristics:
• Phase: 100% vapor (x = 1.0)
• Molecular state: All liquid has evaporated; no liquid droplets present
• Saturation condition: Slightest cooling causes recondensation back to wet vapor
• Dryness fraction: x = 1.0 (fully dry, no moisture)
• Heat addition behavior: Further heat addition increases temperature (becomes superheated)

Physical Properties:
• Density: Much lower than liquid (~3.7 lbm/ft³ for 100 psia)
• Specific volume (vg): Much larger than liquid (~10.5 ft³/lbm for 100 psia)
• Specific enthalpy (hg): Highest value for saturation (hf + hfg)
• Specific entropy (sg): Highest value for saturation (sf + sfg)

Steam Table Access:
Indexed by either saturation temperature or pressure (same table as saturated liquid):
• Notation "vg", "hg", "sg" indicates saturated vapor properties

Practical Examples:
• Steam exiting boiler (ideal case - usually superheated instead)
• Last molecule of steam in condenser inlet (theoretical state)
• Output of steam separator device

Power Plant Importance:
• Represents 100% dry steam (quality x = 1.0)
• Desirable state but seldom achieved in practice
• Real turbines typically use superheated steam instead
• Saturated vapor is unstable (any cooling → condensation)

5. SUPERHEATED VAPOR:
