Feedwater heater: U_o ≈ 100-500 Btu/(hr·ft²·°F)

Rate of Change Important:
• Slow degradation (1-5% per year): Normal, plan maintenance
• Rapid degradation (>10% per month): Emergency condition, plan cleaning

Causes of U_o Degradation:

1. Fouling (Most Common):
Deposits on tube inner or outer surface
• Mineral scale (calcium, magnesium salts)
• Corrosion products (iron oxides)
• Biological growth (algae, bacteria in cooling water)
• Oil/silts from leaking seals

2. Air/Non-Condensable Gases:
• Air in condenser (should be evacuated during startup)
• Released gases (oxygen from feedwater, CO₂ from chemistry)
• Hydrogen from radiolysis or corrosion
• These gases form blanket on tubes, reducing steam contact
• Locally block steam access to tube → Poor condensation

3. Tube Erosion:
• High-velocity steam can erode tubes
• Localized flow patterns cause erosion
• Changes tube geometry, reduces effective U_o

4. Corrosion Layer:
• Corrosion product buildup
• Acts like poor-conducting deposit
• Thickness increases over time

5. Mud Balls (Condenser):
• Particles from cooling water settle in tubes
• Form deposits that partially block flow
• Reduce tube effective area and cooling

FOULING DEPOSIT THICKNESS EFFECT:

Critical Observation:
Small amount of scale creates LARGE resistance increase

Example Calculation:
Condenser tube copper-nickel alloy
k = 23 Btu/(hr·ft·°F)
L_tube wall = 0.035 inch = 0.00292 ft

Resistance of tube wall:
R_wall = 0.00292 / 23 = 0.000127 hr·°F/Btu (negligible)

Now add scale:
k_scale = 0.5 Btu/(hr·ft·°F) (poor conductor)
L_scale = 0.002 inch = 0.000167 ft

Resistance of scale:
R_scale = 0.000167 / 0.5 = 0.000334 hr·°F/Btu

Ratio:
R_scale / R_wall = 0.000334 / 0.000127 = 2.6

Scale resistance is 2.6× LARGER than tube wall!

Effect on U_o:
If dominant resistance was cold-side h before:
1/U_o_original ≈ 0.001
Adding scale: 1/U_o_new ≈ 0.001 + 0.000334 = 0.001334
U_o_new / U_o_original = 1/1.334 = 0.75 = 75%

Result: 25% reduction in U_o from only 2 mils of scale

Even 1 mil deposit creates 12-15% degradation

This demonstrates:
Condenser requires frequent cleaning (2-5 years depending on water quality)
Heat transfer severely impacted by small fouling thickness
Plant efficiency directly dependent on condenser cleanliness

DESIGN COMPROMISE - U_o VALUE:

Why Not Over-Design with Huge U_o?
• Cost: Larger area or enhanced surfaces increase cost
• Diminishing returns: Last 10% of improvement costs 30-50% more
• Design life: Typical plants designed for 10-40 years of operation

Design U_o Selection:
• Conservative enough: Tolerate some fouling before cleaning necessary
• Aggressive enough: Minimize capital cost

Typical Design Practice:
• Assume baseline U_o (clean tubes)
• Apply fouling factor (estimate of expected degradation)
• Design U_o = U_o_baseline × fouling factor
• Example: If expect 20% fouling, design for 80% of clean U_o
• This ensures adequate heat transfer throughout design life between cleanings

MONITORING AND CONTROL:

How Operators Monitor U_o:
1. Calculate Q̇ from primary/secondary heat balance
2. Measure temperatures (T_in, T_out for both streams)
3. Know surface area A (fixed)
4. Calculate ΔT_mean (logarithmic mean)
5. Calculate U_o = Q̇ / (A × ΔT_mean)
6. Compare to design baseline
7. If U_o drops significantly: Plan cleaning or other corrective action

When to Take Action:
• <90% of design: Consider cleaning schedule
• <80% of design: Recommend immediate cleaning
• <70% of design: Emergency condition, impacts plant operation

For Condenser Specifically:
If U_o drops:
• First check: Is air/non-condensables present? (vent if needed)
• If air venting doesn't help: Schedule tube cleaning
• Cleaning involves: Stopping flow, sending brushes through tubes, flushing
• Expect 15-30% improvement in U_o after cleaning
notes.section: OVERALL HEAT TRANSFER COEFFICIENT AND MONITORING:

notes.subject: TH07B
notes.title: RADIATION HEAT TRANSFER:
notes.content:
RADIATION DEFINITION REVIEW:
Heat transfer via electromagnetic waves (primarily infrared radiation) from one surface to another without requiring contact or an intermediate medium.

STEFAN-BOLTZMANN LAW:
Q̇ = σ × A × ε × (T_hot⁴ - T_cold⁴)

Where:
• Q̇ = heat transfer rate [Btu/h, kW]
• σ = Stefan-Boltzmann constant = 0.1714 × 10⁻⁸ Btu/(hr·ft²·°R⁴)
• A = radiating surface area [ft²]
• ε = emissivity (fraction between 0 and 1) [dimensionless]
• T_hot = absolute temperature of hot surface [°R]
• T_cold = absolute temperature of cold surface [°R]

Note: Temperature raised to FOURTH power (T⁴)
This makes radiation extremely temperature-dependent!

STEFAN-BOLTZMANN CONSTANT:
SI units: σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W/(m²·K⁴)
English units: σ = 0.1714 × 10⁻⁸ Btu/(hr·ft²·°R⁴)
Relationships: σ = 4.88 × 10⁻⁸ Btu/(hr·ft²·°R⁴) (sometimes used)

ABSOLUTE TEMPERATURE REQUIREMENT:
Radiation equation MUST use absolute temperature:
• Rankine (°R) in English system
• Kelvin (K) in SI system

Conversion:
°R = °F + 459.67
K = °C + 273.15

Example:
Room temperature: 70°F = 529.67°R ≈ 530°R
Hot surface: 300°F = 759.67°R ≈ 760°R

Critical Point:
Using relative temperatures (°F or °C) in radiation equation produces nonsense!

TEMPERATURE FOURTH-POWER EFFECT:

Radiation very sensitive to temperature:

Room temperature (70°F = 530°R):
Q̇ = 0.1714 × 10⁻⁸ × A × 1 × (530)⁴ ≈ 184 A Btu/(hr·ft²)
This is energy continuously radiated from every surface at room temperature!

Doubling absolute temperature (to 1060°R ≈ 600°F):
Q̇ = 0.1714 × 10⁻⁸ × A × 1 × (1060)⁴ ≈ 2,944 A Btu/(hr·ft²)
16× increase! (Because 2⁴ = 16)

Temperature sensitivities:
• Each 100°F increase → significant radiation increase (roughly 10-20% increase per 100°F)
• At high temperatures, small ΔT changes produce large radiation changes
• Critical during high-temperature accident scenarios

Example Power Plant Temperatures:

Normal operation:
• Primary coolant: 550°F (1009.67°R)
• Q_rad = 0.1714 × 10⁻⁸ × 1 × 1 × (1009.67)⁴ ≈ 1,070 Btu/(hr·ft²)
• Small radiation compared to convection (h ≈ 1000, so Q_conv ≈ 500,000+ Btu/(hr·ft²·°F) if ΔT = 100°F)

Loss of coolant accident:
• Fuel cladding: 2000°F (2459.67°R)
• Q_rad = 0.1714 × 10⁻⁸ × 1 × 1 × (2459.67)⁴ ≈ 44,400 Btu/(hr·ft²)
• Much larger! Radiation becomes significant cooling mechanism
• Comparable to what limited convection still available (no coolant to provide h)

EMISSIVITY (ε):

Definition: Fraction of maximum thermal radiation emitted by a surface.
• ε = 0: Perfect reflector (no radiation emitted)
• ε = 1: Perfect radiator (maximum radiation emitted)
• 0 < ε < 1: Real surfaces

Emissivity depends on:
1. Material type
2. Surface finish (oxidation, corrosion)
3. Temperature (changes with T)
4. Wavelength of radiation (spectral emissivity)

For practical calculations: Use total hemispherical emissivity

EMISSIVITY VALUES AT HIGH TEMPERATURE:

Polished Metals (Poor Radiators):
• Polished copper: ε ≈ 0.05-0.10
• Polished aluminum: ε ≈ 0.05-0.08
• Polished stainless steel: ε ≈ 0.15-0.20
• Polished iron: ε ≈ 0.10-0.20

Oxidized/Rough Metals (Better Radiators):
• Oxidized steel (rusty): ε ≈ 0.80-0.90
• Oxidized stainless steel: ε ≈ 0.60-0.80
• Weathered iron: ε ≈ 0.70-0.90
• Painted metals: ε ≈ 0.85-0.95

Non-Metals (Good Radiators):
• Black paint/soot: ε ≈ 0.95-0.98
• Concrete/brick: ε ≈ 0.85-0.95
• Ceramics: ε ≈ 0.75-0.90

Key Observation:
Shiny polished metals radiate poorly (low ε)
Rough/oxidized surfaces radiate well (high ε)
Opposite of visible light reflection!

KIRCHHOFF'S LAW:
Good absorbers are also good emitters
ε_radiator = α_absorber

Surface that looks dark (absorbs visible light) also radiates well (high ε)
Surface that looks shiny (reflects visible light) also radiates poorly (low ε)

Practical Implication:
Cannot improve cooling by polishing surface (reduces ε)
Painted/oxidized surface actually radiates better for cooling

RADIATION IN POWER PLANT ACCIDENTS:

Normal Operation Radiation Negligible:
• Primary coolant ≈ 550°F
• Convection dominates (h from forced flow ≈ 1000-2000)
• Radiation ≈ 1000-2000 Btu/(hr·ft²)
• Convection ≈ millions Btu/(hr·ft²) (much larger)
• Radiation is < 1% of total cooling

Loss of Coolant Scenario:
• Fuel cladding temperature rises rapidly (no convective cooling)
• At 1800-2000°F, radiation becomes significant
• At 2200°F+, radiation becomes major cooling pathway
• Zirconium-water reaction also occurs (adds heat, accelerates problem)

Effectiveness of Radiation Cooling:
At 2000°F with bare core:
Q_rad ≈ 44,400 Btu/(hr·ft²) (ε ≈ 0.8 oxidized zirconium)
This looks large, but compared to decay heat production:
• Early LOCA: Decay heat ≈ 6-8% of full power
• Full power equivalent ≈ ~400 MW for large reactor
• 6% ≈ 24 MW = 82 million Btu/h
• Fuel surface area ≈ 60,000 ft² (rough estimate for large core)
• Required heat flux = 82 million / 60,000 ≈ 1,400 Btu/(hr·ft²)
• Radiation available ≈ 44,400 Btu/(hr·ft²)

Result: Radiation CAN remove decay heat if cladding reaches critical temperature
But it's inadequate until temperatures very high (dangerous to cladding)
Goal: Maintain liquid cooling (convection) to prevent radiation cooling scenario

notes.subject: TH07B
notes.title: SINGLE-PHASE VS. TWO-PHASE HEAT TRANSFER:
notes.content:
SINGLE-PHASE HEAT TRANSFER:

Definition: Heat transfer where neither fluid changes phase.
Both fluids remain as pure liquid or pure gas throughout heat exchanger.

Examples:
• Heating air through air heater (air → air)
• Heating oil through tube (oil → oil, both liquid)
• Cooling water with cold water (water → water, both liquid)
• Condensate cooling (liquid → liquid cooling water)
• Not phase change, just temperature change

Heat Transfer Equation:
Q̇ = ṁ × cp × ΔT

Where:
• Q̇ = heat transfer rate [Btu/h]
• ṁ = mass flow rate [lbm/h]
• cp = specific heat capacity [Btu/(lbm·°F)]
• ΔT = temperature change [°F]

Energy Balance:
Hot stream loses enthalpy:
Q̇_lost = ṁ_hot × cp_hot × (T_hot,in - T_hot,out)

Cold stream gains enthalpy:
Q̇_gained = ṁ_cold × cp_cold × (T_cold,out - T_cold,in)

At equilibrium: Q̇_lost = Q̇_gained

Three Heat Transfer Layers in Series:
1. Convection from hot fluid to tube: Q̇ = h_hot × A_hot × ΔT
2. Conduction through tube wall: Q̇ = k × A_mean × ΔT / L
3. Convection from tube to cold fluid: Q̇ = h_cold × A_cold × ΔT

Combined:
Q̇ = U_o × A_o × ΔT_mean

Where U_o encompasses all three resistances

Overall Heat Transfer Coefficient:
1/U_o = 1/(h_hot × A_ratio) + L/(k × A_mean) + 1/h_cold

TWO-PHASE HEAT TRANSFER:

Definition: Heat transfer where one fluid changes phase during the process.

Examples:
1. BOILER (Steam Generator):
   • Hot side: Combustion gas (single-phase)
   • Cold side: Water → Steam (two-phase)
   • Phase change: Liquid water vaporizes to steam

2. CONDENSER:
   • Hot side: Steam → Liquid water (two-phase)
   • Cold side: Cooling water (single-phase)
   • Phase change: Steam condenses to liquid

3. FEEDWATER HEATERS:
   • Hot side: Extracted steam → Liquid condensate (two-phase)
   • Cold side: Feedwater heating (single-phase or two-phase in some designs)
   • Phase change: Steam condenses

Energy Balance for Two-Phase:
Q̇ = ṁ × Δh

Where:
• Δh = enthalpy change including latent heat [Btu/lbm]
• Example: h_liquid to h_steam (includes latent heat of vaporization)

Comparison to Single-Phase:
Single-phase: Q̇ = ṁ × cp × ΔT (sensible heat only)
Two-phase: Q̇ = ṁ × Δh (includes latent heat, much larger!)

Example - Boiler Comparison:

Single-phase scenario (only if no phase change):
ṁ = 100 lbm/s, cp = 1.0 Btu/(lbm·°F)
If ΔT = 100°F (increase water temp by 100°F only)
Q̇ = 100 × 1 × 100 = 10,000 Btu/s = 14.2 MW

Two-phase scenario (actual boiler):
ṁ = 100 lbm/s, Δh = 1200 Btu/lbm (liquid to steam)
Q̇ = 100 × 1200 = 120,000 Btu/s = 170 MW

Difference: 12× larger heat transfer for same mass flow!
This demonstrates why latent heat dominates boiler/condenser duty

WHY TWO-PHASE HEAT TRANSFER MORE EFFICIENT:

Latent Heat Much Larger than Sensible Heat:
Heat of vaporization for water: Δh_fg ≈ 700-1000 Btu/lbm
Temperature rise for same energy: ΔT = Δh_fg / cp = 700-1000 Btu/lbm / 1 Btu/(lbm·°F) = 700-1000°F

This huge temperature would be impractical, so two-phase process better

Convection Coefficient During Phase Change:
h during boiling or condensation ≈ 1000-10,000 Btu/(hr·ft²·°F)
Compare to: h for single-phase convection ≈ 100-1000 Btu/(hr·ft²·°F)
Increase of 10-100×!

Reason: Phase change bubbles/droplets create intense mixing
Bubbles scrape off boundary layer constantly
Thin effective thermal layer
Very high effective h

Process Comparison:
Sensible heating:
• Boundary layer develops slowly
• Linear temperature increase
• Moderate h

Boiling (latent heating):
• Bubbles form continuously (intense mixing)
• Phase change converts energy efficiently
• Very high h
• Small ΔT sufficient for large heat transfer

THREE RESISTANCES IN SERIES (Two-Phase):

Path: Hot fluid → Tube → Cold phase-changing fluid

1. Hot Side Convection:
If combustion gas cooling: h ≈ 20-50 (poor)
If steam: h ≈ 1000+ (excellent)

2. Tube Conduction:
k × L / A (usually small compared to convection resistance)

3. Cold Side Phase Change:
If boiling: h ≈ 1000-10,000 (excellent)
If condensing: h ≈ 1000-5000 (excellent)

Result:
Phase-change side (boiling or condensation) usually NOT limiting
Single-phase side usually dominates resistance

Example - Boiler:
h_combustion_gas ≈ 30 (dominant resistance!)
k and thickness: small
h_boiling: 2000+ (not limiting)

Design strategy: Improve combustion gas-side convection

Example - Condenser:
h_steam_condensing ≈ 2000+ (excellent, not limiting)
k and thickness: small
h_cooling_water ≈ 1000-2000 (usually limiting)

Design strategy: Increase cooling water flow to improve h_cold

notes.subject: TH07B
notes.title: CORE THERMAL POWER CALCULATION AND HEAT BALANCE:
notes.content:
DEFINITION:
Core Thermal Power (CTP) is the rate of thermal energy released by fission reactions in the reactor core. Also called "reactor thermal power" or "core power."

Units: MW (thermal), Btu/h, or fraction of rated power (%)

MEASUREMENT METHODS:

Method 1: PRIMARY SIDE HEAT BALANCE (RCS Heat Balance)
Heat removed from core by circulating coolant:

Q̇_primary = ṁ_RCS × cp × (T_h - T_c)

Where:
• ṁ_RCS = reactor coolant mass flow rate [lbm/s]
• cp = specific heat of primary coolant [Btu/(lbm·°F)] ≈ 1.0-1.1
• T_h = hot leg temperature (exiting core) [°F]
• T_c = cold leg temperature (entering core) [°F]
• Q̇_primary = thermal power [Btu/h]

Physical Meaning:
Coolant circulates through core
Absorbs heat equal to: mass flow × specific heat × temperature rise
All heat generated by fission absorbed by coolant
CTP = heat absorbed by primary coolant

Calculation:
Example:
• RCS flow: 150,000 lbm/h
• cp = 1.0 Btu/(lbm·°F)
• T_h = 600°F, T_c = 550°F (ΔT = 50°F)
• Q̇ = 150,000 × 1.0 × 50 = 7,500,000 Btu/h = 2,195 kW ≈ 2.2 MW (thermal)

Method 2: SECONDARY SIDE HEAT BALANCE (Boiler Side)
Heat transferred from primary to secondary through steam generator:

Q̇_secondary = ṁ_steam × (h_out - h_in)

Where:
• ṁ_steam = steam mass flow rate [lbm/s]
• h_out = steam outlet enthalpy [Btu/lbm] (from steam tables)
• h_in = feedwater inlet enthalpy [Btu/lbm] (from steam tables)
• Q̇_secondary = thermal power transferred to secondary [Btu/h]

Physical Meaning:
All heat from core transferred through steam generator
Secondary side receives enthalpy increase equal to: mass flow × enthalpy rise
At steady state: Q̇_primary ≈ Q̇_secondary

Calculation:
Example:
• Steam flow: 500 lbm/s = 1,800,000 lbm/h
• Inlet feedwater: 300°F, 2050 psia (h_in = 276 Btu/lbm)
• Outlet steam: 500 psia, 500°F (h_out = 1469 Btu/lbm)
• Q̇ = 1,800,000 × (1469 - 276) = 1,800,000 × 1193 = 2,147,000,000 Btu/h ≈ 2,147 MW (thermal)

COMPARISON AND DISCREPANCY ANALYSIS:

Ideal Case:
Q̇_primary = Q̇_secondary (perfect energy balance)

Reality:
Small differences due to:
• Pressurizer heater/cooler (maintains pressure, adds or removes small amount)
• RCP motor heat (motor driving pump adds small amount to fluid)
• Heat loss through insulation (very small, usually negligible)
• Measurement errors (instrumentation uncertainty)
• Blowdown from secondary (small amount of steam released)

Calculation:
Q̇_net = Q̇_primary - Q̇_secondary - Q̇_losses

If Q̇_net ≈ 0: System balanced
If Q̇_primary > Q̇_secondary: Energy unaccounted for (check losses)
If Q̇_secondary > Q̇_primary: Indicates measurement error or feedback effect

NUCLEAR INSTRUMENTATION:

Power Indication:
% Reactor Power = (Actual CTP) / (Rated CTP) × 100%

Example:
• Rated power: 3000 MW (thermal)
• Measured CTP: 2100 MW
• % Power = 2100 / 3000 × 100% = 70%

Advantages of Instrumentation:
• Direct measurement (not calculated)
• Fast response (doesn't require waiting for thermal equilibrium)
• Continuous during power changes

Disadvantages:
• Requires accurate calibration
• Sensor locations affect measurement
• Power distribution shape affects accuracy
• Must account for instrument drift

Comparison:
Instrumentation: Measures neutron flux (indicator of power) → fast but requires calibration
Heat balance: Calculates from temperatures → slower but independent verification

Typical Use:
During steady state: Both methods should agree
During power changes: Instruments respond faster, heat balance lags
Verify actual core power: Use heat balance to calibrate instruments
notes.section: CORE THERMAL POWER CALCULATION AND HEAT BALANCE:

notes.subject: TH07B
notes.title: STEAM GENERATOR TUBE PLUGGING AND TEMPERATURE EFFECTS:
notes.content:
SCENARIO:
Some steam generator tubes have been plugged (isolated from service) due to corrosion/cracking.
Effect on system performance when power held constant.

GIVEN CONDITION:
• Original condition: 100% of tubes operational
• New condition: 2% of tubes plugged (cannot carry flow)
• Core power: HELD CONSTANT at same MW thermal

EFFECT ON U_o (Overall Heat Transfer Coefficient):
• Plugged tubes add thermal resistance? NO
• But remaining tubes have better flow distribution?
• Actually, U_o essentially unchanged (still 98% of original tubes active)
• More importantly: Total surface area (A) decreased by 2%

EQUATION ANALYSIS:
Q̇ = U_o × A × ΔT_mean

Same Q̇ (constant power)
A reduced by 2% (98% of original area)
U_o approximately unchanged (per unit area, quality of heat transfer similar)

Rearranging:
ΔT_mean = Q̇ / (U_o × A)
ΔT_mean_new / ΔT_mean_original = A_original / A_new = 1.00 / 0.98 ≈ 1.02

Temperature difference must increase 2% to maintain same heat transfer with 2% less area!

CALCULATION EXAMPLE:

Original Condition:
• Primary coolant: T_h = 600°F (hot leg), T_c = 550°F, ΔT_primary = 50°F
• Secondary: T_steam = 532°F, T_feedwater = 475°F, ΔT_secondary ≈ 57°F
• Average loop T: T_avg = (600 + 550) / 2 = 575°F
• Secondary steam generation: T_sat = 532°F @ system pressure
• Condenser temp: T_cond = 100°F
• T_avg_overall = (575 + 100) / 2 = 337.5°F (average of primary and condenser)

With 2% Plugging:
Required ΔT increased 2% to maintain same Q̇
New ΔT_primary = 50°F × 1.02 = 51°F

New temperatures (maintaining same core outlet T_h strategy):
If keeping power = flow × cp × ΔT
Same flow, same cp, slight increase in ΔT possible by:
• Increasing T_h (hotter outlet) by 1°F
• OR decreasing T_c (colder inlet) by 1°F
• OR combination

Typical operator action (maintaining thermal margin):
• Increase pressurizer temperature setpoint by 1-2°F
• This raises average primary temperature
• T_h increases, power maintained with slightly higher temp

Result:
New T_h = 601°F (1°F increase)
New T_c = 550°F (unchanged)
New ΔT = 51°F (2% increase)

Secondary Side Effect:
Steam generator now operates at:
• Same heat input (power held constant)
• Larger required temperature difference
• Higher primary inlet temperature (551°F for example)

New secondary:
• Inlet feedwater still ~475°F
• Steam outlet: Adjusts to satisfy heat balance
• T_sat_new might be 533°F (slight pressure increase due to higher T_h pushing more energy)

Average coolant temperature:
Original: T_avg = 575°F
New: T_avg = 575.5°F (slightly higher)

Plant Status:
• Power still constant (same MW thermal)
• Average temperature increased slightly
• System still operating normally
• Thermal margin to limits slightly reduced

LONG-TERM IMPLICATIONS:

Continued Tube Degradation:
More tubes plug over time
Every 2% reduction requires ΔT increase to maintain power
Eventually run out of margin:
• Reach maximum allowable pressurizer temperature
• Reach maximum allowable hot leg temperature
• Reach power uprate limit
• Plant cannot maintain power without exceeding limits

Action Required:
Before reaching limits: Perform steam generator maintenance
Options:
• Clean/inspect tubes (remove deposits)
• Plug additional degraded tubes
• Replace steam generator (major outage)
• Request power uprate reduction to lower average temperature

Efficiency Effect:
• Slight temperature increase (1-2°F) negligible for efficiency
• But demonstrates that tube degradation has real plant impact
• Cost: Lower effective heat transfer area → reduced plant output over time

THIS EXAMPLE SHOWS:
• How heat transfer coefficients and areas fundamentally limit power output
• Why steam generator condition critical to plant performance
• Interdependence of primary/secondary systems through heat transfer
• Real-time operating impacts of equipment degradation
notes.section: STEAM GENERATOR TUBE PLUGGING AND TEMPERATURE EFFECTS:

flashcards.subject: CP01
flashcards.front: What is the primary purpose of piping systems?
flashcards.back: Transport fluids/fluid-solid mixtures between equipment. Key factors: temperature, pressure, flow rate, shock loads.

flashcards.subject: CP01
flashcards.front: What five design factors affect pipe material selection?
flashcards.back: Temperature, pressure, flow rate/velocity, shock loads (water/steam hammer, thermal shock), directional changes.

flashcards.subject: CP01
flashcards.front: Which piping material is economical but prone to rust and corrosion?
flashcards.back: Low-carbon steel.

flashcards.subject: CP01
flashcards.front: What material is best for high-temperature and high-pressure applications?
flashcards.back: Nickel alloys (high-cost) or low-alloy steel.

flashcards.subject: CP01
flashcards.front: What are the three types of pipe support systems?
flashcards.back: Rigid restraints (fixed), spring hangers (allow thermal movement), snubbers (limit seismic motion).

flashcards.subject: CP01
flashcards.front: How do piping systems accommodate thermal expansion?
flashcards.back: Thermal loops/bends or expansion joints allow controlled linear expansion.

flashcards.subject: CP01
flashcards.front: What are the five principal valve functions?
flashcards.back: Start/stop flow, throttle flow, control direction, regulate pressure, relieve pressure.

flashcards.subject: CP01
flashcards.front: What type of valve is used to start or stop complete fluid flow?
flashcards.back: Gate valves, ball valves, or plug valves.

flashcards.subject: CP01
flashcards.front: What type of valve controls flow rate without completely stopping flow?
flashcards.back: Globe valves or needle valves.

flashcards.subject: CP01
flashcards.front: Name three basic valve construction components.
flashcards.back: Body (flow path/seats), bonnet (sealing section), disk (opens/closes/throttles).

flashcards.subject: CP01
flashcards.front: What is the purpose of the backseat in a valve?
flashcards.back: Allows packing adjustment without depressurizing system.

flashcards.subject: CP01
flashcards.front: What is the difference between rising-stem and non-rising stem valves?
flashcards.back: Rising-stem: moves upward (visual indicator). Non-rising: position not visually obvious.

flashcards.subject: CP01
flashcards.front: What is pressure defined as?
flashcards.back: Pressure = Force / Area (P = F/A). Units: psi, Pa, bar, atm.

flashcards.subject: CP01
flashcards.front: What is normal atmospheric pressure in psia and kPa?

flashcards.subject: CP01
flashcards.front: What is hydrostatic pressure?
flashcards.back: Pressure from fluid column weight above reference point (P = ρ × g × h).

flashcards.subject: CP01
flashcards.front: What is absolute pressure used for?
flashcards.back: Thermodynamic calculations; measured from perfect vacuum. Example: 10 psig = 24.7 psia.

flashcards.subject: CP01
flashcards.front: What is gage pressure (PSIG)?
flashcards.back: Pressure above atmospheric (Pgage = Pabs - Patm). Common gauge reading.

flashcards.subject: CP01
flashcards.front: What is differential pressure (PSID)?
flashcards.back: Difference between two locations. Used for: filter drop, valve throttling, level measurement.

flashcards.subject: CP01
flashcards.front: What does Pascal's Law state?
flashcards.back: Pressure in confined fluid transmits undiminished in all directions (F1/A1 = F2/A2).

flashcards.subject: CP01
flashcards.front: What is thermal binding in valves?
flashcards.back: Body cools faster than disk → differential contraction binds seat to disk → valve may not reopen.

flashcards.subject: CP01
flashcards.front: How can thermal binding be prevented?
flashcards.back: Crack valve open/re-shut during cooldown. Use proper closing torque. Allow gradual cooling.

flashcards.subject: CP01
flashcards.front: What is pressure locking in valves?
flashcards.back: Liquid trapped in bonnet pressurizes when heated → prevents valve opening (high-temp systems).

flashcards.subject: CP01
flashcards.front: How is pressure locking prevented?
flashcards.back: Provide relief or vent path on bonnet to equalize pressure buildup.

flashcards.subject: CP01
flashcards.front: Should a wrench ever be used on a valve handwheel for extra leverage?
flashcards.back: No. Can overstress actuator gearing/casing → catastrophic failure.

flashcards.subject: CP01
flashcards.front: What does reaching hard stop on a handwheel confirm?
flashcards.back: Nothing. Must verify full travel by counting designed turns; position limit switch is unreliable.

flashcards.subject: TH01
flashcards.front: What are the units for force and mass in American Engineering System?
flashcards.back: Force: lbf (pounds force), Mass: lbm (pounds mass).

flashcards.subject: TH01
flashcards.front: What temperature scale is used in American Engineering System?
flashcards.back: Fahrenheit (°F).

flashcards.subject: TH01
flashcards.front: What is the conversion factor for work in American system?
flashcards.back: Btu = (lbf × ft) / 778.

flashcards.subject: TH01
flashcards.front: What are the main units in SI/Metric System?
flashcards.back: Force: N, Mass: kg, Temperature: °C or K, Pressure: Pa/kPa/bar.

flashcards.subject: TH01
flashcards.front: What is the freezing point of water in °F and °C?

flashcards.subject: TH01
flashcards.front: What is the boiling point of water in °F and °C?

flashcards.subject: TH01
flashcards.front: What is the formula to convert Fahrenheit to Celsius?

flashcards.subject: TH01
flashcards.front: What is Absolute Zero in Rankine and Kelvin?

flashcards.subject: TH01
flashcards.front: What is the formula to convert Fahrenheit to Rankine?

flashcards.subject: TH01
flashcards.front: What is the formula to convert Celsius to Kelvin?

flashcards.subject: TH01
flashcards.front: Why are absolute temperature scales required in thermodynamics?
flashcards.back: All thermodynamic equations require absolute temperature; relative scales produce wrong results.

flashcards.subject: TH01
flashcards.front: What is a system in thermodynamics?
flashcards.back: A quantity of matter or space separated from surroundings by a boundary.

flashcards.subject: TH01
flashcards.front: What is an isolated system?
flashcards.back: No mass transfer, no energy transfer. Theoretical ideal only.

flashcards.subject: TH01
flashcards.front: What is a closed system?
flashcards.back: No mass transfer. Energy transfer (heat/work) allowed. Most common for analysis.

flashcards.subject: TH01
flashcards.front: What is an open system (control volume)?
flashcards.back: Mass transfer across boundary (inlet/outlet flows). Energy transfer allowed.

flashcards.subject: TH02
flashcards.front: What is the First Law of Thermodynamics?
flashcards.back: Energy conserved: E_in - E_out = ΔE_system.

flashcards.subject: TH02
flashcards.front: What is the six-step energy conversion in power systems?
flashcards.back: Heat input → Fluid heating → Turbine work → Generator electricity → Condenser cooling → Pump pressure increase.

flashcards.subject: TH02
flashcards.front: What is the energy balance for power systems?
flashcards.back: Heat in from source = Electrical power out + Heat rejected.

flashcards.subject: TH02
flashcards.front: What is stored energy in a system?
flashcards.back: Potential Energy, Kinetic Energy, Internal Energy, Flow Energy.

flashcards.subject: TH02
flashcards.front: What is transient energy?
flashcards.back: Energy in transit: Heat (temp difference) and Work (force).

flashcards.subject: TH02
flashcards.front: What are sign conventions for heat and work?
flashcards.back: Q added: positive, Q removed: negative. W by system: positive, W on system: negative.

flashcards.subject: TH02
flashcards.front: What is potential energy?
flashcards.back: Energy from position. PE = m × z × g / gc.

flashcards.subject: TH02
flashcards.front: What is kinetic energy?
flashcards.back: Energy from velocity. KE = m × v² / (2 × gc).

flashcards.subject: TH02
flashcards.front: What is internal energy (U)?
flashcards.back: Sum of all microscopic energy in substance. Changes with temperature/pressure.

flashcards.subject: TH02
flashcards.front: What is flow energy (PV energy)?
flashcards.back: Energy from pressure × volume. Specific: P × v. Work to push fluid in/out.

flashcards.subject: TH02
flashcards.front: What is enthalpy (H)?
flashcards.back: H = U + PV. Total energy content of fluid.

flashcards.subject: TH02
flashcards.front: What is specific enthalpy (h)?
flashcards.back: h = u + Pv. Energy per unit mass (Btu/lbm). Used in all cycle calculations.

flashcards.subject: TH02
flashcards.front: How is enthalpy used in turbine calculations?
flashcards.back: Work = h_in - h_out. (Enthalpy drop).

flashcards.subject: TH02
flashcards.front: How is enthalpy used in pump calculations?
flashcards.back: Work = h_out - h_in. (Enthalpy rise).

flashcards.subject: TH02
flashcards.front: What is heat (Q)?
flashcards.back: Transient energy due to temperature difference. Flows hot → cold. Not a property.

flashcards.subject: TH03
flashcards.front: How is the state of a substance defined?
flashcards.back: By two independent intensive properties. Know any two → determine all others.

flashcards.subject: TH03
flashcards.front: What are the four phases of matter?
flashcards.back: Solid (fixed shape/volume), Liquid (fixed volume, container shape), Vapor/Gas (no fixed shape/volume), Plasma (ionized).

flashcards.subject: TH03
flashcards.front: What is melting and vaporization?
flashcards.back: Melting: Solid → Liquid (absorbs heat). Vaporization: Liquid → Gas (absorbs heat).

flashcards.subject: TH03
flashcards.front: What is condensation and solidification?
flashcards.back: Condensation: Gas → Liquid (rejects heat). Solidification: Liquid → Solid (rejects heat).

flashcards.subject: TH03
flashcards.front: What are the three boundary lines on phase diagram?
flashcards.back: Fusion (Solid-Liquid), Vaporization (Liquid-Gas), Sublimation (Solid-Gas).

flashcards.subject: TH03
flashcards.front: What is the triple point on phase diagram?
flashcards.back: Point where all three phases coexist in equilibrium.

flashcards.subject: TH03
flashcards.front: What are the five states of water?
flashcards.back: Subcooled liquid, Saturated liquid, Wet vapor (mixture), Saturated vapor, Superheated vapor.

flashcards.subject: TH03
flashcards.front: What is subcooled liquid?
flashcards.back: Below saturation temp. Resistant to vaporization. Nearly incompressible.

flashcards.subject: TH03
flashcards.front: What is saturated liquid and saturated vapor?
flashcards.back: Saturated liquid: at saturation temp, about to boil. Saturated vapor: 100% vapor, last drop evaporated.

flashcards.subject: TH03
flashcards.front: What is wet vapor?
flashcards.back: Mixture of liquid + vapor at same temperature.

flashcards.subject: TH03
flashcards.front: What is sensible heat?
flashcards.back: Heat that changes temperature without phase change.

flashcards.subject: TH03
flashcards.front: What is latent heat?
flashcards.back: Heat that causes phase change at constant temperature.

flashcards.subject: TH03
flashcards.front: What is latent heat of vaporization (Hfg)?
flashcards.back: Energy to convert saturated liquid → saturated vapor. Released on condensation.

flashcards.subject: TH03
flashcards.front: What is steam quality (X)?
flashcards.back: Fraction of vapor in wet mixture. Range: 0 (all liquid) to 1.0 (all vapor).

flashcards.subject: TH03
flashcards.front: What quality steam is required at turbine inlet and why?
flashcards.back: High quality (>95-99%) to prevent blade erosion and corrosion.

flashcards.subject: TH04
flashcards.front: What is an adiabatic process?
flashcards.back: No heat transfer (Q = 0). Boundary insulated. Common in turbines/pumps.

flashcards.subject: TH04
flashcards.front: What is an isobaric process?
flashcards.back: Constant pressure. Heat added/removed at constant pressure. Boiler, condenser.

flashcards.subject: TH04
flashcards.front: What is an isentropic process?
flashcards.back: No entropy change. Reversible adiabatic. Theoretical ideal for efficiency benchmarks.

flashcards.subject: TH04
flashcards.front: What is isenthalpic process (throttling)?
flashcards.back: No enthalpy change. Occurs in valve/orifice. Pressure drops, entropy increases.

flashcards.subject: TH04
flashcards.front: What is an isothermal process?
flashcards.back: Constant temperature. System in thermal equilibrium.

flashcards.subject: TH04
flashcards.front: What are the three requirements for steady-flow?
flashcards.back: Constant mass flow (m_in = m_out). Constant properties at each point. Constant heat/work rates.

flashcards.subject: TH04
flashcards.front: What is the mechanical equivalent of heat?
flashcards.back: 1 Btu = 778 ft-lbf = 1055 Joules.

flashcards.subject: TH04
flashcards.front: What does Second Law of Thermodynamics state?
flashcards.back: No engine converts all heat to work. Heat rejection required. Max efficiency depends only on temps.

flashcards.subject: TH04
flashcards.front: What is Carnot efficiency formula?
flashcards.back: η = (T_hot - T_cold) / T_hot = 1 - (T_cold / T_hot).

flashcards.subject: TH04
flashcards.front: What is entropy change formula?
flashcards.back: ΔS = Q / T (Btu/lbm-R). More heat at low temp = larger entropy change.

flashcards.subject: TH04
flashcards.front: What is the energy equation for turbines?
flashcards.back: W = h_in - h_out. (Enthalpy drop = work output).

flashcards.subject: TH04
flashcards.front: What is the energy equation for pumps?
flashcards.back: W = h_out - h_in. (Work input = enthalpy rise).

flashcards.subject: TH04
flashcards.front: What does a boiler (steam generator) do?
flashcards.back: Raises feedwater enthalpy to produce steam. Isobaric heat addition.

flashcards.subject: TH04
flashcards.front: What does a condenser do?
flashcards.back: Removes latent heat. Collapses steam. Maintains vacuum. Improves turbine efficiency.

flashcards.subject: TH04
flashcards.front: Why is condensate subcooling important?
flashcards.back: Prevents pump cavitation. Optimal: 10-20°F below saturation.

flashcards.subject: TH04
flashcards.front: What is nozzle function?
flashcards.back: Converts pressure/enthalpy → velocity/kinetic energy through shaped passages.

flashcards.subject: TH04
flashcards.front: What are convergent and divergent nozzles?
flashcards.back: Convergent: area ↓, velocity ↑, pressure ↓. Divergent: area ↑, velocity ↓, pressure ↑.

flashcards.subject: TH04
flashcards.front: What is turbine efficiency?
flashcards.back: Ratio of actual work to ideal work. Typically 80-90%.

flashcards.subject: TH04
flashcards.front: What is pump efficiency?
flashcards.back: Ratio of ideal work to actual work (opposite of turbine). Typically 75-85%.

flashcards.subject: TH04
flashcards.front: What is net cycle work?
flashcards.back: W_net = W_turbine - W_pump. Pump work only 1-5% of turbine work.

flashcards.subject: TH05
flashcards.front: What are the five essential elements of a thermodynamic cycle?
flashcards.back: 1) Working fluid (steam or gas), 2) Engine (turbine or piston) to convert heat to work, 3) Heat source (reactor/boiler), 4) Heat sink (condenser/cooling), 5) Device to move fluid (pump/compressor).

flashcards.subject: TH05
flashcards.front: What is the difference between a thermodynamic process and a thermodynamic cycle?
flashcards.back: A process is a change of state in one direction. A cycle is a series of processes that returns the working fluid to its initial state, forming a closed loop used for continuous energy conversion.

flashcards.subject: TH05
flashcards.front: How is thermodynamic cycle efficiency defined?
flashcards.back: Cycle efficiency (η) = Net work produced / Heat supplied = (Q_added - Q_rejected) / Q_added. Expressed as a percentage, it represents the portion of heat energy converted to useful work.

flashcards.subject: TH05
flashcards.front: Describe the Carnot cycle and why it matters to power plant design.
flashcards.back: The Carnot cycle is an ideal cycle with the highest possible thermal efficiency for an engine operating between two constant temperature reservoirs. It consists of two isothermal processes and two adiabatic processes. The Carnot efficiency sets the theoretical maximum that real cycles can approach but never reach.

flashcards.subject: TH05
flashcards.front: Calculate the Carnot efficiency when a heat engine receives heat at 540°F and rejects heat at 60°F.
flashcards.back: Convert to absolute temperature (Rankine): T_hot = 540 + 460 = 1000°R, T_cold = 60 + 460 = 520°R. η = (T_hot - T_cold) / T_hot = (1000 - 520) / 1000 = 480 / 1000 = 48.0%.

flashcards.subject: TH05
flashcards.front: How does the Second Law of Thermodynamics impact power plant design and operation?
flashcards.back: The Second Law requires that some heat must be rejected for any cycle to operate. Real processes are irreversible and generate entropy. Power plant designers must increase the temperature difference between heat source and sink to improve efficiency, and operators focus on minimizing losses through maintenance and proper operation.

flashcards.subject: TH05
flashcards.front: What are the key differences between the Rankine cycle and the Carnot cycle?
flashcards.back: Rankine is more practical: it uses constant-pressure (isobaric) heat transfer at phase boundaries instead of Carnot's constant-temperature processes. Rankine can be easily analyzed using steam tables. Rankine efficiency is lower than Carnot but achievable in actual power plants.

flashcards.subject: TH05
flashcards.front: Define condensate depression with a numerical example.
flashcards.back: Condensate depression = Saturation temperature at condenser pressure - Hotwell temperature. Example: At 1 psia absolute (saturation temp ≈ 102°F), if hotwell temperature is 96°F, then condensate depression = 102°F - 96°F = 6°F (six degrees of depression).

flashcards.subject: TH05
flashcards.front: List five operational methods to maintain unit efficiency.
flashcards.back: 1) Minimize auxiliary equipment operation to only those necessary for current power output, 2) Minimize steam generator blowdown, 3) Fix steam leaks immediately, 4) Eliminate air leaks into the condenser, 5) Operate air ejector, gland seal, and blowdown heat exchangers to maximize heat recovery.

flashcards.subject: TH05
flashcards.front: How do operators monitor and assess plant efficiency?
flashcards.back: Operators compare electrical generator output (proportional to turbine work) to reactor power output (proportional to heat supplied). Lower-than-expected electrical output for a given reactor power indicates secondary system inefficiency requiring investigation and maintenance.

flashcards.subject: TH06B
flashcards.front: What is mass flow rate and its formula?
flashcards.back: ṁ = ρ × V̇ = ρ × v × A (lbm/hr). ρ = density, v = velocity, A = area.

flashcards.subject: TH06B
flashcards.front: What is volumetric flow rate and common units?
flashcards.back: Q = v × A. Units: gpm (gallons per minute) or cfm (cubic feet per minute).

flashcards.subject: TH06B
flashcards.front: What is continuity equation?
flashcards.back: Mass in = Mass out. ṁ₁ = ṁ₂.

flashcards.subject: TH06B
flashcards.front: What is viscosity and how does temperature affect it?
flashcards.back: Fluid's resistance to flow. Liquids: viscosity ↓ with temp. Gases: viscosity ↑ with temp.

flashcards.subject: TH06B
flashcards.front: What is specific gravity (SG)?
flashcards.back: Density ratio vs water @ 60°F. Water = 1.0. SG < 1 floats, SG > 1 sinks.

flashcards.subject: TH06B
flashcards.front: What is fluid density and typical value for water?
flashcards.back: Mass per unit volume. Water ≈ 62.4 lbm/ft³ (standard). Changes with temp/pressure.

flashcards.subject: TH06B
flashcards.front: What is laminar flow?
flashcards.back: Re < 2,000. Smooth layers, minimal mixing. Parabolic velocity profile.

flashcards.subject: TH06B
flashcards.front: What is turbulent flow?
flashcards.back: Re > 3,500. Cross-currents, mixing. Flattened velocity profile. Requires more energy.

flashcards.subject: TH06B
flashcards.front: What is transitional flow?
flashcards.back: Re = 2,000-3,500. Unstable. Alternates between laminar and turbulent.

flashcards.subject: TH06B
flashcards.front: What is Reynolds number and its formula?
flashcards.back: NRe = (ρ × v × d) / μ (dimensionless). Determines flow regime.

flashcards.subject: TH06B
flashcards.front: What is single-phase flow?
flashcards.back: Fluid either liquid OR gas, not mixed. Easier to analyze and predict.

flashcards.subject: TH06B
flashcards.front: What is two-phase flow?
flashcards.back: Liquid AND vapor mixture. Greater resistance. Head loss increases 100×+.

flashcards.subject: TH06B
flashcards.front: What is elevation head (z)?
flashcards.back: Potential energy in Bernoulli. Height above reference. Path-independent.

flashcards.subject: TH06B
flashcards.front: What is velocity head?
flashcards.back: Kinetic energy in Bernoulli. v²/(2gc). Height if KE converted to PE.

flashcards.subject: TH06B
flashcards.front: What is pressure head (Pv)?
flashcards.back: Pressure-volume energy. Height of column weighing = fluid pressure.

flashcards.subject: TH06B
flashcards.front: What is total head?
flashcards.back: Elevation + velocity + pressure heads. Constant in ideal flow.

flashcards.subject: TH06B
flashcards.front: What is friction head loss (Hf)?
flashcards.back: Pressure/velocity → heat through friction. Expressed in feet of head.

flashcards.subject: TH06B
flashcards.front: What is friction factor (f)?
flashcards.back: Dimensionless Darcy constant. Accounts for pipe roughness. Depends on Re.

flashcards.subject: TH06B
flashcards.front: What is cavitation?
flashcards.back: Vapor bubbles when pressure < saturation pressure. Damages pump impellers.

flashcards.subject: TH06B
flashcards.front: What is choked flow?
flashcards.back: Compressible flow (steam) reaches Mach 1. Limits mass flow. Pout/Pin ≈ 0.5.

flashcards.subject: TH06B
flashcards.front: What is water hammer?
flashcards.back: Sudden flow change → pressure surges. Can spike to 20× normal. Pipe damage, injury risk.

flashcards.subject: TH06B
flashcards.front: What is pump head (Hp)?
flashcards.back: Energy added by pump. Wp = ṁ × Hp × gc/g.

flashcards.subject: TH06B
flashcards.front: What is continuity for variable pipe diameter?
flashcards.back: v₁ × A₁ = v₂ × A₂. Smaller diameter = higher velocity.

flashcards.subject: TH06B
flashcards.front: How does velocity change with pipe diameter?
flashcards.back: Diameter ↑ → velocity ↓. Diameter ↓ → velocity ↑. Proportional.

flashcards.subject: TH06B
flashcards.front: What is Bernoulli's equation?
flashcards.back: z₁ + v₁²/(2gc) + Pv₁ = z₂ + v₂²/(2gc) + Pv₂. Total head constant.

flashcards.subject: TH07B
flashcards.front: What are the three basic modes of heat transfer?
flashcards.back: Conduction (molecular), Convection (fluid motion), Radiation (EM waves).

flashcards.subject: TH07B
flashcards.front: Which heat transfer modes dominate in PWR plants?
flashcards.back: Conduction and convection. Radiation negligible normal op, significant in accidents.

flashcards.subject: TH07B
flashcards.front: What is specific heat capacity (cp) and its formula?
flashcards.back: Heat to raise unit mass one degree. Q = m × cp × ΔT. 1 Btu raises 1 lbm water by 1°F.

flashcards.subject: TH07B
flashcards.front: What is conduction equation and what affects it?
flashcards.back: Q = kAΔT / x. Higher k or A increases rate. Higher x decreases rate. Metals good, gases/ceramics poor.

flashcards.subject: TH07B
flashcards.front: Which materials have high thermal conductivity (k)?
flashcards.back: Copper (133.0), Iron (39.0), 90-10 CuNi (23) Btu/hr-ft-°F. Metals conduct well.

flashcards.subject: TH07B
flashcards.front: Which materials have low thermal conductivity?
flashcards.back: Air (0.0145), Rock Wool (0.03), Concrete (0.2-0.7) Btu/hr-ft-°F. Gases/insulation poor.

flashcards.subject: TH07B
flashcards.front: What is convection?
flashcards.back: Heat transfer between fluid and surface via circulation/mixing. Boundary layer = thin film at surface.

flashcards.subject: TH07B
flashcards.front: What is natural vs forced convection?
flashcards.back: Natural: density-driven. Forced: pump-driven (more efficient). Plants use forced convection.

flashcards.subject: TH07B
flashcards.front: What is boundary layer and what affects it?
flashcards.back: Thin stagnant film at surface. Affected by: temperature ↑ thins layer, flow ↑ thins layer, roughness.

flashcards.subject: TH07B
flashcards.front: What is heat transfer coefficient (hf)?
flashcards.back: hf = kf / xf (boundary layer conductivity / thickness). Higher hf = better heat transfer.

flashcards.subject: TH07B
flashcards.front: What are the three layers in heat exchanger transfer?
flashcards.back: Hot fluid convection → tube wall conduction → cold fluid convection. All in series.

flashcards.subject: TH07B
flashcards.front: What does overall heat transfer coefficient (Uo) represent?
flashcards.back: Uo = 1 / total resistance. Q = Uo × Ao × ΔTo.

flashcards.subject: TH07B
flashcards.front: How does fouling affect heat transfer coefficient?
flashcards.back: Adds extra resistance layer. 2 mil scale can drop Uo ~30%. Monitor to detect degradation.

flashcards.subject: TH07B
flashcards.front: What is radiation heat transfer?
flashcards.back: Transfers heat via EM waves (no medium). Stefan-Boltzmann: Q = σ × A × ε × T⁴.

flashcards.subject: TH07B
flashcards.front: Why is radiation negligible in normal PWR operation?
flashcards.back: Requires very high temp difference (T⁴ term). Critical in accidents only.

flashcards.subject: TH07B
flashcards.front: What is single-phase heat transfer?
flashcards.back: Both fluids remain liquid OR gas (not mixed). Equation: Q = m × cp × ΔT.

flashcards.subject: TH07B
flashcards.front: What is two-phase heat transfer?
flashcards.back: One fluid changes phase (condenser, steam generator). Equation: Q = m × Δh.

flashcards.subject: TH07B
flashcards.front: What does CTP represent?
flashcards.back: Core Thermal Power. Heat input rate from core to Reactor Coolant System.

flashcards.subject: TH07B
flashcards.front: What are the two methods to calculate CTP?
flashcards.back: RCS heat balance: Q = m × cp × ΔT. Secondary heat balance: Q = m × Δh (steam - feedwater).

flashcards.subject: TH07B
flashcards.front: What is condensate depression and optimal range?
flashcards.back: Tsat - Tcondensate. Prevents pump cavitation. Optimal: 10-20°F below saturation.

flashcards.subject: CP04
flashcards.front: What is the fundamental function of a pump?
flashcards.back: Move fluid volume at specific pressure between levels while overcoming flow resistance.

flashcards.subject: CP04
flashcards.front: What are the two main pump categories?
flashcards.back: Kinetic (dynamic) and Positive displacement.

flashcards.subject: CP04
flashcards.front: How do Kinetic pumps operate?
flashcards.back: Convert mechanical energy → kinetic energy (velocity) → pressure energy.

flashcards.subject: CP04
flashcards.front: How do Positive displacement pumps operate?
flashcards.back: Trap fixed fluid volume and force it repeatedly into discharge line.

flashcards.subject: CP04
flashcards.front: What pump type is best for large volumes at moderate/low pressures?
flashcards.back: Centrifugal (kinetic) pumps. Most common in plants.

flashcards.subject: CP04
flashcards.front: What types are positive displacement pumps?
flashcards.back: Gear, screw, piston, diaphragm pumps.

flashcards.subject: CP04
flashcards.front: When are positive displacement pumps preferred?
flashcards.back: Small volumes at high pressures, or viscous fluids.

flashcards.subject: CP04
flashcards.front: What is pump capacity?
flashcards.back: Amount of fluid moved. Units: gpm (gallons/min) or cfs (cubic feet/sec).

flashcards.subject: CP04
flashcards.front: What is static head?
flashcards.back: Difference in fluid levels (elevation head). Stated in feet of water column.

flashcards.subject: CP04
flashcards.front: What does static head represent?
flashcards.back: Pressure energy to lift fluid vertically against gravity (no friction/flow).

flashcards.subject: CP04
flashcards.front: What is dynamic head?
flashcards.back: Energy to set fluid in motion and overcome resistance (velocity + friction heads).

flashcards.subject: CP04
flashcards.front: What is total head?
flashcards.back: Static head + Dynamic head for given condition.

flashcards.subject: CP04
flashcards.front: What is total suction head (Hs)?
flashcards.back: Pressure available at pump suction. Expressed in feet of water column.

flashcards.subject: CP04
flashcards.front: What is positive suction head?
flashcards.back: Suction source fluid level above pump centerline.

flashcards.subject: CP04
flashcards.front: What is suction lift?
flashcards.back: Negative suction head. Suction source below pump centerline. Pump must "lift" fluid.

flashcards.subject: CP04
flashcards.front: What is total discharge head (Ht)?
flashcards.back: Static discharge head + dynamic head downstream of pump.

flashcards.subject: CP04
flashcards.front: What is total head also called?
flashcards.back: Total developed head (TDH). Pressure rise pump must produce.

flashcards.subject: CP04
flashcards.front: What is Net Positive Suction Head (NPSH)?
flashcards.back: Absolute suction pressure minus fluid saturation vapor pressure.

flashcards.subject: CP04
flashcards.front: What happens when NPSH reaches zero?
flashcards.back: Partial vacuum forms. Fluid flashes into vapor. Cavitation risk.

flashcards.subject: CP04
flashcards.front: What is cavitation?
flashcards.back: Vapor bubbles form when suction pressure approaches saturation. Damages impeller/equipment.

flashcards.subject: CP04
flashcards.front: What causes cavitation noise?
flashcards.back: Vapor bubbles collapsing/imploding under high pressure.

flashcards.subject: CP04
flashcards.front: What damage does cavitation cause?
flashcards.back: Impeller pitting/erosion. Reduces efficiency. Creates imbalance.

flashcards.subject: CP04
flashcards.front: What are cavitation indicators?
flashcards.back: Distinctive noise (rocks), vibration, motor current fluctuations, discharge pressure/flow fluctuations.

flashcards.subject: CP04
flashcards.front: Primary cavitation prevention during startup?
flashcards.back: Vent all air from suction lines. Fill completely with fluid before starting.

flashcards.subject: CP04
flashcards.front: How prevent cavitation during operation?
flashcards.back: Maintain adequate NPSH. Raise absolute suction pressure. Keep temp low. Minimize suction restrictions.

flashcards.subject: CP04
flashcards.front: What does pump operational curve show?
flashcards.back: Relationship between flow rate and head (pressure) pump develops at different points.

flashcards.subject: CP04
flashcards.front: Where does pump operating point occur?
flashcards.back: Intersection of pump curve and system resistance curve (system head curve).

flashcards.subject: CP04
flashcards.front: How does pump efficiency vary?
flashcards.back: Decreases as flow deviates from design point. Peak efficiency at specific flow/head.

flashcards.subject: CP04
flashcards.front: Effects of operating outside design point?
flashcards.back: Wastes energy as heat. Accelerates wear. Can cause cavitation.

flashcards.subject: CP04
flashcards.front: What temperature effects impact pump performance?
flashcards.back: Higher temp: viscosity ↓, saturation pressure ↑. Both hurt pump operation and NPSH.

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: What is the main difference between direct and indirect contact heat exchangers?
flashcards.back: Direct: fluids touch each other. Indirect: fluids separated by solid surface (tube/plate).

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: What are common examples of direct contact heat exchangers?
flashcards.back: Cooling towers, lakes, rivers. Fluids in direct contact.

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: What are common examples of indirect contact heat exchangers?
flashcards.back: Steam generators, main condensers. Fluids separated by surfaces.

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: How does a forced draft cooling tower work?
flashcards.back: Fans blow air into tower to exchange heat between water and air.

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: How does a natural draft cooling tower work?
flashcards.back: Convective chimney effect (hot air rises) pulls air through. No fans needed.

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: What two flow configurations are used in cooling towers?
flashcards.back: Cross-flow (air enters side, exits opposite) and Counter-flow (air enters bottom, exits top).

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: What is the purpose of cooling tower fill material?
flashcards.back: Increases air-water contact surface area. Better heat transfer. Usually PVC/plastic.

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: What are the four basic flow paths in shell-and-tube heat exchangers?
flashcards.back: Cross flow, Parallel flow, Counter flow, U-tube.

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: What is crossflow heat transfer?
flashcards.back: Fluids flow perpendicular to each other. Example: main condensers.

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: What is parallel flow heat transfer?
flashcards.back: Fluids flow in same direction. Requires large surface area. Rarely used.

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: What is counter flow heat transfer?
flashcards.back: Fluids flow in opposite directions. Most efficient. Maintains large temp difference.

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: Why is counter-flow more efficient than parallel-flow?
flashcards.back: Maintains larger temp difference throughout, allows more heat transfer in smaller space.

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: What is the formula for heat transfer rate?
flashcards.back: Q = Uo × A × ΔT. (coefficient × area × temp difference).

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: What are three factors that increase heat transfer rate?
flashcards.back: Larger Uo (coefficient), larger A (area), larger ΔT (temperature difference).

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: What is a regenerative heat exchanger?
flashcards.back: Transfers heat from hot to cold sections of SAME system. Example: Feedwater Heaters. Minimizes energy loss.

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: What is a non-regenerative heat exchanger?
flashcards.back: Transfers heat between TWO SEPARATE systems. Heat rejected/discarded. Example: Lube Oil Coolers.

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: What are the major components of shell-and-tube heat exchangers?
flashcards.back: Shell, tube bundle, tubesheets, waterboxes, baffles, nozzles, vents, drains.

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: What is the shell in a heat exchanger?
flashcards.back: Casing surrounding heat transfer region. Houses shell-side fluid.

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: What are tubesheets?
flashcards.back: Perforated metal plates at shell ends. Separate fluids and support tubes.

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: What are baffles?
flashcards.back: Internal dividers directing shell-side flow to cross tubes multiple times.

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: What are two common tube types?
flashcards.back: Straight tubes (easy clean/replace) and U-tubes (simplified expansion, fewer joints).

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: What is thermal shock in a heat exchanger?
flashcards.back: Sudden temp change causing excessive thermal stress. Risk of cracking/brittle fracture.

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: When is thermal shock most likely?
flashcards.back: Startup: hot/cold fluids suddenly introduced. Sudden temp changes during operation.

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: How do you prevent thermal shock during startup?
flashcards.back: Gradually introduce fluids by throttling inlet valves. Minimize sudden temp changes.

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: What is the startup procedure for a heat exchanger?
flashcards.back: (1) Circulate cold fluid with vents open. (2) Slowly valve in hot fluid. (3) Throttle inlet to prevent pressure spikes.

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: What is water hammer in heat exchangers?
flashcards.back: Pressure spike when fluid velocity suddenly changes. Causes pipe movement/damage.

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: How do you minimize water hammer?
flashcards.back: Operate valves slowly. Avoid sudden velocity changes.

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: How do flow rates affect heat exchanger performance?
flashcards.back: Too high: excessive pressure drops, energy loss. Too low: inadequate heat transfer. Must optimize.

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: What is scaling in a heat exchanger?
flashcards.back: Deposit buildup (mineral scale, corrosion). Reduces heat transfer surface/efficiency.

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: What causes tube fouling?
flashcards.back: Mineral deposits, corrosion products, biological growth. Reduces coefficient/area.

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: What happens if a heat exchanger tube fails?
flashcards.back: Cross-contamination of fluids. Loss of heat transfer. Operational hazards.

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: How do you maintain heat exchanger performance?
flashcards.back: Keep surfaces clean. Maintain proper flow. Monitor fouling. Detect failures early.

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: What is the relationship between condenser vacuum and turbine backpressure?
flashcards.back: Higher vacuum (lower pressure) = lower backpressure = greater pressure difference = more turbine work/efficiency.

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: Why is condenser vacuum important?
flashcards.back: Better vacuum improves turbine efficiency. Increases pressure difference. More steam work.

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: What happens when condenser vacuum degrades?
flashcards.back: Backpressure increases. Turbine output decreases. Plant efficiency reduces.

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: How is vacuum measured in condensers?
flashcards.back: As absolute pressure. Lower absolute pressure = better vacuum.

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: How does a main condenser operate?
flashcards.back: Exhaust steam contacts cold tubes → condenses to condensate. Cooling water absorbs latent heat.

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: What is the flow pattern in a main condenser?
flashcards.back: Crossflow: steam flows down perpendicular to cooling water tubes.

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: What is the hotwell?
flashcards.back: Collects condensed steam at condenser bottom. Pumped to feedwater system.

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: How much cooling water is needed per pound of steam?
flashcards.back: 65-100 lbm (8-12 gallons) cooling water per lbm steam condensed.

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: What are non-condensable gases?
flashcards.back: Air and other gases that cannot condense. Accumulate and increase pressure. Reduce vacuum.

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: How do air removal systems work?
flashcards.back: Jet air ejectors or vacuum pumps remove non-condensable gases continuously.

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: How do you monitor condenser efficiency?
flashcards.back: Measure vacuum, outlet water temp, flow rates. Degradation: reduced vacuum, higher outlet temp.

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: What is biofouling?
flashcards.back: Aquatic organism growth. Degrades cooling tower/condenser. Controlled by chemical treatment.

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: What are three key principles of heat exchanger operation?
flashcards.back: (1) Heat transfers hot → cold. (2) Temp difference drives transfer. (3) Minimize losses through design/maintenance.

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: What makes an effective heat exchanger?
flashcards.back: Proper flow patterns, adequate surface area, clean surfaces, correct fluid properties, good thermal design.

flashcards.subject: CP06
flashcards.front: What is an operator's role in heat exchanger performance?
flashcards.back: Monitor conditions, maintain flow, prevent fouling, detect failures, proper startup/shutdown.

questions.subject: CP01
questions.text: What is the primary purpose of piping in a power plant?

options.text: To transport fluids from one piece of equipment to another
To store fluids for later use

questions.explanation: Piping serves as the housing to transport fluids (and sometimes fluid/solid mixtures) between equipment in power plant systems.

questions.subject: CP01
questions.text: Which piping material is typically used for high-temperature applications due to greater resistance to wear, fatigue, and corrosion?
questions.explanation: Low alloy steel is preferred for high-temperature applications due to its superior resistance to wear, fatigue, and corrosion.

questions.subject: CP01
questions.text: Which piping material is normally chosen for systems connected to the reactor because corrosion product generation must be minimized?
questions.explanation: Stainless steel is used in reactor systems where corrosion product buildup must be minimized to protect system integrity.

questions.subject: CP01
questions.text: Which of the following is NOT one of the five principal functions of valves?
questions.explanation: The five principal valve functions are: starting/stopping, throttling, controlling flow direction, regulating pressure, and relieving pressure. Increasing system pressure is not a valve function.

questions.subject: CP01
questions.text: What is the primary function of the backseat in a valve?

options.text: To remove system pressure from the packing to allow packing replacement while the system is pressurized

questions.explanation: The backseat is a critical safety feature that removes system pressure from the packing, allowing maintenance without depressurizing the system.

questions.subject: CP01
questions.text: Gate valves are primarily used as isolation valves rather than for throttling because:

options.text: They are more expensive than globe valves
Positioning the disk in the flow stream causes turbulence and accelerated wear

questions.explanation: Gate valves are unsuitable for throttling because disk positioning in the flow causes turbulence and accelerated wear, damaging the valve.

questions.subject: CP01
questions.text: Why are globe valves preferred for throttling?

options.text: They are cheaper than gate valves
The disk is beveled and seats at nearly right angles to the flow path
They operate faster than other valves

questions.explanation: Globe valves are ideal for throttling because the beveled disk seating at right angles to flow allows smooth, controlled flow regulation.

questions.subject: CP01
questions.text: Which statement is true about Kerotest valves?

options.text: They go from full closed to full open in approximately 1¼ turns
They are best for isolation applications only
They cannot be used for throttling
They have a packing gland design

questions.explanation: Kerotest valves are pack-less globe valves designed to go from full closed to full open in approximately 1¼ turns.

questions.subject: CP01
questions.text: Why should operators avoid over-torquing a Kerotest valve?

options.text: Excessive torque can crush or deform the disk, preventing the valve from opening later
It causes the valve to leak

questions.explanation: Over-torquing a Kerotest valve can crush or deform the disk, potentially making the valve impossible to open later.

questions.subject: CP01
questions.text: What feature makes a needle valve suitable for precise flow control?

options.text: Its long, narrow, cone-shaped stem tip

questions.explanation: A needle valve's long, narrow, cone-shaped stem tip allows fine, precise adjustment of flow rate.

questions.subject: CP01
questions.text: Butterfly valves are typically used in:

options.text: Large diameter, high flow, low pressure applications (e.g., circulating water)

questions.explanation: Butterfly valves are ideal for large diameter, high flow, low pressure service such as circulating water systems.

questions.subject: CP01
questions.text: What is the main advantage of a diaphragm valve with radioactive or corrosive fluids?

options.text: It can handle very high pressures
The fluid is completely separated from the moving parts, resulting in zero stem leakage
It operates faster than other valves

questions.explanation: Diaphragm valves completely separate the fluid from moving parts, preventing stem leakage and protecting against contamination.

questions.subject: CP01
questions.text: What is the primary purpose of check valves?

options.text: To allow flow in only one direction and prevent reverse flow

questions.explanation: Check valves are one-way devices that permit flow in the intended direction while preventing backflow.

questions.subject: CP01
questions.text: What is the key difference between a safety valve and a relief valve?

options.text: Safety valves are used for liquids, relief valves for gases
Safety valves pop fully open with little or no accumulation, while relief valves require accumulation
Relief valves pop fully open, safety valves open gradually

questions.explanation: Safety valves pop fully open at setpoint with minimal accumulation, while relief valves open gradually as pressure rises above setpoint.

questions.subject: CP01
questions.text: What is the primary function of a vacuum breaker?

options.text: To protect a tank or vessel from collapsing due to low internal pressure
To measure vacuum in the system

questions.explanation: A vacuum breaker is a safety device that protects vessels from structural collapse under low internal pressure conditions.

questions.subject: CP01
questions.text: What is the correct definition of 'Fail As Is' for valve actuators?

options.text: The valve opens when power is lost
The valve closes when power is lost
The valve remains in its current position when the actuating medium is lost
The valve springs to a safe position

questions.explanation: Fail As Is (most common in Motor Operated Valves) means the valve maintains its current position when actuating power is lost.

questions.subject: CP01
questions.text: Key precaution when manually operating a Motor Operated Valve (MOV):

options.text: Always tag out the power supply to the motor before using the handwheel (when feasible)
Use a wrench to increase torque application
Operate it as quickly as possible
Do not verify the position afterward

questions.explanation: Tagging out the motor power prevents inadvertent power application during manual valve operation, ensuring operator safety.

questions.subject: CP01
questions.text: When verifying position of a manual valve locally, operators should first attempt to turn the handwheel in which direction?

options.text: Closed direction (negligible effect if already closed)

questions.explanation: Testing closure direction is safe because if the valve is already closed, the handwheel won't move, causing no system impact.

questions.subject: CP01
questions.text: According to SOER 85-2, one primary method to prevent valve mispositioning is:

options.text: Verify that all local and remote indications reflect actual plant conditions before and after manipulation

questions.explanation: Verification of all indications before and after valve operation is essential to prevent dangerous mispositioning events.

questions.subject: CP01
questions.text: What is a major failure mechanism of gate valves discussed in the lesson?
questions.explanation: Thermal binding (differential cooling contraction) and pressure locking (trapped liquid expansion) are critical gate valve failure mechanisms.

questions.subject: CP01
questions.text: What is the primary design consideration for piping in a power plant system?

options.text: Fluid temperature, fluid pressure, flow rate/velocity, chemical/physical properties, and shock loads

questions.explanation: Piping design must account for operating conditions: temperature, pressure, flow rate, fluid properties, contamination, and dynamic loads like water hammer and seismic motion.

questions.subject: CP01
questions.text: Copper alloys are typically chosen for which piping application?

options.text: Corrosive seawater or cooling water systems where corrosion resistance and conductivity are needed

questions.explanation: Copper alloys provide excellent corrosion resistance and thermal conductivity, ideal for seawater, condensate, and cooling water systems.

questions.subject: CP01
questions.text: Which type of pipe support is designed to limit seismic motion while allowing thermal growth?
questions.explanation: Snubbers limit large seismic displacements while allowing normal thermal expansion/contraction of piping systems.

questions.subject: CP01
questions.text: What is the purpose of thermal insulation on piping?

options.text: To protect personnel from hot surfaces and reduce heat loss, also protecting equipment from thermal shock

questions.explanation: Thermal insulation provides worker protection and energy efficiency by minimizing heat transfer between the pipe and environment.

questions.subject: CP01
questions.text: What is thermal binding in valves?

options.text: The bonnet expanding and blocking the stem
Differential thermal contraction between the valve body and disk, potentially binding the disk to the seat
Heat causing the disk to warp

questions.explanation: Thermal binding occurs when the valve body cools faster than the disk, causing the disk to bind against the seat. Prevention: crack open periodically during cooldown.

questions.subject: CP01
questions.text: What is pressure locking in a valve?

options.text: External pressure preventing the valve from opening
Liquid trapped in the valve bonnet pressurizing as it heats, preventing the valve from opening
The disk corroding to the seat

questions.explanation: Pressure locking occurs when trapped liquid in the bonnet heats and pressurizes, making the valve impossible to open. Prevention: provide bonnet relief or vent paths.

questions.subject: CP01
questions.text: What is the primary design characteristic of a swing check valve versus a lift check valve?

options.text: Swing check has a hinged disk; lift check has a globe-like body with higher D/P
Lift check is used only for liquids

questions.explanation: Swing check: hinged disk, low pressure drop when open. Lift check: globe-like, higher D/P but better upstream isolation.

questions.subject: CP01
questions.text: What is a stop check valve designed to do?

options.text: Allow normal check function but also can be forcibly closed by an external actuator, combining check and isolation functions

questions.explanation: Stop check valves combine a check valve's backflow prevention with a globe valve's isolation capability via external actuation.

questions.subject: CP01
questions.text: Which type of actuator is most associated with MOVs (Motor Operated Valves)?

options.text: Fail As Is with gear reduction and declutch lever

questions.explanation: MOVs are electric motors with gear reduction and a declutch lever allowing manual/motor engagement; they typically fail as-is (maintain position).

questions.subject: CP01
questions.text: What hazard can result from using a wrench or valve wrench on an MOV handwheel?

options.text: Exceeding mechanical advantage can overstress the actuator gearing/casing, causing catastrophic failure
It prevents the motor from engaging

questions.explanation: Applying excessive torque via wrenches to MOV handwheels can catastrophically damage the actuator gear train. Operating procedures prohibit this.

questions.subject: TH01
questions.text: According to Pascal's Law, a pressure change applied to an enclosed, incompressible fluid is transmitted:

options.text: Only at the point of application
Undiminished to all points within the fluid and to the walls of the container
Only along the path of least resistance

questions.explanation: Pascal's Law: pressure applied to an enclosed fluid transmits undiminished throughout in all directions.

questions.subject: TH01
questions.text: Gauge pressure plus atmospheric pressure equals which pressure value?
questions.explanation: Pabs = Pgage + Patm. Absolute pressure is always the sum of gauge and atmospheric pressures.

questions.subject: TH01
questions.text: Specific volume is best defined as:

options.text: The total volume of a substance
The volume occupied by a unit mass of a substance (the reciprocal of density)
The volume at standard temperature and pressure

questions.explanation: Specific volume (v) = V/m, measured in ft³/lbm or m³/kg. It is the reciprocal of density.

questions.subject: TH01
questions.text: What is the primary difference between a closed system and an open system in thermodynamics?

options.text: A closed system allows energy transfer across its boundary but not mass transfer, while an open system allows transfer of both mass and energy
A closed system allows no transfer of mass or energy
An open system is always at constant pressure
A closed system is only used in laboratories

questions.explanation: Closed systems have fixed mass boundaries but allow energy exchange. Open systems (control volumes) allow both mass and energy crossing boundaries.

questions.subject: TH01
questions.text: Which type of thermodynamic property depends on the amount of substance present, such as volume or weight?
questions.explanation: Extensive properties (volume, mass, weight) depend on the amount of substance. Intensive properties (pressure, temperature) do not.

questions.subject: TH01
questions.text: On which temperature scale does zero represent the point of no molecular motion (absolute zero) and correspond exactly to zero Kelvin?
questions.explanation: The Rankine scale (absolute scale for Fahrenheit) and Kelvin (absolute scale for Celsius) both have zero at absolute zero.

questions.subject: TH01
questions.text: Which pressure measurement indicates a pressure below atmospheric pressure?
questions.explanation: Vacuum pressure is any pressure below atmospheric. Pvac = Patm - Pabs.

questions.subject: TH01
questions.text: What term describes the difference in pressure between two locations, such as across a filter?
questions.explanation: Differential pressure (psid) is the pressure difference between two points in a system, commonly used across filters and restrictors.

questions.subject: TH01
questions.text: In a hydraulic press, if the output piston has a larger area than the input piston, how does the output force compare to the input force?

options.text: The output force is less than the input force
The output force equals the input force
The output force is greater than the input force
Output force depends only on fluid type

questions.explanation: In a hydraulic press, F = P × A. A larger output piston area produces greater output force (Pascal's Law application).

questions.subject: TH01
questions.text: Why does liquid temperature have a much greater effect on density and specific volume than pressure does?

options.text: Because liquids expand more with heat
Because liquids are relatively incompressible, so pressure has little effect on their volume
Because temperature is more important than pressure

questions.explanation: Liquids are nearly incompressible, so pressure changes have minimal volume effect. Temperature changes cause greater density variations.

questions.subject: TH01
questions.text: Which of the following is an example of an open (control volume) system?

options.text: A sealed cylinder with a fixed amount of gas
A steam turbine where steam enters and exits
A closed tank with no inlets or outlets

questions.explanation: An open system (control volume) has mass crossing its boundary. Turbines, compressors, pumps, boilers, and condensers are examples.

questions.subject: TH01
questions.text: An isolated system in thermodynamics is best described as:

options.text: A system connected to surroundings by a single pipe
A system where neither mass nor energy crosses its boundary
A system insulated from heat transfer

questions.explanation: An isolated system is completely separated from its surroundings; no mass or energy transfer occurs across the boundary.

questions.subject: TH01
questions.text: Hydrostatic pressure in a fluid column is proportional to which of the following?

options.text: The fluid's density and the height of the column above the reference point

questions.explanation: Hydrostatic pressure P = ρgh, where ρ is density, g is gravitational acceleration, and h is height above reference.

questions.subject: TH01
questions.text: In the American Engineering System (English System), what is the standard unit for force?
questions.explanation: The American Engineering System uses pound-force (lbf) for force and pound-mass (lbm) for mass; the mechanical equivalent of heat is 1 Btu = 778 ft-lbf.

questions.subject: TH01
questions.text: Pressure is defined as:

options.text: Total force exerted by a fluid
The weight of a fluid column

questions.explanation: Pressure (P) = F/A, with units of psia (pounds per square inch absolute), psi, Pa, bar, etc.

questions.subject: TH01
questions.text: At which temperature are the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales numerically equal?
questions.explanation: At -40°, both scales read the same: -40°C = -40°F. This is where the conversion lines intersect.

questions.subject: TH02
questions.text: The First Law of Thermodynamics states that energy:

options.text: Cannot be created or destroyed, only converted from one form to another
Can only flow from hot to cold
Is lost as heat in all processes

questions.explanation: The First Law (Energy Conservation): Energy entering a system equals energy stored in or leaving it. E in = E stored + E out.

questions.subject: TH02
questions.text: Heat and work are best classified as which type of energy?

options.text: Transient (energy in transit) forms of energy

questions.explanation: Heat and work are transient energy forms—energy in transit. They exist only during energy transfer between systems and surroundings.

questions.subject: TH02
questions.text: Which equation correctly defines enthalpy (H)?
