questions.explanation: Enthalpy H = U + PV, where U is internal energy and PV is flow energy. This is a fundamental thermodynamic property.

questions.subject: TH02
questions.text: What is the term for energy a substance possesses due to its position or height relative to a reference point?
questions.explanation: Potential Energy (PE) depends on position. PE = mzg/gc, where z is height above a reference point.

questions.subject: TH02
questions.text: What is the term for energy a substance possesses due to its motion?
questions.explanation: Kinetic Energy (KE) = mv²/2gc. It depends on the velocity of the substance.

questions.subject: TH02
questions.text: Internal energy is best described as which of the following?

options.text: The sum of the microscopic energy forms (molecular rotation, vibration, and translation) within a substance

questions.explanation: Internal energy (U) is the sum of all microscopic forms: molecular rotation, vibration, and translational kinetic energy.

questions.subject: TH02
questions.text: Which equation correctly defines specific enthalpy (h)?
questions.explanation: Specific enthalpy h = u + Pv. It represents energy per unit mass of fluid.

questions.subject: TH02
questions.text: For a closed system with no change in potential or kinetic energy, the General Energy Equation reduces to which relationship?

options.text: Change in enthalpy = heat transferred to the system minus work done by the system (Δh = q - w)

questions.explanation: For closed systems with no PE/KE change: Δh = q - w. This is the simplified First Law energy equation.

questions.subject: TH02
questions.text: Which term describes the rate at which work is done?
questions.explanation: Power is work per unit time: P = W/t, measured in watts (J/s) or horsepower (hp).

questions.subject: TH02
questions.text: The mechanical equivalent of heat (Joule's constant) is:
questions.explanation: Joule's constant: 1 Btu = 778 ft-lbf. This converts between heat (Btu) and mechanical work (ft-lbf).

questions.subject: TH02
questions.text: Flow work (PV energy) is the energy a fluid possesses due to:

options.text: Its position above a reference point
Its pressure and volume (the work required to push the fluid into a system)

questions.explanation: Flow energy (PV) is the work required to push a fluid of volume V at pressure P into a system. It equals P×v per unit mass.

questions.subject: TH02
questions.text: In thermodynamic sign conventions, when heat is removed from a system, Q is considered:
questions.explanation: Sign convention: Q added (into system) = positive; Q removed (out of system) = negative. Similarly, W done by system = positive, W done on system = negative.

questions.subject: TH02
questions.text: When work is done ON a system (compression), the work value is considered:
questions.explanation: Sign convention: Work done BY the system (expansion, turbine) = positive. Work done ON the system (compression, pump) = negative.

questions.subject: TH02
questions.text: Entropy (S) is best described as:

options.text: The total energy in a system
A measure of the unavailable energy in a fluid at a given state; increases with irreversibility

questions.explanation: Entropy (S) measures disorder and unavailable energy. Specific entropy (s) has units of Btu/lbm-R. Total entropy increases in real processes.

questions.subject: TH02
questions.text: What is the relationship between enthalpy, internal energy, and specific volume in the definition of specific enthalpy?
questions.explanation: Specific enthalpy h = u + Pv combines internal energy u and flow energy Pv. This property simplifies energy analysis of control volumes.

questions.subject: TH02
questions.text: In a steady flow process, what remains constant by definition?

options.text: The mass flow rate in equals mass flow rate out, and working-fluid properties are constant at any location

questions.explanation: Steady flow: constant mass flow rate in/out, constant properties at each location over time, constant heat/work transfer rates. Most power equipment operates in steady flow.

questions.subject: TH03
questions.text: What is the term for a liquid existing at a temperature below its saturation temperature for a given pressure?
questions.explanation: Subcooled (or compressed) liquid is below saturation temperature for its pressure, meaning it could absorb heat and vaporize.

questions.subject: TH03
questions.text: What is the term for steam that is 100% vapor at its boiling temperature, with no liquid remaining?
questions.explanation: Saturated vapor (dry steam) is at saturation temperature with quality X = 100%. Any further heating produces superheated steam.

questions.subject: TH03
questions.text: What is the term for vapor that exists above its boiling (saturation) temperature?
questions.explanation: Superheated vapor is above saturation temperature. The degrees of superheat = actual T - saturation T.

questions.subject: TH03
questions.text: Heat that changes a substance's phase without changing its temperature is called:
questions.explanation: Latent heat is phase-change heat (melting, vaporization) that doesn't change temperature. Sensible heat does change temperature.

questions.subject: TH03
questions.text: What term describes the fraction of vapor present in a wet steam mixture?
questions.explanation: Steam quality (X) = fraction of vapor in wet steam mixture. Moisture content (M) = liquid fraction. X + M = 100%.

questions.subject: TH03
questions.text: On a P-T diagram, the point at which the solid, liquid, and gas phases can all exist in equilibrium simultaneously is called:
questions.explanation: The Triple Point is where solid, liquid, and gas coexist. For water: 0.01°C, 0.006 atm.

questions.subject: TH03
questions.text: According to Charles' Law, at constant pressure, the volume of a gas is:

options.text: Inversely proportional to its absolute temperature
Directly proportional to its absolute temperature
Proportional to the square of temperature

questions.explanation: Charles' Law: V ∝ T at constant P. V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂ (using absolute temperature).

questions.subject: TH03
questions.text: According to Boyle's Law, at constant temperature, the volume of a gas is:

options.text: Directly proportional to its absolute pressure
Inversely proportional to its absolute pressure
Proportional to the square of pressure

questions.explanation: Boyle's Law: V ∝ 1/P at constant T. P₁V₁ = P₂V₂.

questions.subject: TH03
questions.text: Why should the Ideal Gas Law not be used to determine the properties of steam?

options.text: Steam is always at high pressure
Steam's behavior is considerably more complex than an ideal gas, so steam tables (experimentally derived data) must be used instead
The Ideal Gas Law only works for perfect gases

questions.explanation: Steam deviates significantly from ideal gas behavior, especially near saturation. Steam tables provide experimentally accurate properties.

questions.subject: TH03
questions.text: What is the fraction of liquid in a wet steam mixture called?
questions.explanation: Moisture content (M) = liquid fraction. Quality (X) = vapor fraction. X + M = 100% or 1.0.

questions.subject: TH03
questions.text: What does the 'void fraction' represent in two-phase flow?

options.text: The volumetric fraction of vapor (gas) in the mixture

questions.explanation: Void fraction is the volume fraction of vapor (gas) in a two-phase mixture. Different from quality, which is mass fraction.

questions.subject: TH03
questions.text: On a P-T diagram, what is the significance of the Critical Point?

options.text: The highest pressure at which solid can exist
The highest temperature and pressure at which liquid and gas can exist as distinguishable phases
The point where all phases coexist
The freezing point of the substance

questions.explanation: At the Critical Point, the distinction between liquid and gas phases disappears. Above the critical point, only a supercritical fluid exists.

questions.subject: TH03
questions.text: What are 'degrees of superheat' in a thermodynamic process?

options.text: The absolute temperature of the vapor
The difference between the actual temperature and the saturation temperature of the vapor
The heat added to the system

questions.explanation: Degrees of superheat = T_actual - T_saturation. For example, if steam is at 350°F when saturation is 300°F, superheat = 50°F.

questions.subject: TH03
questions.text: What are 'degrees of subcooling' for a liquid?

options.text: The absolute temperature of the liquid
The difference between the saturation temperature and the actual (lower) temperature of the liquid

questions.explanation: Degrees of subcooling = T_saturation - T_actual. Condensate at 100°F when saturation is 110°F has 10°F of subcooling.

questions.subject: TH03
questions.text: Why does cavitation occur in a pump?

options.text: The liquid pressure drops below saturation pressure, causing vapor bubbles to form; they collapse later, causing erosion and damage
Too much flow through the pump

questions.explanation: Cavitation: local pressure < saturation pressure → vapor bubbles form → downstream, pressure increases → bubbles collapse violently → erosion and vibration.

questions.subject: TH03
questions.text: In the context of steam table usage, what is a 'saturated steam table' indexed by?

options.text: Either by saturation temperature or saturation pressure (corresponding conditions)

questions.explanation: Saturated steam tables list properties indexed by either saturation temperature or saturation pressure; the two are uniquely related.

questions.subject: TH04
questions.text: In a process where no heat is transferred to or from the system, what term describes this condition?
questions.explanation: Adiabatic process: Q = 0 (no heat transfer). Temperature and pressure can change in adiabatic processes.

questions.subject: TH04
questions.text: For a turbine, the work output is typically expressed as the difference between which two values?
questions.explanation: Turbine work: W = h_in - h_out. The enthalpy drop across the turbine equals the mechanical work output.

questions.subject: TH04
questions.text: What does the term 'isenthalpic' describe in a thermodynamic process?
questions.explanation: Isenthalpic process: enthalpy remains constant. Throttling (through a valve) is an isenthalpic process.

questions.subject: TH04
questions.text: Which of the following is the correct expression for the work input to a pump?
questions.explanation: Pump work: W = h_out - h_in (positive value). Work is input to increase fluid pressure and enthalpy.

questions.subject: TH04
questions.text: Condensate depression is defined as the difference between which two temperatures?
questions.explanation: Condensate depression = saturation temperature minus actual condensate temperature. A few degrees prevents pump cavitation.

questions.subject: TH04
questions.text: A process that occurs at constant pressure is called:
questions.explanation: Isobaric process: P = constant. Boiler heat addition and condenser heat rejection are isobaric processes.

questions.subject: TH04
questions.text: A process that occurs at constant temperature is referred to as:
questions.explanation: Isothermal process: T = constant. Often occurs during condensation or with isothermal compression/expansion.

questions.subject: TH04
questions.text: What does the Second Law of Thermodynamics state about a heat engine operating in a cycle?

options.text: All heat can be converted to work
No engine, actual or ideal, can convert all the heat supplied into work; some heat must always be rejected
Heat only flows from cold to hot
The amount of entropy always decreases

questions.explanation: Second Law: No cyclic heat engine can achieve 100% efficiency. All engines must reject heat to the surroundings.

questions.subject: TH04
questions.text: The change in entropy of a system is defined as which of the following?

options.text: The heat added to the system multiplied by temperature
The heat transferred to or from the system divided by the absolute temperature at which the transfer occurs
The change in internal energy of the system

questions.explanation: Entropy change: ΔS = Q/T_abs. Total entropy increases in any real irreversible process (Second Law).

questions.subject: TH04
questions.text: In a convergent nozzle, what happens to the velocity and pressure of the fluid?
questions.explanation: In convergent nozzles: flow area decreases → velocity increases, pressure decreases (kinetic energy increases).

questions.subject: TH04
questions.text: Why is a few degrees of condensate subcooling desirable at the condenser hotwell?

options.text: To prevent cavitation in the condensate pumps

questions.explanation: Condensate depression prevents pump cavitation (vapor bubbles) but excessive depression wastes heat and increases corrosion.

questions.subject: TH04
questions.text: An ideal turbine or pump work process is described as isentropic because:

options.text: Friction is not considered, so there is no change in entropy of the working fluid

questions.explanation: Isentropic process: ΔS = 0 (reversible). Real turbines/pumps add entropy through friction, reducing their efficiency.

questions.subject: TH04
questions.text: Turbine efficiency is defined as which of the following ratios?
questions.explanation: Turbine efficiency = Real work output / Ideal isentropic work. Real turbines are always less efficient than ideal.

questions.subject: TH04
questions.text: Why is the First Law of Thermodynamics essential for analyzing heat exchangers?

options.text: It predicts the type of heat exchanger needed
It relates energy input and output; for a heat exchanger, heat gained by one fluid equals heat lost by the other (no work done)

questions.explanation: In heat exchangers: Q gained = Q lost (First Law). The energy equation q = h_out - h_in applies directly.

questions.subject: TH04
questions.text: What is the function of a divergent nozzle?

options.text: To increase velocity and decrease pressure
To decrease velocity and increase pressure

questions.explanation: In a divergent nozzle: flow area increases → velocity decreases, pressure increases (kinetic energy converts to pressure energy).

questions.subject: TH04
questions.text: What process occurs when steam flows through a partially open valve, resulting in pressure drop and entropy increase?
questions.explanation: Throttling: constant enthalpy (h_in = h_out), pressure drops, entropy increases. No work done, no heat added. Used for flow control.

questions.subject: TH04
questions.text: What is pump efficiency defined as?

options.text: Ideal work (fluid power) / Real work (shaft power)

questions.explanation: Pump efficiency = ideal (isentropic) work / real (shaft) work. Real pumps require more shaft power than ideal due to friction.

questions.subject: TH04
questions.text: How does superheating steam in the boiler affect turbine work output?

options.text: It increases turbine work and also improves cycle efficiency
It has no effect on turbine work

questions.explanation: Superheating increases the enthalpy of steam entering the turbine (h_in increases), resulting in greater work output (W = h_in - h_out).

questions.subject: TH04
questions.text: What is the effect of friction losses in a real turbine compared to an ideal isentropic turbine?

options.text: Real turbine produces less work and adds entropy to the system
Real turbine has lower outlet pressure

questions.explanation: Friction in real turbines increases entropy (ΔS > 0), reducing the enthalpy drop available for work. Turbine efficiency accounts for this.

questions.subject: TH05
questions.text: What are the five essential elements of a thermodynamic cycle?

options.text: A working fluid, an engine to convert heat to work, a heat source, a heat sink, and a device to move the working fluid
A compressor, turbine, pump, condenser, and boiler
Temperature, pressure, volume, enthalpy, and entropy
Input, output, efficiency, work, and heat

questions.explanation: The five essential elements of a thermodynamic cycle are: a working fluid, an engine to convert heat to work, a heat source, a heat sink, and a device to move the working fluid.

questions.subject: TH05
questions.text: The Carnot cycle consists of which four processes?

options.text: Two isothermal processes and two adiabatic (isentropic) processes
Two isochoric processes and two isobaric processes

questions.explanation: The Carnot cycle consists of two isothermal processes and two adiabatic (isentropic) processes, operating between two heat reservoirs.

questions.subject: TH05
questions.text: According to the Carnot efficiency equation, the efficiency of a Carnot cycle depends only on:

options.text: The absolute temperatures of the heat source and heat sink
The type of working fluid used
The size and design of the engine

questions.explanation: The Carnot efficiency depends only on the absolute temperatures of the heat source and heat sink: η = 1 - (Tcold/Thot).

questions.subject: TH05
questions.text: What are the two ways to increase the Carnot efficiency of a cycle?

options.text: Increase the temperature of the heat source or decrease the temperature of the heat sink
Increase the amount of working fluid and reduce system pressure
Use a more efficient turbine and condenser
Add more heat exchangers to the system

questions.explanation: Carnot efficiency increases by raising the heat source temperature or lowering the heat sink temperature, both of which increase the temperature ratio.

questions.subject: TH05
questions.text: What is the primary purpose of a Moisture Separator Reheater (MSR) in a steam cycle?

options.text: To reduce moisture in the steam entering the low-pressure turbine, protecting the final blading stages from wear
To improve overall cycle efficiency by increasing work output
To reduce the amount of feedwater heating required
To increase the condenser vacuum and lower rejection temperature

questions.explanation: The MSR protects turbine blades from erosion and damage caused by moisture, not to improve efficiency directly.

questions.subject: TH05
questions.text: How does feedwater heating (using extraction steam) affect cycle efficiency?

options.text: It increases cycle efficiency because less heat must be added by the heat source
It decreases efficiency because energy is extracted from the turbine
It has no effect on efficiency
It only improves reliability, not efficiency

questions.explanation: Feedwater heating improves efficiency by reducing the amount of heat that must be added in the boiler to achieve the desired cycle conditions.

questions.subject: TH05
questions.text: How does increasing condenser vacuum (lowering absolute condenser pressure) affect cycle efficiency?

options.text: It increases efficiency, because more work is extracted from the steam and less heat is rejected
It decreases efficiency due to higher pumping losses
It has no effect on efficiency
It increases efficiency only if feedwater heating is also used

questions.explanation: Lower condenser pressure increases the expansion ratio in the turbine, extracting more work per unit of steam and improving efficiency.

questions.subject: TH05
questions.text: What is heat rate, and how does it relate to plant efficiency?

options.text: Heat rate is the energy input (BTU) required per unit of electrical output (kW-hr); it is inversely related to efficiency
Heat rate is the temperature rise across the condenser
Heat rate is the amount of heat added by the boiler per hour
Heat rate is the same as efficiency expressed in different units

questions.explanation: Heat rate (BTU/kW-hr) is inversely proportional to efficiency. A lower heat rate indicates higher efficiency.

questions.subject: TH05
questions.text: What is the correct formula for Carnot cycle efficiency when using absolute temperature?
questions.explanation: Carnot efficiency η = 1 - (T_cold/T_hot) where temperatures are absolute (R or K). Higher source temperature or lower sink temperature increases efficiency.

questions.subject: TH05
questions.text: In the Rankine cycle, which process has constant pressure in the boiler?

options.text: Constant-pressure heat addition to produce steam

questions.explanation: The Rankine cycle boiler process is isobaric (constant pressure). Heat addition occurs at constant system pressure to generate steam.

questions.subject: TH05
questions.text: Which of the following factors does NOT typically improve cycle efficiency?

options.text: Increasing steam temperature in the boiler
Increasing steam flow rate to the turbine

questions.explanation: Increasing steam flow rate increases power output but does not improve efficiency. Efficiency (%) is determined by cycle temperatures/pressures and losses.

questions.subject: TH05
questions.text: Why is a higher steam quality important in power plant turbines?

options.text: To protect turbine blades from moisture erosion damage and improve steam expansion efficiency
To reduce the condenser cooling water requirement

questions.explanation: Wet steam (low quality) damages turbine blades through moisture impingement. High quality steam (>99%) ensures protection and optimal expansion characteristics.

questions.subject: TH06B
questions.text: Mass flow rate is defined as:

options.text: The volume of fluid passing a reference point per unit time
The mass of fluid passing a reference point per unit time
The velocity of fluid at a reference point
The pressure of fluid at a reference point per unit time

questions.explanation: Mass flow rate (ṁ) is the mass of fluid that passes a reference point per unit time, typically expressed in lbm/hr.

questions.subject: TH06B
questions.text: The mass flow rate equation can be expressed as ṁ = ρ × V̇ = ρ × v × A. Which variable represents the cross-sectional area of flow?
questions.explanation: In the mass flow rate equation, A represents the cross-sectional area of flow in square feet (ft²).

questions.subject: TH06B
questions.text: Volumetric flow rate (Q) is commonly expressed in which of the following units?
questions.explanation: Volumetric flow rate is the volume of fluid passing a reference point per unit time, commonly expressed as gallons per minute (gpm) or cubic feet per minute (cfm).

questions.subject: TH06B
questions.text: Steady flow (continuity of flow) occurs when:

options.text: The velocity is constant throughout the pipe
The mass flow rate into and out of a system are equal
The pressure is constant throughout the system

questions.explanation: Steady flow (continuity of flow) occurs when the mass flow rate into and out of a system or component are equal.

questions.subject: TH06B
questions.text: Viscosity is best defined as:

options.text: A fluid's ability to conduct heat
A fluid's density relative to water
A fluid's ability to resist flow

questions.explanation: Viscosity is a measurement of a fluid's ability to resist flow. Free flowing fluids have low viscosity while fluids that resist flow have high viscosity.

questions.subject: TH06B
questions.text: How does viscosity of liquids change with increasing temperature?
questions.explanation: For liquids, viscosity decreases with increasing temperature, primarily due to increased molecular spacing.

questions.subject: TH06B
questions.text: Water at 68°F is used as the reference standard for viscosity measurement. At this temperature, water has a viscosity of:
questions.explanation: Water at 68°F is the standard reference point for viscosity measurement, with a value of 1.0 centipoise.

questions.subject: TH06B
questions.text: Specific gravity is defined as:

options.text: The mass per unit volume of a fluid
The ratio of a fluid's density compared to water at 60°F
The ability of a fluid to resist flow
The pressure exerted by a fluid per unit area

questions.explanation: Specific gravity (SG) is the ratio of a fluid's density compared to water at 60°F (which has an SG of 1.0).

questions.subject: TH06B
questions.text: For liquids, as temperature increases, how do viscosity and specific gravity change?
questions.explanation: For liquids, as temperature increases, both viscosity and specific gravity decrease, resulting in less energy required for flow.

questions.subject: TH06B
questions.text: Laminar flow is characterized by:

options.text: High turbulence and cross-currents throughout the pipe
Layers of fluid moving smoothly over adjacent layers
Maximum velocity at the pipe walls and zero at center
Uniform velocity profile across the pipe diameter

questions.explanation: In laminar flow, layers of fluid move smoothly over adjacent layers with minimal mixing. Flow conditions exist where Reynolds number is less than about 2,000.

questions.subject: TH06B
questions.text: Turbulent flow is characterized by:

options.text: Smooth, layered movement of fluid with no cross-currents
Cross-currents set up that disturb the fluid layers
Parabolic velocity profile similar to laminar flow
Velocity that is zero everywhere in the pipe

questions.explanation: In turbulent flow, cross-currents are set up that disturb the fluid layers. This flow exists when Reynolds number is greater than 3,500.

questions.subject: TH06B
questions.text: The Reynolds number is used to determine:

options.text: The pressure drop across a valve
Whether flow is laminar, transitional, or turbulent
The total head of the fluid system

questions.explanation: Reynolds number (NRe) determines the mode of flow: laminar (NRe < 2,000), transitional (2,000-3,500), or turbulent (NRe > 3,500).

questions.subject: TH06B
questions.text: Single-phase flow occurs when:

options.text: The fluid is a mixture of liquid and vapor
The fluid is either completely in liquid state or completely in gaseous state
The flow passes through multiple pipe sections
The pressure remains constant throughout the system

questions.explanation: Systems and components are normally designed for single-phase fluid flow where the fluid is either in its liquid state or in its gaseous state, not a mixture of both.

questions.subject: TH06B
questions.text: Two-phase flow greatly increases the resistance to flow primarily because:

options.text: The fluid is a mixture of liquid and vapor with different flow velocities

questions.explanation: Two-phase flow is when liquid and vapor coexist, greatly increasing resistance to flow and can increase head loss by a factor of 100 or more.

questions.subject: TH06B
questions.text: The elevation head term in Bernoulli's equation represents:

options.text: The kinetic energy due to fluid velocity
The potential energy due to elevation above a reference level
The energy due to fluid pressure

questions.explanation: Elevation head (z) represents the potential energy the fluid possesses due to its elevation above a reference level, expressed in feet.

questions.subject: TH06B
questions.text: The velocity head term in Bernoulli's equation represents:

options.text: The height to which flowing fluid would rise if all kinetic energy were converted to potential energy
The height of a column of fluid equivalent to pressure
The vertical distance above a reference level
The energy lost due to friction in the pipe

questions.explanation: Velocity head represents the kinetic energy the fluid possesses due to its velocity - the height to which the fluid would rise if all kinetic energy converted to potential energy.

questions.subject: TH06B
questions.text: The pressure head in Bernoulli's equation is expressed as:

options.text: The absolute pressure divided by velocity
The height of a column of fluid whose weight equals the pressure
The pressure multiplied by the flow rate
The gauge pressure plus atmospheric pressure

questions.explanation: Pressure head (Pv) represents the PV energy the fluid possesses due to its pressure - expressed as the height of a fluid column equivalent to that pressure.

questions.subject: TH06B
questions.text: According to Bernoulli's principle, the sum of elevation head, velocity head, and pressure head is called:
questions.explanation: The sum of elevation head, velocity head, and pressure head is called total head. Bernoulli's equation states that total head is constant when ideal conditions apply.

questions.subject: TH06B
questions.text: Head loss is best defined as:

options.text: A decrease in the fluid's temperature due to radiation
The conversion of fluid pressure and velocity to heat energy through friction
The total height of fluid above a reference point
The pressure drop across a closed valve

questions.explanation: Head loss is the conversion of fluid pressure and velocity to heat energy through friction. Although it represents a loss of flow energy, it increases the fluid's internal energy.

questions.subject: TH06B
questions.text: In Darcy's equation for head loss (Hf = f × (L/d) × (v²/2gc)), what does the friction factor (f) account for?

options.text: The surface roughness of the pipe and type of flow
The elevation change in the system

questions.explanation: The friction factor (f) in Darcy's equation takes into account the surface roughness of the pipe and depends on Reynolds number (type of flow).

questions.subject: TH06B
questions.text: According to Darcy's equation, which of the following changes would INCREASE head loss?
questions.explanation: Head loss increases with: increased friction factor (f), increased pipe length (L), and increased velocity squared (v²). Head loss decreases with increased pipe diameter (d).

questions.subject: TH06B
questions.text: Head loss varies with the square of fluid velocity. This means if velocity doubles, head loss will:
questions.explanation: Since head loss is proportional to v², if velocity doubles (2×), head loss increases by (2)² = 4 times.

questions.subject: TH06B
questions.text: A system characteristic curve graphically represents:

options.text: Head loss versus volumetric flow rate

questions.explanation: A system characteristic curve shows head loss versus volumetric flow rate for a given system configuration. The exponential shape results from the velocity squared term.

questions.subject: TH06B
questions.text: Water hammer is defined as:

options.text: The sound produced when water flows through a pipe
Pressure fluctuations that develop when flow through a pipe is suddenly changed
The erosion of pipe material caused by high velocity water
The vibration of pipe hangers due to system operation

questions.explanation: Water hammer is the name given to pressure fluctuations (surges) that develop in a piping system when flow is suddenly changed, such as by valve closure.

questions.subject: TH06B
questions.text: In a single-phase water hammer event, the pressure wave is created when:

options.text: Water enters a pipe at high velocity
Moving water is suddenly decelerated by a flow restriction

questions.explanation: In single-phase water hammer, moving water is suddenly decelerated by a restriction (valve closure). The momentum (kinetic energy) converts to pressure-volume energy.

questions.subject: TH06B
questions.text: Two-phase water hammers are typically more severe than single-phase hammers because:

options.text: Higher velocities are involved when water slugs collide

questions.explanation: Two-phase water hammers are more severe due to the higher velocities involved when water slugs (entrained water accelerated by steam) collide with obstructions.

questions.subject: TH06B
questions.text: The Joukowsky equation describes water hammer pressure change as ΔP = ρ × c × Δv. The term 'c' in this equation represents:

options.text: The pressure drop across the restriction
The speed of sound in the fluid

questions.explanation: In the Joukowsky equation (ΔP = ρ × c × Δv), 'c' represents the pressure wave speed (speed of sound in the fluid), typically expressed in ft/sec.

questions.subject: TH06B
questions.text: According to the Joukowsky equation for water hammer pressure, peak pressure depends on:

options.text: The velocity change and fluid density

questions.explanation: Peak water hammer pressure (ΔP) is primarily dependent on velocity change (Δv) and fluid density (ρ), NOT on pipe length.

questions.subject: TH06B
questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a recommended method for preventing water hammer?

options.text: Ensure systems are water-solid before starting pumps
Initiate flow as slowly as possible
Rapidly close valves to stop flow immediately
Ensure steam traps are functioning to remove condensate

questions.explanation: Rapidly closing valves causes water hammer. Prevention methods include filling systems completely, initiating flow slowly, and closing valves slowly when required.

questions.subject: TH06B
questions.text: A 'keep fill' system is used primarily to:

options.text: Prevent void formation and water hammer from column rejoining

questions.explanation: Keep fill systems are low-volume pump systems designed to keep another system's piping full for correct system response time and to prevent water hammer.

questions.subject: TH06B
questions.text: When adding heat to a closed system, the pressure increases because:

options.text: The density of water changes with temperature increase

questions.explanation: As heat is added to a closed system, the density of water decreases, resulting in a pressure increase. Isolation of heat exchangers before cooling can cause rupture.

questions.subject: TH06B
questions.text: When heating a closed system, NPSH (Net Positive Suction Head) decreases because:

options.text: The system temperature approaches saturation temperature

questions.explanation: As heat is added, the system temperature gets closer to saturation. The lowest pressure is at pump suction, so when saturation is reached, cavitation occurs.

questions.subject: TH06B
questions.text: High point casing vents on centrifugal pumps should be opened before pump start to:

options.text: Remove non-condensable gases and prime the pump

questions.explanation: High point casing vents allow pump priming and removal of non-condensable gases that could be trapped in the case, preventing pump damage and water hammer.

questions.subject: TH06B
questions.text: When filling a closed system, high point vents should remain open until:

options.text: A solid stream of fluid comes out

questions.explanation: High point vents should remain open until a solid stream of fluid comes out, ensuring all air is removed and the system is properly filled.

questions.subject: TH06B
questions.text: Starting a pump in a system that has been drained is avoided mainly because:

options.text: It increases system pressure too much
It could damage the pump due to lack of cooling and lubrication

questions.explanation: Starting a pump in a drained system risks pump damage from cavitation and lack of cooling/lubrication. Pumps should be stopped and tagged before draining systems.

questions.subject: TH06B
questions.text: In the operating experience case OE22415 (Condensate Motor Bearing Failure), the bearing failure was caused by:

options.text: High viscosity oil due to cold bearing temperatures
Cavitation in the bearing cooling system

questions.explanation: At the starting temperature of 52°F, oil viscosity was approximately 700 SUS, causing excessive friction and bearing pad contact with shaft, resulting in bearing wipe.

questions.subject: TH06B
questions.text: The key lesson from operating experience case SER 16-96 (Reheater Drain Pipe Failure) was that:

options.text: Water hammer only causes minor damage
Water hammer could rupture large bore piping and cause personnel injury
Reheater systems never experience water hammer
Valve materials determine water hammer severity

questions.explanation: The September 1996 Oconee event resulted in an 18-inch pipe rupture and seven personnel injuries, demonstrating water hammer's potential for catastrophic failure.

questions.subject: TH07B
questions.text: What is the definition of heat transfer?

options.text: The transfer of energy that occurs as a result of a temperature difference
The movement of mass between systems
The conversion of work to heat only
The storage of thermal energy in a substance

questions.explanation: Heat transfer is the transfer of energy due to a temperature difference, from higher to lower temperature.

questions.subject: TH07B
questions.text: Which of the following is NOT one of the three basic modes of heat transfer?
questions.explanation: The three basic modes are conduction, convection, and radiation. Evaporation is a phase change process, not a mode of heat transfer.

questions.subject: TH07B
questions.text: What is specific heat capacity (cp)?

options.text: The heat required to raise the temperature of a unit mass of a substance by one degree
The total heat capacity of a system
The heat required to change phase without temperature change
The ratio of heat to work in a cycle

questions.explanation: Specific heat capacity cp is the heat required to raise the temperature of one unit mass by one degree Fahrenheit or Celsius.

questions.subject: TH07B
questions.text: In conduction heat transfer through a slab, what happens to the heat transfer rate if the material thickness (x) is doubled?
questions.explanation: From Equation 5: Q = kAΔT / x. Doubling thickness x halves the heat transfer rate.

questions.subject: TH07B
questions.text: Which material has the highest thermal conductivity from the typical values table?
questions.explanation: Copper has the highest thermal conductivity at 133.0 Btu/hr-ft-°F, making it an excellent conductor.

questions.subject: TH07B
questions.text: What is the overall heat transfer coefficient (Uo) in a heat exchanger?

options.text: The reciprocal of the total thermal resistance for all layers (tube wall and boundary layers)
The thermal conductivity of the tube material only
The convection coefficient of the hot fluid only
The sum of all individual heat transfer coefficients

questions.explanation: Uo is the overall coefficient accounting for conduction through the tube wall and convection in both boundary layers, as the reciprocal of total resistance.

questions.subject: TH07B
questions.text: How does fouling affect the overall heat transfer coefficient Uo?

options.text: It increases Uo by adding a conductive layer
It decreases Uo by adding an additional layer with its own thermal resistance
It has no effect on Uo
It only affects the fluid velocities

questions.explanation: Fouling adds an extra layer with its own U, increasing total resistance and thus decreasing the overall Uo, sometimes dramatically.

questions.subject: TH07B
questions.text: Why is radiation heat transfer not a workable mode in a nuclear power plant during normal operation?

options.text: It requires extremely high temperature differences to transfer significant heat
It cannot occur in the presence of water
It is too efficient and would overheat the core
It violates the First Law of Thermodynamics

questions.explanation: Radiation requires very large ΔT for meaningful heat transfer due to the T^4 dependence, making it impractical for normal operation.

questions.subject: TH07B
questions.text: What is core thermal power (CTP)?

options.text: The measure of heat input per unit time from the core to the reactor coolant system
The electrical power output of the generator
The total heat rejected in the condenser
The power consumed by the reactor coolant pumps

questions.explanation: CTP is the rate of heat transfer from the core into the RCS, calculated via heat balance.

questions.subject: TH07B
questions.text: Which equation is used for reactor coolant system heat balance to calculate CTP?
questions.explanation: For RCS heat balance with no phase change: Q = m × cp × ΔT, where ΔT is TH - TC.

questions.subject: TH07B
questions.text: In a secondary system heat balance, why is the change in enthalpy (Δh) used instead of cp × ΔT?

options.text: Because boiling occurs on the secondary side, requiring both sensible and latent heat accounting
Because cp is not constant for steam
Because there is no temperature change in the steam generator
Because feedwater flow is not measured

questions.explanation: Secondary side involves phase change (sensible + latent), so total enthalpy change Δh = hSteam - hFeedwater is used.

questions.subject: TH07B
questions.text: What two methods are commonly used to calculate core thermal power?

options.text: RCS heat balance using m × cp × ΔT and secondary heat balance using m × Δh
Direct neutron flux measurement and electrical output measurement
Condenser heat rejection and pump heat input
Steam flow and feedwater temperature only

questions.explanation: Two methods: RCS heat balance (Q = m cp ΔT) and secondary heat balance (Q = m Δh).

questions.subject: TH07B
questions.text: What is percent reactor power?

options.text: Actual core thermal power divided by rated core thermal power
Electrical output divided by thermal input
Steam flow divided by design steam flow

questions.explanation: Percent reactor power = CTP actual / CTP rated × 100%. It is what nuclear instrumentation indicates.

questions.subject: TH07B
questions.text: From the fuel centerline to the coolant, what is the approximate temperature drop across the helium-filled gap?
questions.explanation: Gap temperature drop ~200°F due to helium's relatively low thermal conductivity compared to solids.

questions.subject: TH07B
questions.text: What is the primary mode of heat transfer from the fuel pellet centerline to the outer edge of the pellet?
questions.explanation: Through the solid ceramic pellet, heat transfers by conduction, with a large ~1000°F drop due to low k of UO2.

questions.subject: TH07B
questions.text: What is the zirc-water reaction and at what temperature does it become self-sustaining?

options.text: Rapid oxidation of zirconium with steam producing heat and hydrogen; becomes self-sustaining at ~2200°F
A cooling process that prevents fuel melting
A corrosion reaction that starts at 5000°F
A phase change in the cladding material

questions.explanation: Zirc-water reaction begins ~1800°F and becomes self-sustaining ~2200°F, producing heat and hydrogen that can damage cladding.

questions.subject: TH07B
questions.text: What is the purpose of the overall heat transfer coefficient monitoring in heat exchangers?

options.text: To detect early degradation due to fouling or corrosion

questions.explanation: Monitoring Uo allows early detection of fouling or corrosion that reduces heat transfer capability.

questions.subject: TH07B
questions.text: In combined conduction and convection heat transfer in a heat exchanger, heat flows through which sequence of layers?

options.text: Convection from hot fluid to tube, conduction through tube wall, convection from tube to cold fluid
Convection from cold to hot fluid only

questions.explanation: Sequence: hot fluid convection → tube wall conduction → cold fluid convection.

questions.subject: TH07B
questions.text: What effect does nucleate boiling have on the film convection heat transfer coefficient hf?

options.text: It increases hf by creating turbulence that thins the boundary layer
It decreases hf by adding insulation
It has no effect on hf
It only affects radiation heat transfer

questions.explanation: Nucleate boiling creates bubble motion that thins the boundary layer and increases hf, improving heat transfer.

questions.subject: TH07B
questions.text: What is the primary reason forced convection is used in nuclear power plants instead of natural convection?

options.text: It is more efficient and easier to control the flow rate
Natural convection cannot occur in water

questions.explanation: Forced convection via pumps is more efficient and allows precise flow control for heat transfer management.

questions.subject: TH07B
questions.text: According to the example, what is the approximate temperature drop from fuel pellet centerline to outer edge?
questions.explanation: Large ~1000°F drop across the pellet due to low thermal conductivity of ceramic UO2.

questions.subject: TH07B
questions.text: What happens to cladding integrity if departure from nucleate boiling (DNB) begins?

options.text: Cladding surface temperature rises sharply, potentially initiating zirc-water reaction

questions.explanation: DNB causes sharp rise in cladding surface temperature, risking zirc-water reaction and cladding damage.

questions.subject: TH07B
questions.text: What is the function of a heat exchanger in a power plant?

options.text: To remove heat from or add heat to a working fluid without mixing the fluids
To increase the pressure of the working fluid

questions.explanation: Heat exchangers transfer heat between two fluids without mixing them, used for heating, cooling, or steam generation.

questions.subject: TH07B
questions.text: In the heat exchanger performance equation for single-phase fluids, Q = m × cp × ΔT, what does a negative Q indicate?

options.text: Heat is being lost by that fluid
Heat is being gained by that fluid

questions.explanation: Negative Q means heat loss from the fluid; positive means heat gain. The other fluid has the opposite sign.

questions.subject: TH07B
questions.text: What is one example of conduction and one example of convection in a nuclear power plant?

options.text: Conduction: heat transfer across heat exchanger tubes; Convection: heat transfer from fuel rod surface to coolant
Conduction: steam flow in pipes; Convection: through fuel pellet
Conduction only in condenser, convection only in core

questions.explanation: Conduction through solid tube walls; convection from rod surface into flowing coolant.

questions.subject: CP04
questions.text: What is the primary function of a pump?

options.text: To move fluids and overcome flow resistance

questions.explanation: The fundamental purpose of all pumps is to move a given volume flow rate of fluid at a specific pressure from one level to another, overcoming all flow resistance encountered between the fluid levels.

questions.subject: CP04
questions.text: Which type of pump is best for moving large volumes at relatively low pressure?
questions.explanation: Kinetic or dynamic pumps use rotating impellers to impart velocity to fluid and are best for moving large volumes at moderate to low pressures. Centrifugal pumps are the most common kinetic type.

questions.subject: CP04
questions.text: How does a positive displacement pump differ from a kinetic pump?

options.text: It traps fixed volumes and forces them through, not velocity-based
It uses rotating impellers to gain velocity
It operates only at low pressure

questions.explanation: Positive displacement pumps trap a fixed volume of fluid and force it into the discharge line. They work by volume displacement rather than velocity conversion, making them ideal for high-pressure or viscous fluid applications.

questions.subject: CP04
questions.text: What is pump capacity typically measured in?

options.text: Gallons per minute (gpm) or cubic feet per second (cfs)

questions.explanation: Pump capacities are normally expressed in gallons per minute (gpm) or cubic feet per second (cfs). The rated volumetric flow rate for a specific set of parameters is the pump's capacity.

questions.subject: CP04
questions.text: Static head is best described as:

options.text: The difference in fluid levels (elevation head)
The energy to set fluid in motion
The pressure drop due to friction

questions.explanation: Static head is a difference in fluid levels (elevation head), normally stated in feet of water column. It represents the pressure energy needed to lift fluid vertically against gravity.

questions.subject: CP04
questions.text: Dynamic head includes which of the following components?
questions.explanation: Dynamic head is the energy required to set the fluid in motion and overcome resistance, including velocity head (kinetic energy) and friction head (energy lost to friction in pipes and fittings).

questions.subject: CP04
questions.text: Total suction head becomes negative when:

options.text: The fluid source is below the pump centerline (suction lift)

questions.explanation: When the suction source fluid level is below the pump centerline, the pump must 'lift' the fluid, creating a negative suction head called 'suction lift'. This increases the demand on the pump and increases cavitation risk.

questions.subject: CP04
questions.text: Using the formula Hs = hs – hfs + ps, what does 'hfs' represent?

options.text: Pressure drop in suction line (dynamic head)

questions.explanation: In the total suction head equation, hfs represents the pressure drop in the suction line due to friction and velocity effects. This dynamic head component reduces available pressure at the pump suction.

questions.subject: CP04
questions.text: Total discharge head (Ht) does NOT include:

options.text: The static suction head of the source tank
Pressure in discharge tank if pressurized

questions.explanation: Total discharge head (Ht = ht + hft + pt) includes static discharge head, friction losses in discharge piping, and tank pressure. It does not include suction head, which is part of the total head calculation separately.

questions.subject: CP04
questions.text: If a pump has Ht = 40 ft and Hs = -5 ft, what is the total head (H)?
questions.explanation: Using the equation H = Ht – (+Hs): H = 40 – (+(-5)) = 40 + 5 = 45 feet. Total head is the pressure rise the pump must develop to move fluid through the system.

questions.subject: CP04
questions.text: Net Positive Suction Head (NPSH) is the difference between:

options.text: Absolute suction pressure and saturation (vapor) pressure

questions.explanation: NPSH = Psuction – Psat, where Psat is the saturation pressure (vapor pressure) of the fluid. NPSH determines whether cavitation will occur and is critical for safe pump operation.

questions.subject: CP04
questions.text: Cavitation occurs when:

options.text: Pump suction pressure drops to saturation pressure of the fluid
Flow rate increases above rated capacity

questions.explanation: Cavitation occurs when pump suction pressure approaches the saturation pressure of the fluid, causing vapor bubbles to form. These bubbles can cause severe damage to the pump impeller and reduce capacity.

questions.subject: CP04
questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a consequence of cavitation?

options.text: Pitting and erosion of the impeller
Flow oscillations and discharge pressure fluctuations

questions.explanation: Cavitation causes pitting and erosion, flow oscillations, excessive vibration, pump overheating, and reduced flow. It does not improve filtration; in fact, it can create more contamination from erosion debris.

questions.subject: CP04
questions.text: A pump that sounds like it is pumping rocks most likely indicates:
questions.explanation: Distinctive noise that sounds like pumping rocks is a primary indicator of cavitation. Other indicators include vibration, motor current fluctuations, and pressure/flow variations. This noise warrants immediate investigation.

questions.subject: CP04
questions.text: Which method does NOT prevent cavitation?

options.text: Increasing discharge pressure limit beyond design rating
Using a head tank to create static pressure

questions.explanation: Proper cavitation prevention methods include head tanks, booster pumps, large-diameter suction piping, temperature reduction, and proper system design. Increasing discharge pressure beyond design limits is dangerous and won't solve suction-side cavitation problems.

questions.subject: CP04
questions.text: What must be done to suction lines before pump startup to prevent cavitation?

options.text: Air must be vented and suction lines completely filled with fluid
Discharge valve must be fully open

questions.explanation: Vapor bubbles and free air are much more compressible than liquid, leading to flow instability and cavitation risk. All air must be vented from suction lines before startup and lines completely filled with fluid.

questions.subject: CP04
questions.text: The operating point of a pump occurs where:

options.text: The pump performance curve intersects the system resistance curve

questions.explanation: The pump's operating point occurs at the intersection of the pump performance curve (provided by manufacturer) and the system head curve (determined by system design). This is where actual pump performance meets system requirements.

questions.subject: CP04
questions.text: Pump efficiency typically decreases when:

options.text: Flow rate deviates significantly from design point

questions.explanation: Most pumps operate at peak efficiency in a specific range of flow rates and heads. Operating outside this design range wastes energy, accelerates wear, reduces efficiency significantly, and can lead to cavitation. Part-load operation is particularly inefficient.

questions.subject: CP04
questions.text: How does fluid temperature affect pump operation?

options.text: Higher temperature increases saturation pressure and decreases viscosity, affecting NPSH and flow resistance
Temperature has no effect on pump performance
Lower temperature always improves pump reliability
Temperature only affects motor, not pump performance

questions.explanation: As temperature increases, viscosity decreases (easier flow) but saturation pressure increases (higher cavitation risk). Temperature affects fluid properties, NPSH, and overall pump performance. Regular temperature monitoring is important.

questions.subject: CP04
questions.text: For safe and reliable pump operation, operators must:

options.text: Understand pump theory and recognize abnormal conditions early
Never check pump vibration or temperature
Run pumps continuously at maximum discharge pressure

questions.explanation: Operators trained in pump theory can diagnose problems early and take corrective action. Understanding pump operation, monitoring vibration, thermal performance, and fluid condition enables preventive maintenance and ensures reliable operation throughout the pump's service life.

questions.subject: CP06
questions.text: What is the primary purpose of a heat exchanger?

options.text: To measure temperature differences between fluids
To transfer heat from one fluid to another
To mix two different fluids together
To increase the pressure of fluids

questions.explanation: A heat exchanger is a device designed to transfer heat from one fluid to another. Heat transfer requires a temperature difference between substances.

questions.subject: CP06
questions.text: What is the key difference between direct contact and indirect contact heat exchangers?

options.text: Direct contact requires higher temperatures than indirect contact
In direct contact, fluids mix together; in indirect contact, fluids are separated by a solid surface
Indirect contact is less efficient than direct contact
Direct contact is used only for cooling towers

questions.explanation: Direct contact heat exchangers allow two fluids to contact each other directly. Indirect (surface) heat exchangers separate fluids with a solid surface such as tubes or metal plates.

questions.subject: CP06
questions.text: Which type of cooling tower uses fans to blow air into the tower?
questions.explanation: Forced draft cooling towers use fans to blow air into the tower, facilitating heat exchange between cooling water and air.

questions.subject: CP06
questions.text: What is the primary function of cooling tower fill material?

options.text: To increase the weight of the tower
To increase surface area for air-water contact and atomize water for efficient heat transfer
To reduce the noise from falling water

questions.explanation: Cooling tower fill material (traditionally redwood, now mostly PVC or plastic) increases surface area for air-water contact and helps atomize water for effective heat exchange.

questions.subject: CP06
questions.text: What describes the flow pattern in a main condenser?

options.text: Parallel flow with fluids moving in the same direction
Cross-flow with steam flowing downward perpendicular to cooling water tubes
Counter-flow with steam and water flowing in opposite directions
U-tube flow with steam circulating around the tubes

questions.explanation: Main condensers operate as classic cross-flow heat exchangers where exhaust steam flows downward perpendicular to tubes containing circulating cooling water.

questions.subject: CP06
questions.text: Why are parallel-flow heat exchangers rarely used in power plants?

options.text: They operate at too high a pressure
They require larger surface area than other types for the same heat load because temperature difference decreases as fluids travel through
They are more expensive than counter-flow exchangers
They cannot handle liquid-to-liquid heat transfer

questions.explanation: Parallel-flow exchangers are inefficient because as heat transfers, temperatures converge and the temperature difference (ΔT) becomes smaller, reducing heat transfer rate.

questions.subject: CP06
questions.text: What is the heat transfer rate equation used by heat exchanger designers?

options.text: Q = m × Cp × ΔT (mass times specific heat times temperature change)
Q = Uo × A × ΔT (heat transfer coefficient times surface area times temperature difference)
Q = P × V × T (pressure times volume times temperature)
Q = F × D × H (flow rate times diameter times head)

questions.explanation: The overall heat transfer rate is calculated as Q = Uo × A × ΔT, where Uo is the overall heat transfer coefficient, A is surface area, and ΔT is temperature difference.

questions.subject: CP06
questions.text: What is the main advantage of counter-flow heat exchangers compared to equally-sized parallel-flow exchangers?

options.text: They produce a higher rate of heat transfer because temperature difference is maintained throughout the exchanger
They are less expensive to construct

questions.explanation: Counter-flow heat exchangers maintain a higher temperature difference throughout because fluids flow in opposite directions, resulting in greater heat transfer for their size.

questions.subject: CP06
questions.text: What is a primary advantage of U-tube heat exchangers?

options.text: They allow for easier tube surface cleaning
Thermal expansion is simplified and they require only half as many tube-to-sheet joints as straight tube designs
They operate at higher pressures than straight tubes
They are cheaper to manufacture than other types

questions.explanation: U-tube heat exchangers simplify thermal expansion handling and reduce the number of tube-to-sheet joints needed compared to straight tube designs.

questions.subject: CP06
questions.text: What is a regenerative heat exchanger?

options.text: A heat exchanger that recycles the same fluid continuously
A heat exchanger that transfers heat from high temperature fluid to low temperature sections of the same system, minimizing energy loss
A heat exchanger that requires periodic regeneration or cleaning
A heat exchanger used only in secondary systems

questions.explanation: Regenerative heat exchangers transfer heat within the same system (e.g., feedwater heaters), minimizing energy loss since heat is not rejected to a separate system.

questions.subject: CP06
questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a major component of a shell and tube heat exchanger?
questions.explanation: Major components include shell, tube bundle, tubesheets, waterboxes, baffles, nozzles, vents and drains. A compressor pump is not part of the heat exchanger structure.

questions.subject: CP06
questions.text: How much does a typical 30-foot feedwater heater tube expand when heated from 70°F to 470°F?
questions.explanation: A typical 30-foot tube expands approximately 1.4 inches when heated from 70°F to 470°F. Floating head designs allow one tubesheet to slide to accommodate this expansion.

questions.subject: CP06
questions.text: What is the purpose of baffles in a shell and tube heat exchanger?

options.text: To increase the shell thickness for higher pressure rating
To direct flow over tubes and provide lateral tube support while maintaining overall counter-flow direction
To measure the temperature of the shell side fluid
To separate scale and fouling deposits from tubes

questions.explanation: Baffles direct shell-side fluid to cross tubes multiple times while maintaining counter-flow direction, improving heat transfer efficiency and supporting tubes.

questions.subject: CP06
questions.text: What is thermal shock in heat exchangers and why is it a concern?

options.text: Thermal shock is when a heat exchanger operates above its design temperature briefly
Thermal shock is sudden temperature changes that cause differential metal expansion/contraction, potentially causing brittle fracture if pressure is high
Thermal shock is the vibration that occurs during startup
Thermal shock is when tubes become corroded from thermal cycling

questions.explanation: Thermal shock occurs when temperature suddenly increases or decreases, causing differential expansion/contraction between tubes and shell. This can challenge structural integrity and cause brittle fracture under high pressure.

questions.subject: CP06
questions.text: What is the correct startup procedure to avoid thermal shock in a heat exchanger?

options.text: Introduce hot fluid first, then gradually add cold fluid
Introduce cold fluid first using throttled inlet valves, then gradually add hot fluid to prevent differential thermal expansion
Fill the exchanger rapidly with both fluids simultaneously
Operate at full flow rate from the beginning of startup

questions.explanation: Cold fluid is circulated first to minimize differential thermal expansion. Hot fluid is then introduced gradually through throttled inlet valves to prevent thermal shock.

questions.subject: CP06
questions.text: What is water hammer in heat exchangers and how is it minimized?

options.text: Water hammer is corrosion; minimized by using stainless steel tubes
Water hammer is a pressure spike from sudden flow velocity changes; minimized by slowly operating isolation valves
Water hammer is vibration from tube friction; minimized by reducing flow rate
Water hammer is sediment buildup; minimized by frequent flushing

questions.explanation: Water hammer occurs when fluid velocity suddenly changes. It is minimized by slowly operating inlet valves and opening drain connections to prevent trapped liquids from pressurizing.

questions.subject: CP06
questions.text: What operational factor causes excessive pressure drops and energy loss in heat exchangers?

options.text: Flow rates that are too low
Flow rates that are too high

questions.explanation: Flow rates that are too high create excessive pressure drops and energy loss. Flow rates that are too low result in inadequate heat transfer.

questions.subject: CP06
questions.text: What does scaling or tube fouling in heat exchangers reduce?

options.text: The heat transfer surface area available and the overall heat transfer coefficient

questions.explanation: Scaling and fouling deposits (mineral scale, corrosion products, biological growth) reduce effective heat transfer surface area and lower the overall heat transfer coefficient.

questions.subject: CP06
questions.text: What is the relationship between condenser vacuum and turbine backpressure?

options.text: Vacuum and backpressure are independent of each other
Higher vacuum reduces backpressure, creating greater pressure difference across turbine and improving turbine efficiency
Lower vacuum increases backpressure, improving plant efficiency
Vacuum has no effect on turbine output

questions.explanation: Higher condenser vacuum (lower absolute pressure) creates a greater pressure difference between turbine inlet and outlet, driving more work from steam and improving efficiency.

questions.subject: CP06
questions.text: Approximately how much cooling water is needed to condense one pound of steam in a condenser?
questions.explanation: Approximately 65 to 100 pounds or 8 to 12 gallons of cooling water is needed per pound of steam condensed. This large quantity is necessary to absorb the latent heat of condensation.

questions.subject: CP06
questions.text: What is the primary purpose of the air removal system in a condenser?

options.text: To prevent moisture from entering the condenser
To remove non-condensable gases (primarily air) that accumulate and reduce condenser vacuum
To measure the condenser pressure continuously
To cool the circulating water temperature

questions.explanation: Non-condensable gases (primarily air) cannot condense and accumulate in the condenser, increasing pressure and reducing vacuum. Air removal systems (jet air ejectors or vacuum pumps) continuously remove these gases.

questions.subject: CP06
questions.text: What indicators suggest that a condenser is experiencing performance degradation?

options.text: Increased flow rate through the condenser tubes
Reduced vacuum despite stable load, increased outlet water temperature, and fouling of tubes
Lower pressure readings on the secondary system

questions.explanation: Condenser degradation is indicated by: (1) Reduced vacuum despite stable load, (2) Increased outlet water temperature, (3) Fouling of tubes, (4) Air in-leakage.

questions.subject: CP06
questions.text: What is biofouling in cooling tower and condenser systems?

options.text: Corrosion of tube surfaces from acidic water
Growth of aquatic organisms in cooling water systems that reduces cooling effectiveness and increases backpressure
Accumulation of mineral deposits on tube surfaces
Thermal stress from rapid temperature changes

questions.explanation: Biofouling (SOER 84-1) occurs when aquatic organism growth degrades cooling tower and condenser performance. Control measures include chemical treatment and system monitoring.

questions.subject: CP06
questions.text: How does the heat transfer rate equation Q = Uo × A × ΔT help optimize heat exchanger performance?

options.text: It shows that only temperature difference matters for heat transfer
It shows that increasing the overall heat transfer coefficient, surface area, or temperature difference increases heat transfer rate
It proves that heat exchangers cannot be made more efficient
It is used only for condenser calculations, not other heat exchangers

questions.explanation: The equation Q = Uo × A × ΔT shows that heat transfer rate increases with larger heat transfer coefficient (U), increased surface area (A), or greater temperature difference (ΔT).

questions.subject: CP06
questions.text: What is the significance of logarithmic mean temperature difference (ΔTlm) in counter-flow heat exchanger design?

options.text: It indicates the average temperature of the fluids
It accounts for the changing temperature difference throughout the exchanger and is used to calculate overall heat transfer rate
It measures the maximum temperature the exchanger can tolerate
It has no practical application in modern heat exchangers

questions.explanation: In counter-flow heat exchangers, the logarithmic mean temperature difference (ΔTlm) is used because the temperature profile changes throughout the exchanger, requiring this mathematical correction for accurate heat transfer calculations.
